The Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs has amassed substantial size over recent years, representing an impressive compilation of research and offering a diverse range of opportunities for statistical exploration in the field of theorem proving. Despite the numerous contributions made so far, the ever-expanding nature of the archive still poses certain challenges: locating specific content has become increasingly difficult, and it can be challenging to keep pace with the latest material without devoting substantial time. In this research paper, we examine the potential of employing information retrieval techniques to enhance search functionality within the Isabelle Archive, given that query terms frequently revolve around concepts related to theorem statements, authors, and other contextual attributes. As a preliminary step, we conducted an in-depth examination of two significant Isabelle directories using a range of automatic and semi-automatic tools, including data mining approaches, sentiment analysis, named entity recognition, and manual coding. This investigation focused on two research questions: Firstly, we sought to assess the effectiveness of information retrieval methods in extracting valuable insights from the Isabelle Archive. To this end, we evaluated the performance of these methods across various directories and found that a support vector machine achieved an impressive 80% accuracy, surpassing the 60% attained by the best word retrieval method. Secondly, we aimed to determine the feasibility of categorizing the Isabelle Archive using topic models, with a particular emphasis on distinguishing between Isabelle directories based on their thematic attributes. Through the application of two competing models – LDA and structural topic modeling – we identified substantial similarities in the topics associated with MLSS data from consecutive years, but also observed a notable distinction between directories when utilizing the proposed STM approach, with a particular emphasis on the introduction of “meta-topics” to differentiate between Isabelle directories. Ultimately, we discuss the potential of further developing the Isabelle Archive by integrating the extracted information, and present a range of future research directions, including the application of supervised information extraction techniques to other repositories of formal proof data. In addition, we make available our research code through OpenSource, enabling the reproduction of our results and potentially serving as a foundation for similar explorations into other formal proof repositories, such as Coq or Lean. Finally, we provide a concise summary of this research in the form of a pre-print document.

Deep learning models' adaptability is a long-standing mystery. Recent studies have indicated that incorporating transfer learning enhances the performance of graph neural networks (GNNs). This work introduces a novel framework for understanding and quantifying adaptability in GNNs through the lens of node embeddings. Building on this concept, the study develops a metric to measure the shift in node embeddings resulting from new GNN model training after domain adaptation. This metric, along with others, such as accuracy and reconstruction error, provides insight into the effectiveness of transfer learning. Moreover, the framework provides instructions for determining the optimal pre-training period for specific target graphs. Employing this framework on both synthetic and real-world datasets (e.g., Cora and Citeseer), various experiments have been conducted to investigate the shift in node embeddings and evaluate the effectiveness of transfer learning. The results demonstrate that incorporating transfer learning significantly boosts GNNs' performance. Additionally, the framework accurately anticipates the optimal pre-training period for these GNNs. It is worth noting that the shift in node embeddings can be anticipated based on the overlap between the node embedding distributions of the source and target graphs. This overlap information is derived from the final layer's last dimension, which carries essential characteristics of node embedding. Consequently, training the subsequent layers on the target dataset may fail to replicate this shift. This phenomenon is responsible for the limited effectiveness of previous methods like DeepSet, MesoGCN, and GNNChem, as evidenced by their poor performance on datasets like Adience and NCI-1. On the other hand, the proposed metric has successfully captured the adaptability of DeepSet and MesoGCN on Adience and NCI-1 and GNNChem on NCI-1. Moreover, the study demonstrates the practical application of the understanding of transfer learning in the inductive setting for cheminformatics tasks. As an example, the study finds that incorporating transfer learning on the source dataset NCI-1 and then training on NCI-2 results in a performance boost of 2.3%. A similar approach also yields a 3.2% and 3.5% improvement on datasets NCI-1 and MACEUCI, respectively. Consequently, the study suggests training GNNs over a broader set of target datasets to enhance their adaptability. This paper presents a unified approach to addressing certain complex optimization challenges. Problems of control, estimation, and system design can be redefined as optimization problems subject to specific constraints. However, given the infinite dimensionality of these issues, it becomes necessary to employ numerical techniques to approximate a solution. We explore specific methods used in simultaneous direct approaches, specifically the transcription process. Our focus is on two widely used methods: collocation and Galerkin approaches. Collocation methods involve finding a solution that simultaneously satisfies multiple constraints, while Galerkin methods involve deriving a solution that meets multiple boundary conditions. Both methods have their advantages and disadvantages. Collocation methods often rely on rough polynomial bases, while Galerkin methods utilize smoother (but less representative) bases. Nevertheless, both approaches can achieve comparable results with appropriate selection of bases. We demonstrate the utility of this framework by applying it to a challenging optimization problem, specifically the minimal-time problem. This problem, which involves tracking a specific trajectory while accounting for time delays and constraints, proves difficult to solve analytically. As such, we employ numerical methods to approximate a solution when analytical solutions are not available. Ultimately, we demonstrate that using a discrete-time formulation can simplify the problem, but a continuous-time formulation is generally preferred. Using the discrete-time formulation, we identify several critical factors that must be considered to ensure an accurate approximation of the solution, specifically the choice of time points, basis elements, and weighting parameters. By leveraging the \texttt{PcOpt}\
toolbox, we provide a framework for implementing these methods and validating the resulting approximations. By utilizing the Levenberg-Marquardt algorithm, we ensure that the necessary conditions for optimality are met. Our numerical experiments reveal that using the discrete-time formulation allows us to achieve a stable time scaling while obtaining a minimal-time control law. This control law is applied to the capture maneuver in both the continuous-time and discrete-time formulations. When employing the discrete-time formulation, we derive a solution that minimizes the time required to execute the capture maneuver. However, this approach corresponds to an analytical formulation that yields an infinite time. As such, we identify a contradiction, demonstrating that using the discrete-time formulation can simplify the problem but also leads to pathological results. Conversely, this approach can provide valuable insights into the complexity of the problem when combined with analytical results. Ultimately, this research highlights the utility of the direct simultaneous approach in tackling complex optimization challenges when analytical solutions are not available. By leveraging this framework, we can approximate a solution when analytical solutions are not feasible

Rubin Observatory Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST), are projected to observe approximately 10 million time-varying celestial sources each night for a decade, sending real-time data streams to brokers for evaluation. Brokers will then utilize machine learning to filter these sources and select the most relevant for various scientific applications. Our investigation explores the merits and complexities of employing Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) in classifying transients for real-time community selection. BNNs, a type of neural network that incorporates uncertainty, have the advantage of providing reliable source predictions while maintaining privacy. Our study involved developing a BNN classifier and benchmarking its performance against a standard Neural Network on a dataset of 200,000 transients, including 50,000 classes of interest. The results indicate that BNNs offer comparable performance to Neural Networks on classification tasks, but also exhibit increased agreement in their uncertainty measurements. Notably, BNNs have the advantage of being invertible, allowing for the recovery of their input data. This property could potentially be used to ensure the privacy of source measurements, an essential consideration for future large-scale sky surveys. While full privacy preservation remains a challenging issue (particularly in instances where more information is desired from the data than can be safely retained), our results suggest that BNNs can significantly contribute to this effort. Recent observations from ALMA and Spitzer have uncovered a population of large, distant galaxies that are too faint to be seen in UV images captured by the Hubble Space Telescope. These galaxies have been referred to as HST-dark due to their elusive nature. Available data have revealed information on their age, metal content, and the presence of hot dust, but many aspects of their characteristics, such as spatial extent and star formation patterns, remain poorly understood. This study utilizes a detailed, multi-scale, and shroud-based analysis of data from optical, near-infrared, sub-millimeter, and mid-infrared wavelengths to investigate the properties of these galaxies, integrating data from different observations and images. The research also compares the morphology of star-forming regions within HST-dark galaxies with that of galaxies that are easily seen in UV images. These comparisons, along with other analyses, provide insights into the similarities and differences between HST-dark galaxies and more readily detected galaxies of similar masses. This study further explores the relationship between the amount of dust in galaxies and their overall mass, investigating whether galaxies that are easily seen in UV images have more or less dust than those that are not. Additionally, the research assesses whether galaxies that are easily seen in UV images are more or less efficient at creating stars than those that are not. These comparisons, while conducted at different scales, provide consistent results, contributing to a deeper understanding of the characteristics of galaxies across a wide range of masses. This study also suggests that galaxies that are easily seen in UV images are more efficient at creating stars, have more prominent regions of gas and dust, and are more massive, with masses above approximately 10 billion solar masses, than those that are not. These findings are consistent with observations from optical, near-infrared, sub-millimeter, and mid-infrared wavelengths. However, the research does not detect a significant difference in the star formation efficiency of galaxies of all masses when data from different wavelengths are examined. These findings suggest that, despite their elusive nature, the characteristics of galaxies that are easily seen in UV images can be understood through a detailed analysis of data from multiple and varied observations. These findings also highlight the importance of combining data from different wavelengths and scales to gain a deeper understanding of the properties of galaxies across a wide range of masses. Contrasting a two-dimensional model where disk centers lie on a plane, the inclusion of a third dimension alters the local disk arrangements and consequently the number of jammed patterns. Specifically, it has been discovered that the disk stack configuration also appears at higher packing densities when all disk centers reside on a plane. A scaling approach was used to determine the area of the jamming phase diagram that follows a power-law scaling of the channel height and packing density, resulting in the derivation of a numerical scaling law for the jamming threshold in terms of the aspect ratio of the channel. Furthermore, the jambed patterns exhibit similarities to column jammed patterns where disks are confined to separate channels. Specifically, it has been found that the number of column jammed patterns increases with the aspect ratio of the channel. Moreover, the current research cannot rule out whether the jambed patterns observed resemble those in two-dimensional disk packings or if they exhibit distinct patterns that arise from the inclusion of a third dimension. Finally, the impact of disk size variations on various jammed patterns has also been explored. While disk size variations tend to reduce the number of jammed patterns, the exact jammed patterns obtained when all disk sizes are identical cannot be recovered through simulations with varying small numbers of disks. This implies that the patterns observed when allowing size variations may resemble those obtained when all disk centers lie on a plane. Comprehensive listings of jammed patterns, the transitions between jammed patterns, and the area of the jamming phase diagram have been made available online. Additionally, the observed patterns suggest the possibility of developing algorithms that could aid in optimizing the filling of complex container geometries used in industrial processes. Moreover, the current research may serve as a starting point for investigating the packing properties of more intricate container geometries in future investigations. A preliminary examination of larger systems has also been conducted to confirm the applicability of the derived results. Lastly, the current work includes supplementary findings regarding the stability of active states, which are explored in detail. Research into El Ni\~no's two main flavors - East Pacific and Central Pacific types - has become a significant focus in climate variability studies. Recent investigations heavily rely on statistical techniques such as multivariate analysis, which often require continuous data and can be influenced by human biases, or independent component analysis, which may lack objectivity. Unlike these traditional methods, this research uses two cutting-edge techniques, teleconnection mapping and multivariate analysis, that are considered relatively unbiased and effective in identifying spatial correlations within large datasets. Our findings, which are based on 1980-2019 ERA5 reanalysis data and quantitatively verified, show distinct differences between the two types of El Ni\~no. We create a map illustrating the consistent geographical patterns of El Ni\~no's effects and quantify the linear relationships between the two. Our results also reveal significant changes in these patterns over time, which are particularly noticeable in the influence of Central Pacific El Ni\~no on the African Monsoon. Our research contributes to the ongoing debate about the differing impacts of East Pacific and Central Pacific El Ni\~no in various regions. We hope that our research will lead to a better understanding of the complex mix of linear climate responses and non-linear dynamic interactions that vary over time. We encourage the scientific community to build on our research in three key areas - investigating the causes of the changes in linear climate responses, expanding the scope of our findings to include other climate phenomena, and developing models of dynamic interactions. Our research is available in full on the Knowledge Hub at https://knowledgehub.ecmwf.cloud/displaydoco/Research%3A+Investigating+the+two+flavours+of+ENNO. The behavior of disordered materials under mechanical stress is often characterized by nonaffine deformation of their constituent particles, a phenomenon long acknowledged yet still not fully understood. A fundamental question regarding the nonaffine behavior has persisted: does it arise inherently from the existing structural constraints? To investigate this, we employed machine learning to analyze the nonaffine deformation of fibers subjected to uniaxial tension via discrete element simulations. Our research revealed that nonaffine deformation could be achieved within systems devoid of any restrictions, thereby shedding light on the underlying nature of this phenomenon. Moreover, the degree of nonaffine deformation was found to be modifiable through adjustment of energy penalties, which would be applicable to systems governed by affine constraints as well. Ultimately, the nonaffine deformation has both intrinsic and extrinsic origins, stemming from both inherent material properties and external boundary conditions. A refined theoretical framework has been proposed, taking into consideration the diverse influence of various system parameters on the nonaffine deformation and constraints present in the system. Through the application of machine learning, the nonaffine deformation has been effectively described through its association with specific discretely encoded structural patterns, which can be identified in the displaced particles immediately following mechanical loading. These patterns, or features, correlate with the local spatial arrangement of the particles and their nearest neighbors. Moreover, the importance of each pattern has been quantified through a kernel-based machine learning method, which utilizes a weighted sum of the patterns to predict the nonaffine deformation. The predicted nonaffine deformation has been found to be in agreement with experimental measurements, thereby validating the developed approach. The method has been found suitable for use with experimental data, which contains discrepancies and gaps due to technical limitations. In addition to existing factors like natural death and predation, we incorporate predation influenced by age and pollution-induced effects, where adults can mitigate pollution's detrimental impact, thereby reducing the growth rate of pollutants, thus showing a beneficial relationship between adult population and environmental pollution levels. Hierarchical taxonomies have immense value in numerous applications, but their applicability is restricted by the costly and time-consuming process of manual maintenance. Current research has sought to automatically enhance taxonomies by learning concepts from structured data, but the results are hampered by limitations of Euclidean space in representing hierarchical relationships. This has led to inaccurate child concept predictions due to the neglect of overlapping relationships between concepts. To overcome these limitations, we propose representing taxonomies in hyperbolic space, which better captures hierarchical nuances and facilitates the preservation of overlapping relationships. We introduce a novel prediction model that leverages this representation to accurately forecast parent-child relationships within taxonomy structures. To further improve performance, we integrate an attention mechanism, which considers the relevance of ancestor nodes in relation to target concepts, in addition to incorporating self-attention for enhanced attention weighting. We validate the effectiveness of our approach through experiments conducted on two large, extensively used taxonomies. These experiments demonstrate that our proposed method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving improvements of 4% or more in precision. The results suggest that representing taxonomies in hyperbolic space is beneficial for maintaining hierarchical context while facilitating accurate concept prediction. Additionally, incorporating attention mechanisms can further augment performance by focusing predictions on relevant concept aspects. Although related work has explored hyperbolic taxonomy representation, it primarily concentrates on learning concept hierarchies. In contrast, our proposed framework uniquely integrates hyperbolic space with the contexts of concept embeddings and attention mechanisms to facilitate accurate prediction of parent-child relationships within taxonomy structures. This novel framework is validated through experiments on two large, extensively used taxonomies, showing that it significantly surpasses state-of-the-art baselines, achieving improvements of 4% or more in precision. The code for our proposed method has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/hi-gh/hyperbolic-concept-learn. Furthermore, we have donated our developed code to the open-source knowledge graph embedding framework, SPaRQL, with contributions made to the repository at https://github.com/linkeddatakg/SPaRQL. As one of the first implementations of hyperbolic graph embedding learning in the field, this contribution is intended to facilitate the adoption of this innovative technique in the industry. With the donation of the hyperbolic extension to SPaRQL, the repository is now referred to as SPaRQL-H. The updated repository can be accessed at https://github.com/hi-gh/SPaRQL-H. The fourth Industrial Revolution has significantly improved industrial productivity and efficiency, incorporating data analytics and cyber-physical systems for enhanced planning and scheduling. Nonetheless, uncertainties inherent in environmental factors and operator subjectivity often go unaccounted for in decision-making, causing shipment delays and inaccuracies in budget projections. This widespread issue demands correction, and power analytics offers an effective solution, offering an interpretable and computationally efficient approach for creating predictive models. By integrating power analytics with industrial scheduling, companies can develop actionable models addressing their key concerns, such as shipment delays and product quality issues. This study provides a comprehensive review of power analytics and related concepts, exemplifying its applications in multiple industries and presenting a novel framework for creating power models tailored to scheduling needs. The proposed framework addresses existing limitations, enabling model scalability and flexibility in performance forecasting with minimal dependency on data volume. Furthermore, a case study illustrating the application of power analytics in forecasting lead times and product quality has been conducted using actual data from a Mexican company. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of power analytics in producing valuable insights, addressing complex problems, and influencing business decisions. The approach enables companies to choose from various models, depending on their specific needs and data availability. The method allows users to establish a minimal set of critical features and targets, making the solution easily adoptable by companies. The framework's versatility is showcased through its application in diverse industries and scenarios, such as manufacturing and service-based businesses, highlighting its scalability and adaptability. Finally, future research directions and potential applications of power analytics in other business domains are explored. These directions include the development of an automated toolset for power model creation, the integration of power analytics with social media data, the application of deep learning in power analytics, the extension of power analytics to non-numerical fields, and the investigation of causal relationships between features and targets. The results of this research provide valuable insights for practitioners and scholars, addressing questions such as: Can companies improve forecasting accuracy and model complexity simultaneously? Can the feature extraction process be automated for better results? Can the analysis yield meaningful results even with limited data? Can the method be scaled up to diverse industries and scenarios? Can the method address complex issues such as low product quality and shipping delays? Can the method be used to identify critical features and targets in different domains? Can the method be used to make strategic decisions through data analysis? The answers to these questions are affirmative, indicating the feasibility and effectiveness of power analytics in scheduling and other scheduling-related tasks. Cyber-Physical Systems require robust resilience properties to withstand disruptions, yet a standardized approach remains lacking. We introduce a novel framework for evaluating system resiliency based on a specific logical structure called a Resiliency Specification, which is comprised of STL formulas. By integrating time bounds and individual performance metrics, the Resiliency Evaluation Framework provides an in-depth analysis of a system's ability to recover and maintain stability following an adverse event. Additionally, the framework calculates the expected resiliency time and caps the likelihood of non-recovery. We provide theoretical proof of our approach and demonstrate its applicability through a case study. The framework, along with its resources, can be accessed online. (Figure updated in January 2021)

One of the most pressing enigmas in modern physics is the existence of dark matter. Although it's confirmed that dark matter gravitationally affects luminous matter, this interaction makes accelerometer-based searches particularly intriguing. This article details ongoing and future searches for dark matter particles such as feebly interacting matter trapped on Earth, scalar domain walls, and scalar halos, all of which are susceptible to being detected by accelerometers due to their weak interaction with gravity. Furthermore, we propose the 'Gravity And Accelerometer Sensors Together' (GAST) concept, integrating accelerometers with gravitational sensors for enhanced sensitivity. Several viable configurations, such as utilizing feebly interacting matter trapped on Earth, where a single kilogram device has the potential to detect signals from domain walls originating from masses of at least $10^{16}$ grams, or the scalable GAST gravitational sensor, capable of setting limits on short-range gravitational forces with distances below $10^{-2}$ meters, and detecting frequencies in the 100 kHz to 100 MHz range, are discussed. Finally, we outline future opportunities and potential collaborations, such as the DAPHNE II storage ring, the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), and the International Linear Collider (ILC), which could supply large numbers of narrow uncharged mesons for searches for vanishing feebly interacting matter.

Radio sources powered by an Active Galactic Nucleus have significant magnetic fields influencing their polarization properties, affecting observations of plasma and contaminating cosmic microwave background measurements. Understanding the polarization-statistics relationship with source characteristics is essential. By analyzing large radio source samples from 1.4 GHz surveys, this study calculates the median fractional polarization in relation to angular size. It finds a strong correlation between polarization and source size below ~5", with a weaker correlation above ~8". The results indicate depolarization due to the host galaxy and surrounding environment up to ~5 kpc. Additionally, the curvature of magnetic fields in radio sources appears to be a key factor in polarization statistics. The findings also suggest that depolarization curves may be used to determine the magnetic field strength and radius. However, a relationship between depolarization and magnetic field radius was not found. Furthermore, the study sets new lower bounds on the magnetic field strength for sources with small angular sizes. The study's predictions are consistent with earlier research on large radio sources, suggesting a significant impact of cosmic magnetic fields on polarization statistics. The study's methodology provides a reliable framework for estimating polarization statistics from future radio source surveys. Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) are a type of mathematical model based on Markov processes, but with the critical difference of having an inaccessible set of states, known as hidden states. Markov chains that operate under the principles of HMMs can only transition between accessible states, making the hidden state set a form of non-accessible information. HMMs are often represented through a graphical layout consisting of arrows indicating state transitions along with associated probability values. Additional information is provided through observation probabilities, which make predictions about what is being observed in a system, but also take into account the current accessible state. HMMs, along with related variants, known as Bayesian Networks, are fundamental models used in machine learning and probabilistic inference. They are applied across multiple fields including speech recognition, natural language processing, and computer vision. HMM-based processes can be represented mathematically by combining Markov processes with a complete separable Banach space for observation notes. However, a practical challenge arises when attempting to establish the existence of accessible states. This issue becomes particularly prominent when attempting to create compact Hausdorff topologies from transition- invariant metrics. This work addresses the existence of accessible states for HMM-based processes by providing compact topology definitions for the state space and demonstrating the existence of accessible states under specific conditions. Additionally, this research offers implications for HMM-based processes and extends existing topologies from transition- invariant metrics to observation note spaces, while also exploring the topological implications for HMM-based processes. It, however, remains unclear whether the topological definitions proposed in this research are applicable to a wide range of HMM-based processes. This work specifically investigates the existence of compact topology definitions for the dual HMM-based processes under the assumption of a finite number of accessible states. We develop a class of stochastic advection problems to investigate turbulent transport properties, where the flow field statistics are represented as continuous complex Gaussian fields. This representation accurately captures turbulence's essential feature of rapid change, passivity, and nonlocal effects, as well as the phenomenon of intermittency. By solving these problems using Monte Carlo methods, we demonstrate that the asymptotic behavior of the solutions can be described through Fractal Fourier law, a PDE involving both Fourier and fractional derivatives. A special case of this problem, in one spatial dimension, is analytically solvable, and we derive the exact solution using semi-spectral methods. Through numerical examples, we verify that the Fourier law is well-approximated both statistically and asymptotically. Furthermore, we show that the speed of the advection can be significantly decreased by increasing the intensity of turbulence, and discuss the implications for scaling properties of the diffusion coefficient. A generalization of the problem to any dimension reveals that higher dimensions lead to a decaying exponential factor in the diffusion coefficient, rather than the stretched exponential factor observed in one dimension. A preliminary investigation into the Monte Carlo method's convergence properties is also conducted. Overall, our findings indicate that the stochastic advection problems provide a suitable framework for understanding turbulent transport properties, and the resulting solutions can be used to inform the development of a closure model for turbulent diffusion. By combining the closure model with the averaged equations of the problems, we achieve a measure of self-consistency, as shown in one dimension. A possible extension of the framework to understand the scattering of particles in turbulent flows is also contemplated. Ultimately, our work lays a theoretical foundation for a general, first-principles-based model of turbulent transport across various fields of study. With sufficient computational power, the model can provide novel insights and descriptions that are currently inaccessible. As an example of this, we show that the model reveals a previously unknown factor of $\sqrt{2\pi}$ in the diffusion coefficient, leading to a factor of 2 that was missing in earlier studies. A related extension of the model to understand the thermodynamic effects of turbulence, an area of study previously unexplored with similar methods, is also considered. By employing stochastic advection problems and developing first-principles-based closure models, we achieve a deeper understanding and clearer description of the underlying physical laws governing turbulent transport properties and their asymptotic behavior. By averaging these models, we identify key properties and parameters that are indicative of turbulence, and our work provides a more nuanced perspective on the origins and consequences of these phenomena.

Protecting users of location-based services with significant privacy requirements is extremely difficult when multiple locations are shared within a short time frame due to the significant relationships anticipated between those locations. Our proposed R\'enyi divergence based framework measures and bounds expected privacy losses for interrelated data sets, further demonstrated through an algorithm incorporating conditional Gaussian process priors. This framework is utilized in a practical method for preserving the privacy of aggregate statistics of user location over a period, involving transforming a user's location history into a distorted record that incorporates noise, such that the distorted record appears to originate from an artificially constructed database with a specified amount of desired privacy. The proposed method is quantitatively evaluated in terms of both the expected privacy level and the added noise necessary for achieving that privacy level, utilizing R\'enyi divergence as the privacy metric. This approach is additionally assessed through a concept of universal privacy applicable to any privacy mechanism and independent of the database distribution. The proposed privacy-preserving scheme and its performance evaluation contribute knowledge in the following ways: (1) they identify a meaningful upper limit on the expected privacy loss associated with a given privacy mechanism, (2) apply a R\'enyi divergence based framework to a real-world problem, and (3) analyze a realistic user location data scenario, unlike prior research which primarily targets private release of single locations or sparse locations. Furthermore, the proposed framework offers a meaningful evaluation of the expected privacy loss for interrelated data sets, unlike prior research which primarily focuses on upper limits of privacy loss for discrete data sets or scenarios with low entropy. Moreover, the framework provides a meaningful evaluation of the expected privacy loss for continuous data sets, unlike prior research which focuses on approximating a R\'enyi divergence based metric for discrete data sets. Experimental results show that maintaining a meaningful upper limit on the expected privacy loss does not significantly compromise location utility, while employing a practical method achieving a bounded expected privacy loss may result in a slight sacrifice of location utility. The proposed framework and its resources are made available at https://github.com/kuo-hsun-tseng/infusion. This research is further supported by the grant DMS-1615468 from the National Science Foundation.

In this context, we examine a privacy issue related to federated learning that divides data between participants. There are two primary forms of vertical federated learning and horizontal federated learning which have diverse applications and differ in their ability to release data. Firstly, vertical federated learning involves releasing attribute information from participants, while revealing user information is prevented. Secondly, horizontal federated learning involves combining data across participants, generated from the same study, with participant identities remaining confidential. This problem is framed as a minimax game where participants aim to maximize utility while minimizing reliance on unreliable participants, and the server seeks to minimize training loss by selecting reliable participants. This problem is solved using an algorithm that alternates between utility maximization and loss minimization at each participant and server step. Experiments demonstrate that compared to other methods, this approach trains faster and reaches a better loss position. Results indicate an inverted shape in the microwave conductivity spectrum as it varies with energy, displaying a peak in the conductivity at intermediate temperatures, which declines with further increases in temperature. Notably, the microwave conductivity exhibits a reversal compared to the optimal doping regime, peaking at under and over doped states and plummeting around optimal doping, instead. One of the most efficient distributed training algorithms for machine learning is stochastic gradient descent (SGD). However, the process involves constant communication of large data transfer, consuming a substantial amount of bandwidth and potentially slowing down training speed. We've developed a novel technique called Communication-Avoiding SGD (CA-SGD) that minimizes the need for communication. This technique takes advantage of data parallel training, where a parameter server sends optimized communication by combining gradients in bulk, while also using techniques such as gradient compression and parameter quantization to further reduce the bandwidth required. Additionally, the technique allows for asynchronous communication, which can lead to significant performance gains on systems with high variability in communication latency. Our experimental results demonstrate that CA-SGD can reduce the total communication complexity by multiple orders of magnitude across different deep learning applications, such as training ResNet-50 and Transformer-Large, compared to traditional SGD. Furthermore, the technique leads to a performance speedup of 2.3 to 6.2 times on Kubeflow systems with high communication variability. The code for our technique is openly available. The widespread dissemination of misinformation through the internet and social media significantly impacts public perception and user behavior, with generative models now making it easier to create fake content. Such deep learning-based content creation techniques are producing highly realistic outcomes. Despite the simple goal of consuming a short article to determine its origin, users find it difficult to identify fabricated information, including artificially generated headlines. This paper focuses on developing effective methods to both create and detect origin-locked text, specifically headlines and conversations. Our investigation into the topic involves exploring the differences between detecting the origin of a article with detecting the origin of a headline, due to conversations being a longer form of generated content. Two datasets were developed for this research, one containing origin-locked article headlines and another containing origin-locked conversations. Our dataset includes both a large amount of natural misinformation and a smaller amount of misinformation that was generated by a computer. We also developed and tested several methods for identifying misinformation, including machine learning and computer-generated clues, and found that using a combination of clues significantly improves the accuracy of detecting misinformation. Interestingly, we found that using a combination of clues is especially effective at identifying misinformation when the origin of a article is known. This research highlights the importance of origin-locked article identification, specifically when it comes to computer-generated content. Our findings suggest that using a combination of clues is a strong approach for identifying misinformation, regardless of whether the origin of a article is known. This research has the potential to impact various fields, such as public policy and fact-checking, in various ways. Our dataset and code are publicly available, allowing for future research to be conducted on detecting misinformation. This research was supported by National Science Foundation Award CNS-1940352. A groundbreaking method using Bayesian neural networks enhances the accuracy of classifying gamma-ray sources. The study focuses on identifying Fermi-LAT blazar candidates, consisting of BL Lacertae objects and Flat Spectrum Radio Quasars, from a large group of candidates. In contrast to traditional classifier assessments, this method produces classification confidence, crucial for analyzing noisy or imbalanced datasets. The Bayesian neural network model was trained utilizing both internal and external training sets, resulting in robust performance even with external data. The model was compared to a conventional neural network classifier, producing more reliable outcomes when provided with external information. The model was then applied to a set of noisy BL Lacertae data, generating a probability distribution to classify this data. Following a thorough assessment, the model demonstrated high efficacy in classifying gamma-ray sources, achieving a precision of 82% and a recall of 83%, with an ionization coefficient of 0.95. Notably, the model's predictions were largely independent of the volume of the considered sources, indicating its reliability in assigning classes to Fermi-LAT blazar candidates. The model's code is available online for replication and further research purposes. 

Note: This research was facilitated by the computational resources provided by DC2 at the French National Center for Scientific Research (CNRS). 

In Addition, the paper's findings include the following points:
- A strong correlation exists between the model's output and the luminosity of gamma-rays for BL Lacertae objects.
- There is a notable gap in the model's performance for objects with low luminosity.
- A similar correlation exists for FSRQs, but it is less pronounced than for BL Lacertae objects.
- The model's predictions are less confident for FSRQs, indicating a greater uncertainty in their classification. 
- A comparison with existing blazar classification models revealed notable differences in their outcomes. 

Ultimately, the model's outcomes demonstrate that Bayesian neural networks are a powerful tool for classifying gamma-ray sources, offering a more accurate assessment of blazar candidates compared to traditional methods. The model's predictions are available online for replication, and it is recommended to consult the provided link for access to the model's results. Active participation and user engagement are crucial components of social networking, 
fueled in large part by user-generated content that comes in various forms like 
images, videos, and GIFs. However, this content remains inaccessible to many users, 
despite available solutions that aim to reduce this form of exclusion. Our research 
involved surveying 258 social media users and interviewing 20 participants, with 7 of 
them having visual impairments, to understand their perceptions of online content 
and how support tools are utilized. Our analysis of the results reveals that 
platforms' efforts are inadequate, and that mainstream users often aren't aware 
of accessible practices. By exploring the views of end-users on accessible 
practices, barriers they face, and motivating factors, we also suggest further 
approaches to boost user engagement and raise awareness about accessibility. 
Ultimately, this research aims to influence platform policies and practices to 
make online interactions more inclusive. The associated GitHub repository contains

Specifically, we can interpret the tensor join as an equivalent representation of the hypergraph intersection operation, and demonstrate that the tensor intersection operation corresponds to the hypergraph contraction operation. Furthermore, we can express the hypergraph M\"{o}bius function in terms of the tensor intersection operation, and derive a formula for calculating the hypergraph M\"{o}bius function through the tensor join operation. Moreover, we can generalize the tensor Laplacian matrix based on the tensor join operation, and prove its equivalence to the hypergraph Laplacian matrix under certain conditions. Ultimately, we can extend our findings from hypergraphs to halfgraphs and circumsgraphs. Our results provide a valuable mathematical formulation for calculating hypergraph invariants and analyzing the properties of the tensor Laplacian matrix, which has the potential to lead to new algorithms for hypergraphs. Finally, we can generalize our operations to other types of tensor networks. In clinical trials for Alzheimer's and progressive diseases tracked with continuous data over time, the mixed model repeated measures approach often dominates. However, treating time as a categorical variable can introduce complications, particularly when appointments are missed or rescheduled due to events like the COVID-19 pandemic, which risks inducing bias. To address this limitation, a novel method employing natural cubic splines is presented to model time as a continuous variable and utilize treatment effect variations over time. The proposed method surpasses established models such as mixed model repeated measures and those relying on proportional treatment effects in real-world and simulation studies. Furthermore, this method has been successfully implemented in R and R-shiny code, demonstrating its practicality in real-world data analysis. The code includes a global optimal model fitting process using the "optim" function and interactive dashboard allowing users to specify individual subject weights, which is then made available online. Additionally, this research involves an in-depth exploration of patient weight influences on treatment variation across time. Moreover, an adaptive Bayesian model employing the "distracted Bayesian" approach from Gilks et al. (1995) is also presented, which can offer more efficient Bayesian alternatives to the implemented frequentist model. The adaptive Bayesian approach successfully addresses common issues, such as the need for informative priors or the requirement of prior distributions for model parameters. The model employs a non-informative prior for the treatment effect over time and relies on local information from surrounding data points. Importantly, this approach achieves frequency properties equivalent to the established model. Furthermore, an illustrative case study employing real-world data is employed to show the effectiveness of the adaptive Bayesian model in prior-free analysis, which can offer more frequentist performance benefits. The implemented adaptive Bayesian model also addresses additional challenges, such as the existence of outliers and rare missing data due to events like the COVID-19 pandemic, which can further enhance its practicality in real-world scenarios. In the adaptive Bayesian model, the treatment effect over time is modeled as a linear regression equation, which can offer more flexibility and allow for the incorporation of additional covariates. Furthermore, an adaptive prior for the outlier parameter has also been employed, which can offer more local information. The model's performance in the presence of outliers is then demonstrated through real-world data. Finally, the adaptive Bayesian model also employs a unique approach to address the rare missing data problem by modeling the probability of missing observations using a multivariate logistic regression model. The model incorporates the predictive distribution for the missing data and employs an adaptive prior for the probability of missing data over time.

In massive machine-type communications (mMTC), granting numerous users low-latency connections is made possible by non-orthogonal grant-free access with low signaling overhead. This research proposes a novel two-stage approach using a genetic algorithm (GA) to generate user-specific sequences for low-latency grant-free uplink access. First, the initial GA finds a subsampling strategy to transform a unitary matrix into a closely-packed, uniform pattern. Subsequently, a second-stage GA is employed to conceal "distortion-inducing" data within the matrix, ensuring even power distribution for multi-carrier transmissions. These modified sequences are proposed for mMTC uplink grant-free access, where simulation results showcase superior performance for joint grant-free uplink channel estimation and data transmission, surpassing traditional sequences like Zadoff-Chu and Frank-Zadoff in various error-rate benchmarks for moderate to high active user ratios. This genetic-algorithm-based method also offers advantages in terms of low signaling overhead and simplified process complexity compared to other recent approaches. Ultimately, the proposed sequences demonstrate high success rates under practical, time-varying environmental conditions. Furthermore, the modified sequences are compatible with current standardization efforts for uplink grant-free access access, such as those in the 5G-NURRC. These sequences can be made open-source upon request. Additionally, the genetic-algorithm code used for this research can also be made available for public viewing. These objects include $\mathbb{F}_1^\pm$-algebras that incorporate elements with superscripts, which can be thought of as generalised adic exponents. Research on spoken dialogue has typically relied on a shortlist of the top ASR hypotheses for decoding.  Recent studies, however, have shown that incorporating multiple ASR possibilities can improve accuracy.  Confusion networks, which combine multiple ASR paths, offer such an option but have been underutilized due to difficulties in training and implementation.  This paper explores alternatives to confusion networks, specifically dynamic confusion graphs and flows, which can be more easily trained and incorporated into a decoder.  We also propose an efficient method for generating these alternatives to ASR hypothesis lists, and demonstrate their potential for reducing word error rates, particularly in cases where language understanding is complex.  An added benefit is that this information can be shared across dialogue turns, reducing the need for repeated network requests.  We also investigate the potential for incorporating this information in a decoder and explore the trade-offs between accuracy, complexity, and latency.  Specifically, using the dynamic flow representation and incorporating it into the decoder yields a 1.9% relative reduction in WER over the top ASR hypothesis alone, at a cost of 33% increase in decoding time.  This improvement is at the expense of a 2.1% increase in speech recognition complexity.  We also observe that incorporating this information early in the recognition process yields better results than incorporating it later.  Ultimately, this work lays the groundwork for future research into the use of confusion information in spoken dialogue systems.  We also offer a basic implementation of the information and decoder modifications, which is available online at https://github.com/nlphub/flow-decoder.  This implementation is based on the NLPHUB software suite and utilizes the Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence's AllenNLP framework.  Specifically, the project draws on the use of WFSTs, WFSTM, and the use of the Moses decoder, all of which are incorporated into the NLPHUB library.  This implementation is further documented in the accompanying README file.  We hope this work and the accompanying code will serve as a foundation for future research into the incorporation of confusion information in spoken dialogue systems.  We also hope that the use of the NLPHUB library and interactions with the code will provide valuable hands-on experience with spoken dialogue systems.  Finally, while the use of confusion information is generally applicable to language understanding, we specifically explore its use in task-oriented dialogue systems in this study. As social media increasingly influences public perceptions globally, researchers have focused on tackling the pervasive issue of hate speech online. This pernicious problem gives rise to real-world consequences, such as heightened social divisions and violent crimes. Previous studies have employed automated hate speech detection methods, but they often fall short by overlooking broader social and contextual nuances. Furthermore, few approaches demonstrate explainability and are prone to system bias. We introduce the first known hate speech dataset, AGHared, which is an extraordinary and extensive collection of hate speech samples, along with associated contextual information. This data was generated by scraping online discussions from various Hebrew-language forums over a period of time. We then develop a contextual hate speech model, which incorporates the intricate interplay of social context and hate speech, to enhance hate speech detection accuracy. We also create a summary representation of this context, aiding researchers in addressing critical issues like system bias and explainability. Our proposed model achieves a remarkable 88.2% Mackey-precision in detecting hate context on AGHared. Furthermore, our analysis of contextual information reveals significant correlations between hate context and hate labels, while contextual error rates are significantly lower than those of hate speech classification alone. These results illustrate the importance of considering broader social context in hate speech detection. We believe that the AGHared dataset and our proposed model will have a profound impact on researchers and practitioners, empowering them to tackle the complex issue of hate speech more effectively. We explore the behavior of large networks of theta neurons, deriving degree-based mean field equations that capture the overall dynamics of these networks. By assuming random connections, we analyze the effects of varying in- and out-degree distribution widths on synaptically and gap junction coupled networks. Our findings reveal that the out-degree distribution has no impact on synaptically coupled network dynamics. Broadening the in-degree distribution of inhibitory networks eliminates oscillations and narrows the bistability range in excitatory networks. Conversely, in gap junction coupled networks, in-degree distribution variations shift the onset points for collective oscillations. Many of these results persist in networks of more biologically accurate neurons. Additionally, we observe delayed responses and oscillation delays in out-degree distributed networks, and derive conditions for delayed responses in synaptically coupled theta networks. These studies confirm our previous findings on neuron pair interactions and extend them to large networks. They also demonstrate that mean field equations provide an accurate representation of large networks. By analyzing the properties of these channel capacity regions, we derive explicit formulas that express the boundaries of their achievable rates in terms of the spectral features of the input signals. Conversely, we also develop methods to compute channel capacity when only the spectral characteristics of the input signals and noise are known, without requiring knowledge of the channel's transfer function. Furthermore, we present a practical approach to estimating the capacity of Gaussian interference channels when the signal distributions are unknown, by leveraging the spectral properties of the channel and optimal rate allocations. The efficacy of this method is validated through simulations that compare its performance with that of other approaches based on non-linear precoding and multi-user techniques. In Brazil, the situation is particularly dire, with the country ranking second in the world's homicide death tolls among those under the age of 20.  Despite the widespread nature of this issue, the complex interplay of factors driving it is still poorly understood.  In addressing this knowledge gap, our research draws upon a comprehensive review of the literature, combining quantitative analyses of data to identify associated factors with qualitative examinations of case studies to explore underlying mechanisms.  Our findings indicate that certain factors, such as being young, male, and of lower socioeconomic status, significantly increase an individual's likelihood of becoming a homicide victim.  Our case-study results, which were based on over 70 in-depth interviews with key stakeholders, revealed that these demographic characteristics frequently intersect with factors like family dynamics, education levels, and access to firearms to give rise to a multifaceted profile of high-risk individuals.  In particular, factors unique to each demographic group contribute to their elevated homicide risk, such as a tendency towards violent conflict among young men and a lack of social connections among those from lower socioeconomic backgrounds.  Furthermore, our research found that certain 'tipping points' exist that can trigger violent outcomes among individuals, such as exposure to guns or the influence of criminal leaders.  Our results also highlight the importance of individual characteristics, like mental health or substance abuse issues, in shaping an individual's likelihood of becoming a homicide victim.  Ultimately, our findings emphasize the critical nature of incorporating both quantitative and qualitative approaches in order to develop a more nuanced understanding of this complex issue.  In practice, this means that policy makers must be able to adapt their strategies in response to emerging trends and patterns in homicide data in order to effectively address this problem.  Our research provides a number of policy recommendations, including the creation of community-based programmes aimed at providing support to at-risk individuals and the implementation of targeted initiatives to reduce gun violence.  In Brazil, this could involve building on existing programmes like the 'Cadeira de Bicicleta', which provides support to young people at risk of dropping out of school, by expanding this model to other demographics and environments.  Similarly, programmes aimed at identifying and removing firearms could be tailored to specific high-risk regions, such as the city of Rio de Janeiro, to increase their effectiveness. We propose InDistill, a novel model compression approach, combining the principles of knowledge distillation and channel pruning to efficiently transfer critical information flow from a powerful teacher model to a more efficient student model. Unlike previous techniques that collapse this information, InDistill leverages layer-wise pruning of the teacher's intermediate stages, aligning their widths with those of the student, thereby enabling direct information flow and facilitation of knowledge distillation without an intermediate encoding stage. Furthermore, our approach undertakes a detailed examination of the teacher's intermediate outputs, pruning them based on distillation uncertainty to ensure a tailored compression strategy. Through thorough evaluation on multiple image classification datasets, such as CIFAR, ImageNet, and Tiny ImageNet, as well as incorporation of various pruning techniques, such as PRNN, Soft Pruning, and Exact Pruning, the InDistill method has demonstrated superior performance compared to the current state-of-the-art model compression methods. Notably, evaluations on the ImageNet dataset have shown that InDistill has achieved a 2-fold reduction in parameters with minimal loss in accuracy, specifically a 1.8% drop, while surpassing the compression capability of Soft Prunning by 0.6% in a channel pruning scenario. A well-known dimensionality reduction technique called CountSketch employs randomized linear measurements to map vectors into a lower-dimensional space, particularly effective at identifying the top elements (with the largest squared magnitude) of a given vector. However, the CountSketch sketch falls short in situations where subsequent vectors rely on feedback from previous inputs. Under such circumstances, the classic estimator can be compromised by a relatively low number of inferences, essentially making the top elements' estimates inaccurate with high probability. Research has proposed a novel strategy, taking only a small number of inferences, that offers significant improvements by requiring fewer queries while maintaining nearly optimal results. A key part of this approach involves a process for determining optimal weights, which can be efficiently sample-average calculated. Interestingly, the weights possess unique properties, being mutually independent and optimally optimized for CountSketch. Furthermore, the provided query upper bounds hold true even for scenarios where the feedback is used to infer the dynamics of changing networks, dynamic channels, and other complex systems. For instance, it's shown that the CountSketch sketch is susceptible to approximately $O(\sqrt{n})$ queries rather than $O(n)$. This study focuses on the application of the Euler characteristic for advanced topological data analysis in multi-variable spaces. Euler characteristic is a fundamental, widely recognized topological invariant with numerous past uses, especially in studies involving random fields. Our primary objective is to illustrate its application in high-dimensional spaces. While employing more powerful invariants like homology remains an active area of research, the theoretical and computational feasibility of the Euler characteristic make it an attractive intermediate step for multi-variable topological analysis. We demonstrate its practicality by using it as a tool for partitional data clustering in spaces of any dimension, as well as for the efficient computation of topological features in high-dimensional spaces. Specifically, we utilize extensions such as combined and weighted Euler characteristics. We create a novel, highly scalable algorithm with near-linear complexity for computing combined Euler characteristic in high-dimensional spaces. Moreover, we apply weighted Euler characteristic in a context inspired by Bayesian approximation for sampling-based fields. The theoretical validity of these methods is established through combinatorial topology connections, and their performance is evaluated in different scenarios through extensive numerical experiments. Additionally, we present an application of combined Euler characteristic for spatial data partitioning. We compare the performance of the proposed methods with existing alternatives that involve Monte Carlo sampling in various case studies. The results show that weighted Euler characteristic offers a balance between accuracy and speed, making it a suitable choice for data topological analysis in high-dimensional spaces. The study further introduces a Python library, called PyEuler, for efficient and scalable implementation of the proposed methods. The library's modular structure allows for easy application of different advanced topological invariants in the future. The methods discussed in this study have been published in a research report (Iijima et al., 2021) and were also presented at the workshop Topological Data Analysis in High-Dimensional Spaces (2021). The concept of an effective, time-independent Floquet Hamiltonian underpins the Floquet engineering of isolated systems, describing their evolution over driving periods. In open systems, this approach remains limited due to driving-induced fluctuations. We develop a theory for a quantum system driven both strongly and periodically, focusing on its behavior governed by the open-system Floquet master equation. Under conditions where the system remains well-defined despite the driving, we identify a phase characterized by time-indistinguishable Floquet generators. In this phase, where the generator's phase factors cancel out, we determine the Floquet master equation's general form and demonstrate its reduction to the closed-system Floquet Hamiltonian in the isolated-system limit. Both the delocalized Floquet generator's phase and its influence on dynamics are directly related to the driving's geometric structure, highlighting a time-indistinguishable phase with and without driving-induced fluctuations. Furthermore, we illustrate the theoretical localizer's failure to remove the generator's phase, contrasting it to more conventional quench drivers. Lastly, we show both the driving-induced fluctuations and the ineffectiveness of localizers in eliminating the delocalized Floquet generator's phase at the single-particle level. The proposed theory has broad implications, applicable to various driven quantum systems across diverse fields, including photonics, electronics, and ultra-cold atoms. Ultimately, it may facilitate the design and analysis of Floquet-engineered open quantum systems, enabling the realization of non-unitary quantum dynamics. To contribute to this area, we present a universal method for obtaining universal dynamical invariants, applicable to both unitary and non-unitary dynamics. In the case of a non-unitary phase with a delocalized Floquet generator, these invariants provide insight into the system's dynamics, quantifying its dissipation rate and defining criteria for phase transitions. Even when the generator becomes localized with a time-distinguishable phase, these invariants retain significant physical relevance, offering a framework for classifying non-unitary quantum dynamics. As demonstrated by its application to a non-Hermitian quasiperiodic system, this approach may lead to significant advancements in the field of non-unitary quantum engineering. The discovered universal dynamical invariants provide a general framework for obtaining similar invariants in both unitary and non-unitary quantum dynamics, highlighting the importance of phase classification. Despite recent advancements in Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), explaining their predictive decisions remains an unresolved issue. Current methods primarily address the interpretation of individual cases (i.e., important graph structures and node attributes) to understand model predictions, but generate instance-specific explanations that fail to provide a broader understanding of the GNN model, restricting their general applicability in the inductive setting. Moreover, these methods struggle to provide natural explanations, as they involve assigning arbitrary importance to graph features, disregarding their inherent meanings. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel explanation method based on text, specifically Graph Prompts, that generates general, interpretable explanations for GNN predictions using natural language, independent of the dataset used for model training or testing. By combining prompt-based explanation techniques with graph classification tasks, our research demonstrates that these explanations hold equal significance for both understanding the model itself and providing transfer knowledge to similar applications. Moreover, we utilize these explanations as constraints in the inductive setting, showcasing their potential to enhance downstream task performance, such as zero-shot learning. Formal verification offers critical correctness assurances, yet it often necessitates an adaptable and easily modifiable proof framework. Hoare logic serves as a general and versatile method for software verification but may not be well-suited for automatic verification due to the complexity of automated proving and the need to incorporate human expertise. In some situations, Hoare logic can be adapted for automatic verification, while in others, more tailored logics might be required. Distributed consensus is crucial for various distributed systems, such as distributed databases and blockchains, to function correctly. The Canopus protocol efficiently manages large-scale distributed consensus without the need for a single leader, achieving this through a virtual tree structure that limits network traffic and hardware redundancies within the network. The existing Canopus protocol excels at performance, however, struggles when dealing with failures that don't directly affect performance, leading to a need for an improved version. This study enhances Canopus to not only tolerate various types of failures but also to be more adaptable to dynamic changes in the network and individual component failures without relying on a single leader. The proposed modification involves introducing a new failure detection method using partial messages to improve the protocol's robustness. The improved protocol achieves this by utilizing a partial message-based method to detect failures when a node detects an anomaly, it sends the partial message to its neighbors, which are then used to confirm the failure. If a failure is confirmed, the node initiates a recovery process to re-integrate the failed node or perform a rollback of the correct value to the correct node. This improved protocol not only tolerates failures but also minimizes the latency caused by a failure, with the difference in latency being proportional to the network's height and the cost of broadcasting a message is proportional to the square of the width of the network. Furthermore, we modify Canopus to adapt to dynamic changes in the network and individual component failures by introducing a new phase in the protocol's agreement phase to re-calculate the values of the correct node and perform a rollback of the correct value to the correct node. This improved protocol achieves a time complexity of $O(\sqrt{m} + \sqrt{h})$ when dealing with a static network and $O(\sqrt{m})$ when dealing with dynamic changes in the network and individual component failures. All the pseudocode for the protocol is written in the Go programming language and all simulations are run using this programming language. Recent studies utilizing neutron spin echo and nuclear magnetic resonance relaxation methods, which examine linear transport properties, have yielded contrasting results when evaluating the impact of cholesterol on the bending modulus of lipid bilayers. This inconsistency arose despite earlier research employing solely equilibrium experiments, not linear transport properties, indicating that one may be misled by data from the latter. A general discussion is presented to illustrate how this occurs, which in turn prompts the introduction of a criterion that distinguishes between general linear operators and those possessing a physical basis within the context of system of equations. Using the condition of physical necessity, it is demonstrated that one specific method – neutron spin echo – is prone to misinterpretation, which may explain the discrepancy between its findings and those of nuclear magnetic resonance relaxation methods. Furthermore, it is suggested that the latter actually measures what it claims – the challenge of fluidity within the membrane. In an effort to clarify this, a simplified model of a membrane is analyzed. This model significantly decreases the challenge of fluidity when compared to a purely fluid system of the same weight and demonstrates how this decrease occurs through the introduction of cholesterol, which in turn increases the membrane's resistance to bending. A more comprehensive model, which incorporates membrane components beyond cholesterol and lipids, also reveals that the challenge of fluidity is negligible. Consequently, nuclear magnetic relaxation methods may be used in the future to directly measure the presence of other membrane components, which is not currently the case. In an effort to address the inconsistency between neutron spin echo and nuclear magnetic relaxation methods regarding the impact of cholesterol on the bending modulus of lipid bilayers, it is proposed that the latter actually finds evidence of increased fluidity within the membrane. A comprehensive discussion is presented to illustrate how this may occur through the interaction of cholesterol and the membrane's other components, which in turn increases the challenge of fluidity within the membrane. In an effort to further increase the understanding of how this may occur, a simplified model of a membrane is analyzed. This model, which incorporates one type of molecule called anchidic acid, demonstrates how this may lead to increased fluidity within the membrane through the anchoring of this molecule. A more comprehensive model, which incorporates multiple types of molecules, also reveals how these may interact and increase the challenge of fluidity within the membrane. Consequently, nuclear magnetic relaxation methods may be used in the future to directly measure the presence of other membrane components or interactions beyond cholesterol. A broader interpretation of this is also provided, which in turn increases the understanding of how this may lead to increased fluidity within the membrane.

In recent research, Berman developed the concept of Gray categories as stable tricategories, serving as intermediate points between pseudofunctors in 2-categories of categories and functors. This paper introduces refined Gray categories, incorporating equivariant components and dihomotopy, which can be seen as a refined version of Berman's definition. These categories are then linked to 2-categories of homotopy coherent simplicial categories through a construction similar to that used by Shulman, establishing a connection to the study of adjoint correspondences. This relationship further allows for the definition of refined Gray categories using a more general construction. A comparison with tricategories defined by Bourdeau-Bondy-Horel reveals that refined Gray categories, including those derived from pseudofunctors, match their "homotopy-in-the-source" variant, ensuring consistency across definitions. This study also explores how refined Gray categories, including those derived from equivariant pseudofunctors, provide a suitable framework for the interpretation of Cisinski's relative total left fibrations, establishing a connection to the work of Berger-Mogilski on equivariant fibrations. A final result shows the correspondence between stable refined Gray categories and tricategories, along with some key equivalences involving equivariant components and dihomotopy. 
This research dually develops the concept of refined Gray groups, providing a simplified model that can be used to describe total left fibrations in 2-categories of categories and functors up to homotopy. A comparison with the work of Shulman on adjoint correspondences yields new insights, and the definition of refined Gray groups, including equivariant components, provides a straightforward framework for the study of total left fibrations in 2-categories of categories and functors up to homotopy. 
A preliminary outline of (2,2)-equivariant dihomotopy categories, along with the definition of refined Gray categories, is presented, offering a simplified model that can be used to describe these categories. A comparison with the work of Mandell-Segal-Shulman on mixed fibrations yields new insights, and the definition of refined Gray categories, including equivariant components and dihomotopy, provides a straightforward framework for the study of (2,2)-equivariant fibrations up to 2-homotopy.

Automatic hippocampus segmentation on magnetic resonance imaging is a critical factor in diagnosing and treating neuropsychiatric disorders. Current deep learning-based methods primarily utilize data from patients with healthy or Alzheimer's disease. This raises concerns about their performance in other domains, such as patients with epilepsy and hippocampal resections. We have developed and validated an open-source, state-of-the-art deep learning method for automatic hippocampus and parahippocampal gyrus segmentation, using 3D multi-contrast MRI data. We have also created and distributed a large, diverse dataset with 85 patients who have epilepsy, hip fracture, hypoxia-ischemia, and hippocampal resections, collected using 3T MRI. We have compared our method against 11 state-of-the-art and recently published techniques and demonstrated significantly better results. A Python package, ehpseg, is now available for download at https://doi.org/10.1016/J.Nicl.2022.103161, allowing for replication of results and segmentation of new data. A web-based interface can be accessed at https://hpseg.cometaweb.org/. We have achieved a mean absolute error of 2.1 mL for hippocampus segmentation and 1.4 mL for parahippocampal gyrus segmentation, with a coefficient of variation of 0.53 for hippocampus segmentation and 0.42 for parahippocampal gyrus segmentation.
