We scrutinize an experiment claiming to showcase the quantum pigeonhole effect by having three parties navigate a two-path interferometer with no pair of them using the same path simultaneously. Through an analysis based on weak values, we uncover inconsistencies in the interpretation of the protocol's classical model, particularly in the treatment of path detection and photon counting. Furthermore, we propose an alternative scenario for testing the quantum pigeonhole effect, drawing from the no-go theorem for entangled particles. In the context of the path interferometer, we demonstrate that the quantum pigeonhole effect is equivalent to the principle of wave packet superposition, thereby resolving any perceived paradox.}

Our research identifies the Cosmic Ray Albedo Neutron Decay (CRAND) as the primary factor responsible for the formation of high-energy inner proton radiation belts. A Monte Carlo simulation model is created to calculate proton radiation at low Earth orbit by simulating the interaction between cosmic ray particles and the Earth's atmosphere, followed by transportation in the magnetosphere. This includes modeling proton generation from neutron decay and trapping within the geomagnetic field, taking into account factors such as spatial distribution, energy, and momentum of these trapped protons. This effort contributes to the development of a comprehensive radiation environment simulation at low Earth orbit and geostationary satellites. The simulated proton radiation at an altitude of 600 km is consistent with measurements from the Proton Radiation Sensor on the Chinese space station Tiantan, which provides 200.8 kg mass and 6 m length radiation protection. Moreover, this simulation is validated by comparing it with measurements from the Binary Neutron Telescope on board PSB-SPC. The Binary Neutron Telescope uses a unique binary coincidence technique to detect neutrons and determine their energy by calculating the time projection of the detected event. This detection method enables the calculation of neutron energy by comparing measured event time with simulated neutron trajectory time. The results of this simulation reveal a high degree of consistency between measured data and simulated neutron energy. This successful validation of the Monte Carlo method allows for the calculation of neutron energy with an accuracy of approximately 0.2 MeV. A comparison with previous studies of CRAND neutron energy has also revealed the superiority of this new method. The simulated data indicates that radiation pressure may play a significant role in transporting protons from the outer radiation belt to an altitude as low as 600 km. Consequently, the total number of trapped protons at this altitude is estimated to be as low as 70 per second. This study's findings suggest that radiation pressure could be the primary mechanism responsible for the transportation of protons from the outer radiation belt to an altitude of 600 km. As a result, the total number of trapped protons at this altitude is estimated to be significantly lower than what would be expected through diffusion. The results of this simulation provide the basis for generating a proton radiation spectrum at an altitude of 600 km, which can be used as a reference for designing spacecraft radiation protection at low Earth orbit and geostationary satellites. The simulated data has been applied to generate a proton radiation spectrum at an altitude of 600 km, which can be used in designing space radiation protection at various spacecraft configurations and orbitals

A network's expressivity is a crucial factor in assessing deep neural networks, 
as it correlates with the limitations of achievable performance gains. This paper 
establishes a framework for generating a series of network architectures, 
each with increasing complexity, to quantify a network's expressivity. We use 
the expressivity metric to create a step-by-step protocol for designing more 
effective networks based on prior examples. This protocol generates new 
architectures by combining redundant sub-networks. We apply this framework to 
a variety of image classification tasks, involving various network architectures, 
and also investigate the effect of training data on the step-by-step protocol. 
We find that the generated architectures, known as SymNet, exhibit enhanced 
performance on the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets, as well as the ImageNet 
dataset. This research provides insights into the nature of expressivity in deep 
neural networks and offers a practical method for improving network design. We 
also present a novel, more efficient approach to proxy-based network 
optimization, where the goal is to eliminate unnecessary parameters while 
maintaining performance. We propose two novel symmetric proxy-based optimization 
algorithms and apply them to ResNet-50 and ViT-21, achieving significant 
parameter reduction while preserving accuracy on the ImageNet dataset. The 
source code is available at https://github.com/azhu2021/SymNet. This research 
is supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (No. 62176203), 
the Beijing Natural Science Foundation (No. GJHZ202113), and CRC-CAAI-1033.

We propose a novel approach to modelling interstellar dust where larger grains are directly observed as compact, aligned pahticles, while the smaller components are absorbed or scattered out of detection. Using a two-component model based on the conjunction of Mwille et al's recent observation of aligned graphene-like material in tau Aurigae's circumstellar envelope and the PAH studies of Druard et al, we are able to replicate the observed extinction and continuum sub-mm spectra of both the Red Rectangle and tau Aurigae with high accuracy. Notably, this model also predicts the presence of PAH emission features in the spectral range of 7.5-11 micrometers for both the Red Rectangle and tau Aurigae, in accordance with the findings of Schmidt et al. Additionally, the model suggests that the observed emission at 7.3 micrometers in the Red Rectangle is primarily caused by the vibration of hydrogenated amorphous carbon, rather than the vibration of hydrogenated PAHs as previously assumed. However, the model does predict the presence of emission at 7.3 micrometers for tau Aurigae, in accordance with the findings of Schmidt et al. Building upon the model of Druard et al, we introduce a correlation between the fluorescence of PAHs and the polarization of photon polarization, and demonstrate that the observed features in the spectral range of 7.5-11 micrometers can be attributed to a combination of polarized fluorescence from aligned PAHs and the polarization of photon polarization by graphitic grains. Research on exoplanets has led to a realization that hot Jupiter planets are more common around low-mass stars than initially thought.  Recent studies using SOPHIE at the Observatoire de Haute-Provence have re-examined data for a sample of M dwarfs, searching for signs of planetary activity.  Three stars in the sample showed radial velocity variability that could be interpreted as signals from orbiting planets.  Using simulations and further analysis, scientists estimated the possible masses and orbits of these putative planets.  Estimates for minimum planet mass ranged between 5 to 16 times that of Jupiter, with possible masses between 20 to 60 times that of Jupiter, suggesting these planets may form earlier, before their stars reach maximum contraction phase.  Further verification is needed, with a combination of photometric and spectroscopic methods, to confirm these findings and gain a deeper understanding of planetary formation and evolution across a variety of star types.  It appears that smaller planets may form in the habitable zones around low-mass stars and it is possible that current detection methods are not yet refined enough to identify these planets.  With an emphasis on exploring the diversity of planetary systems surrounding all types of stars, scientists aim to break the historical distinction between planets orbiting high-mass and low-mass stars, with an emphasis on understanding the unique characteristics of each system.  Furthermore, by studying the formation of planets in the solar neighborhood, scientists may uncover previously unknown aspects of planetary formation and evolution, such as relationships between planetary mass, period, and metallicity.  Ultimately, a comprehensive understanding of planetary mass-period relations may be derived from this research, with implications for space missions such as MEISORP and TRES. A crucial next step will be the inclusion of these results in a combined dataset during the Tres4GAPS workshop in October 2014.

A extensive examination of phonon topology in 52 compounds has been conducted, covering a broad range of binary and ternary materials. The study focuses on halides of group I and II (Li, Na, K, Be, Mg, Ca), sulfur, and transition metal compounds of group IV and group VB. Computational investigations of phonon dispersion relations and temperature-dependent phonon-spectrum evolution were performed. Specifically, we used first-principles calculations based on density functional theory and employed the Vienna ab initio simulation package. In our research, we identified topological phonons in S, SnSe, PbTe, CaSi, MgGe, CaGe, and Li6.5Si1.5. Other compounds that exhibit phonon topology include LiS, NaS, BeSe, BeTe, CaSb, MgSb, MgBi, and Mn4Ge. Excluding S, however, we discovered phonon cascades in all other compounds studied. In most of these materials, instability is present at low pressure. Specifically, we found phonon instability in S, SnSe, PbTe, CaSi, MgGe, CaGe, and Li6.5Si1.5, while phonon-spectrum changes lead to dynamic instability in others, such as LiS, BeSe, BeTe, CaSb, MgSb, MgBi, Mn4Ge, and Mn3Ge. The results indicate a wide range of phonon topology examples, underscoring the feasibility of designing stable phonon states through alloying and chemical composition modulation. Therefore, these materials may hold promise for phonon engineering and potential applications in resonant phonon devices. The study's computational data are freely accessible via the GitHub repository https://github.com/PhonTibrary/PhonTibrary-TopologicalPhonons.

As applications relying on graph representations grow, the focus has shifted from global fairness to incorporating fairness at the node level, considering that Graph Neural Network (GNN)-based models primarily operate within local neighborhoods. To address this, we propose a framework that captures the concept of neighborhood fairness. Our method is built on two core components - the first enables the construction of equitable neighborhoods for any node in a graph and the second allows adaptation to accommodate specific data constraints. Notably, while numerous studies have explored link prediction, we delve into fair link classification as part of the MesoMotif Fairness Challenge, focusing on identifying functional motifs within graphs. Our approach highlights the importance of neighborhood fairness in capturing meaningful graph patterns through selective node inclusion. By leveraging the capabilities of both graph-based and node/edge-based metrics, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, achieving an F1 score of 0.8135 compared to the baseline F1 score of 0.8131. Furthermore, our neighborhood-based metric surpasses the baseline in almost every aspect, except for edge homogeneity,, underscoring the significance of neighborhood fairness. Our implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/quantifying-fairness/Neighborhood-Fairness.

Two proposed expectation models for temporary financial bubbles, involving individuals with varied predictions and positive influences on the market, have been examined through simulation and analysis. The first model, based on a study by Dang, Chakrabarti, and Chakraborty in 2015, uses an exponential decay function to represent arbitrageurs' altered predictions, while the second, inspired by a 2011 study of Arthur, Durlauf, and Davis, accounts for varied predictions through a mixture of arbitrageurs with mixed signals. Simulated markets revealed that both models produced sustainable bubbles, characterized by a dramatic decline in trading volume and price, followed by a rapid collapse. Notably, the first model allowed for an indefinite extension of the bubble, whereas the second model predetermined its duration. The simulation outcomes also showed that both models generated price distributions with extreme outliers and long tails. Interestingly, in markets where prices were often significantly lower than their potential, the first model tended to produce higher prices, whereas the second model resulted in lower prices. A key difference between the two models lies in the average price, with the first model yielding higher averages and the second model yielding lower, possibly due to varied predictions leading to more frequent and severe market crashes. Overall, the simulation results indicate that heterogeneous positive expectations can lead to sustainable bubbles, potentially explaining the emergence and persistence of temporary bubbles in financial markets. The models' ability to replicate real market patterns suggests potential benefits for investors in terms of market forecasting. Further investigation is required to examine the models' implications for market crashes and their consequences. common link in their objectives, allowing them to complement each other in the
process of predicting a subject-object pair in a sentence. While a relation
extraction model identifies the object corresponding to a particular subject
within a set of candidates, a knowledge graph link prediction model suggests
possible objects for a given subject. However, the traditional approach has
two key drawbacks: the focus on a specific subject and the reliance on prior
knowledge. In an effort to break free from these constraints, a new model
called CoLink has been developed. This model involves using attention to derive
general representations of subjects from large knowledge graph data and then
using these subjects in conjunction with objects from relation extraction data to
predict possible objects for a given subject. Results indicate that CoLink
outperforms the existing state-of-the-art model, specifically on the English
sub-set of TAC-KBP. Furthermore, a new state-of-the-art model called CoLink+,
achieving up to 7.5% absolute improvement over CoLink, has been developed by
integrating it with cross-attention. This cross-attention mechanism allows for
the direct access of a specific subject's representation by an object, while
co-training enhances the robustness of the model. These findings suggest that
subject representations obtained through large-scale knowledge graph data are
more informative than relation-specific models, achieving better results than
general baselines that rely on relation-specific models. Moreover, a cross-
attention mechanism allows a specific subject to directly access its subject's
representation, bringing CoLink+ in line with existing state-of-the-art link
prediction models. All implementation details can be accessed at the CoLink+
GitHub repository.

The inverter is an integral building block in CMOS technology. In the realm of variability-driven design, characterizing the inverter's robustness in the face of process fluctuations is of significant interest. Among CMOS technologies of different generations and fabrication processes, the impact of different types of fluctuations on the inverter's delay, particularly its rise and fall times, has been observed to be quite distinct. Thermal-mott and piecewise-linear models have been found to accurately represent the inverter's delay under specific conditions, whereas delay parameters have been shown to be tightly correlated with the inverter's edge positions. Furthermore, the inverter's edge positions and delay have been observed to respond differently to variations in device parameters, with different parameters affecting rise and fall times equally. Notably, this research uncovered a distinct set of critical regions where the inverter's delay becomes severely impacted due to fluctuations. In the context of SPICE simulations involving 45 nm, 65 nm, and 130 nm CMOS technologies, it has been demonstrated that a relatively small change in process fluctuations can result in a massive increase in the inverter's delay. The findings presented in this study are applicable to a wide range of CMOS technologies. Building on this understanding, this research proposed a simple yet efficient method for optimizing the inverter's edge positions and delay under the influence of process fluctuations. By incorporating this optimization technique, a traditional CMOS inverter-based circuit achieved improved performance in terms of its delay, particularly rise and fall times. The optimization technique can be easily integrated into existing design flows, making it a practical and effective solution to variability-driven design problems. Quasi-periodic oscillations type C, typically observed in low-hard and hard-intermediate states of black hole X-ray transients, have been investigated using the MAXI J1535-571 data collected by Insight-HXMT. By applying a novel time-dependent Comptonization model and a relativistic reflection model, researchers have demonstrated its ability to accurately describe X-ray data up to 100 keV. Observations suggest that an almost constant frequency for type C QPOs around 12-13 Hz exists across different hardness levels, indicating a decaying frequency with increasing color temperature. These findings support earlier studies suggesting a boundary layer as the source of type C QPOs. However, since type C QPOs are primarily seen in low-luminosity states with a low accretion rate, it is proposed that they may also be generated by mass transfer between the primary star and a previously discovered 2.5-s X-ray pulsation source, rather than solely due to the accretion process. Furthermore, in states with very low X-ray luminosities below 10^35 erg/s, type C QPOs might be triggered by an alternative mechanism, possibly attributed to an alternative boundary layer associated with a secondary object sharing a shared equatorial plane. Despite both objects being in a relatively close orbit, their mass is estimated to be under a certain limit, specifically under 2.2 times solar mass for the object with a 2.5-s X-ray pulsation period, and under 1.2 times solar mass for the other object, for them to produce the observed QPOs and pulsations by generating an alternative boundary layer. In the context of multi-agent reinforcement learning, particularly for tasks requiring cooperation and communication, MARL agents are prone to being brittle due to their potential for overfitting on the policies of their training partners. As a result, they may adapt strategies centered on preconceived expectations of other agents' actions rather than truly reacting to their behaviors. To address this issue, we developed transfer empowerment as a method that quantifies the influence between MARL agents, aiming to measure how much one agent can impact another within a shared environment. This quantification serves as a starting point for developing agents whose actions have a significant impact on their counterparts. Importantly, our framework allows for the assessment of the effectiveness of inter-agent influences in cooperation settings. Through theoretical analysis and empirical testing, we have found that our proposed method yields better results in non-selfish settings and significantly improves the ability of MARL agents to work together effectively in cooperative tasks. Additionally, the measures derived from transfer empowerment provide valuable insights into the qualities that one agent can influence another to perform. Moreover, we have observed that the central idea behind our approach - the focus on how one agent can affect another - naturally facilitates the development of non-parametric models for communication between agents, which in turn leads to improved performance in both cooperative and competitive settings. Overall, our proposed method offers a novel and powerful approach to understanding and improving the interactions among MARL agents. The framework may also be applied to other MARL settings, such as those focused on fairness, to explore the uncharted space of influence evaluation and design. As such, it serves as a versatile tool for creating more intelligent and cooperative AI agents. All relevant code and data can be accessed at https://github.com/azazza91/transfer-emp. Lastly, our research provides a new perspective on the fundamental nature of influence evaluation in the context of MARL, shedding light on the inherent properties and requirements of this framework. As a result, the measures derived from transfer empowerment can be viewed as fundamental characteristics of multi-agent systems. In contrast, the methods proposed to design agents according to these characteristics can be seen as approaches aiming to leverage these fundamental properties. Furthermore, the methods proposed in this study can be viewed as non-parametric techniques, whereas previous works based on transfer empowerment have been parametric. Nonetheless, the central idea behind our approach - the focus on how one agent can affect another - leads to a novel framework for non-parametric model development, highlighting the potential for future research in this direction. Material identification in images has a wide range of practical applications, such as assisting people with disabilities and acting as a sensory for individuals who cannot see. This study investigates the recognition of visual materials using a deep-learning approach. Differing from typical object classification tasks, material recognition is more challenging due to variations in appearance, limited data, and poor image quality. In response to these obstacles, we introduce the Residual Rectangular Transform for Rhythmic Patterns (3R) method. First, we develop an algorithm to extract and align image features in a way that mimics human perception. Next, we employ an encoder-decoder architecture to capture contextual information and preserve the richness of the data. Furthermore, we introduce an encoder-sharing strategy to enhance performance and reduce the complexity of the network. Lastly, we use an attention mechanism to refine the classification results and improve accuracy. Our proposed approach has achieved exceptional performance on the MaterialImage-130 dataset, yielding state-of-the-art results. Additionally, we conducted a thorough analysis of our approach, including a parameter efficiency assessment. This study contributes not only a highly effective material recognition method but also offers insights into the design of the model and can serve as a reference for future work in this field. The research code and dataset are publicly available at https://github.com/ziyi525/material-recognition.

In contrast to other dense methods, we leverage self and cross attention mechanisms in the Transformer model to derive feature descriptors that are context-dependent for both images. This approach allows our method, termed LoFTR, to identify dense matches without relying on a complicated pipeline and accurately place keypoints despite low-texture surroundings. This research paper explores a real-world scenario in which consumers can avoid paying high prices for energy consumption during peak hours by shifting their consumption patterns in exchange for discounted rates. To achieve this, a two-layer neural network is proposed, consisting of an encoder that aggregates sequential energy data and an decoder that regresses sequential labels, both trained end-to-end. By applying the encoder-decoder model, consumers can forecast optimal consumption schedules, thereby taking advantage of temporary price reductions. Given the sparse and high-dimensional nature of energy consumption data, the paper addresses this issue by using a transformer-based encoder and a linear translator for decoding, as well as applying an encoder with a reduced number of neurons to process energy consumption sequences. Additionally, the study includes a comparison of proposed approaches with existing methodologies, evaluating their performance using the F1-score and Mean Squared Error metrics. With the goal of making real-time linear transformer predictions feasible for resource-constrained devices, the paper proposes an efficient encoding method to reduce memory usage and computational costs. Furthermore, the study demonstrates the effectiveness of proposed schemes through experiments using both synthetic and actual energy consumption data. Lastly, the paper highlights the potential real-world applications of these approaches by illustrating real-time linear transformer predictions on real energy consumption data. The study's implementation will be made available on GitHub under the MIT License, including the associated code with the ID 615181. Based on the experimental findings, the paper shows that the proposed schemes successfully forecast energy consumption with a high F1-score (approximately 0.973) and mean squared error (much less than 0.01). In terms of the decoding method, the study finds that the transformer-based encoder performs better than the linear translator but slightly worse than the reduced encoder with F1-scores of 0.9738, 0.9731, and 0.9739, respectively. Conversely, the paper finds that the linear transformer decoder excels over the reduced encoder with a much lower MSE (approximately 0.002) and reports a computational complexity analysis based on the number of neurons in the encoder. Finally, the study suggests a real-world application of these approaches by illustrating a consumer agent's ability to dynamically change energy consumption patterns in response to temporal price variations. The paper's associated code is available at https://github.com/ashishkaps/Real-time_linear_transformer. The research data can be found at https://doi.org/10.21924/prism/101.2. https. //github.com/ashishkaps/Real-time_linear_transformer.

These measures have been calculated for 102 languages, enabling a comprehensive comparison. Our analysis reveals a positive correlation between these metrics, suggesting they are loosely associated with a common underlying factor. Firstly, we investigated the intrinsic characteristics of each measure using principal component analysis, revealing some interesting insights. For example, Germanic languages tend to score high on Relative Complexity and Morphological Density, while Outcome languages and Indo-Aryan languages score well on Derivational Complexity and Paradoxical Complexity, respectively. We establish the optimal Lipschitz regularity of very weak solutions for the measure-valued elliptic PDE $-\mathrm{div}(A(x) \nabla u) = Q \; \mathcal{H}^{n-1} \llcorner \Gamma$ within a smooth domain $\Omega$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$. Here, $\Gamma$ represents a $C^{1,\alpha}$-smooth hypersurface, with $Q$ defined as a $C^{0,\alpha}$ density on $\Gamma$, and $A$ characterizes a symmetric, uniformly elliptic and $W^{1,q}$-regular tensor $(q > n)$. Furthermore, the article discusses the optimality of these conditions applied to the problem. This particular equation essentially represents a non-Newtonian fluid equation when considering flow within a smooth domain, with the additional factor of a measure-valued source term on a smooth surface. It is notable that the case where the domain is $\mathbb{R}^n$ was previously addressed in a paper by the authors, with different prerequisites and results reported. Ultimately, the article provides a complementary outcome to previously published results related to the given problem. $\diamondsuit$\\

In the field of display advertising, real-time bidding has become the predominant approach. Each ad impression resulting from user interaction is instantly auctioned off, with demand-side platforms (DSPs) providing bids typically based on the impression's value. Nonetheless, since the impression's utility is unknown at bidding time, DSPs must strategically bid in anticipation of uncertainty. This research addresses this challenge by incorporating the variable reward probability and the optimal bidding strategy, which maximizes expected return, into a single model. Additionally, this model is characterized as a complex nonlinear equation with interdependence, for which a deep neural network is proposed as a solution to solve the equation by framing it as a function approximation task. Finally, this approach is tested using a large-scale dataset and comparative analysis is performed with a benchmark method. Experimental results reveal the neural network's ability to accurately solve the equation and increase revenue by 18.4% over the existing standard method. Further analysis confirms the neural network's effectiveness across various risk tolerance levels. This research contributes to the advertising field by providing a flexible framework for bidding strategy adjustment according to the level of risk preference and reward probability. Nonclassical properties in continuous-variable quantum systems are often marked by quantum correlations and Wigner negativity. This study explores how these two nonclassical traits are connected in the context of remotely generating Wigner negativity through local measurements. Our research indicates that when two parties share a Gaussian state, any Wigner negativity in one subsystem can be eliminated in favor of creating it in the other subsystem simply by having the other party perform local measurements on their share of the state. This behavior is consistent across a range of Gaussian states, including thermal states, where the magnitude of the negativity is directly related to the temperature of the thermal state and the local measurements in question. What's more, our research shows that while quantum steering is a prerequisite for Wigner negativity, it is not a necessary condition for the remote generation of Wigner negativity in this system. This research is significant because it highlights an intriguing mechanism through which quantum correlations can be manipulated and engineered in continuous-variable quantum systems. Furthermore, our research offers novel insights into the behavior of Wigner negativity across a range of quantum states, including thermal states, which are often overlooked in favor of more traditional nonclassical states like coherent and squeezed states. This research has implications for the field of quantum key distribution, where Wigner negativity has been proposed as an alternative nonclassical trait. Since remote generation of Wigner negativity in this system does not preclude the possibility of steering-based quantum key distribution, this research is particularly relevant to this application. However, our research also reveals a counterintuitive scenario in which remote generation of Wigner negativity results in a condition known as single-mode squeezing, which is a resource that is mutually exclusive with Wigner negativity and cannot be used in conjunction with it in this particular application. This research therefore sheds light on a crucial distinction between steering-based and other forms of quantum key distribution. Furthermore, our research offers novel insights into the connection between Wigner negativity and other nonclassical traits in continuous-variable quantum systems, paving the way for future applications and contributions to the field of quantum information science. Utilizing the two-decoy BB84 protocol, which is a common QKD implementation, we simulate and calculate the secure boundary analysis under diverse source conditions, including the influence of random seed non-uniformity. Notably, our analysis shows that the contribution of random seed non-uniformity significantly impacts the secure boundary, particularly when the random seed's min-entropy is below 0.5 bits. We also experimentally generate the photonic states of the two-decoy BB84 QKD protocol, providing a comprehensive, quantitative demonstration of the secure boundary analysis in practice. By combining these findings, we compare and contrast the two-decoy BB84 with other QKD protocols from a secure boundary perspective. To conclude, the research outcomes are further discussed as potential solutions to mitigate the impact of random seed non-uniformity in QKD protocols. A typical strategy for modelling extreme events involves considering occurrences beyond a high threshold as events of a non-homogeneous Poisson process. While this method has the advantage of using threshold-independent extreme value parameters, it comes with the challenge of parameter uncertainty. To address this, we propose a novel estimation strategy that incorporates Bayesian updating into the framework. Specifically, we first derive the likelihood and prior distributions of the parameters of the Poisson process, and then introduce a procedure to update these parameters using the P\'{o}lya-Gamma sampler. Notably, this method enables simultaneous estimation of the parameters governing both the exceedance process and the distribution above a high threshold. To demonstrate the feasibility of this approach, we present an illustrative numerical study of a real-world dataset. Our study models the number of extreme daily mean-excess losses of automobile insurance policies in Taiwan, and reveals a significant correlation between this model and the AC-AR(1) model in the existing literature. Furthermore, we parameterise the autoregressive component as part of the Bayesian model to showcase the feasibility of this parameterisation. Through a series of numerical experiments, we verify the efficacy of the proposed method and its performance in overcoming issues of data sparsity. Ultimately, we apply the estimated parameters to predict future extreme values, and evaluate the predicted performance of the Bayesian model through the Quantile Score and the Grandt Score. When compared to the non-Bayesian estimator with Independent Metropolis-Hastings, our proposed method demonstrates notable advantages in terms of its faster convergence and superior estimation accuracy. A computational implementation of the proposed method is available online through the GitHub repository. In particular, the modelEst function can be used for parameter estimation, the SimFun function for simulation, and the Grandt function for evaluation. To facilitate reproducibility, we also provide the code used in our numerical study in the supplementary materials. Specifically, the code is stored in the modelEst.R file and the R package modelEst can be installed via the install.packages("modelEst") command. To address these issues, we propose a new framework for refining and expanding the graph's content by leveraging both human and artificial intelligence to improve its accuracy and utility. A key component of this framework is ATOMIC, a massive database containing over 350,000 everyday causes and effects that can be used to infer the relationships between concepts. We believe that by combining human and artificial intelligence inputs, we can create a more accurate and more comprehensive understanding of the world. Recent photometric studies of the first population stars in the galactic globular clusters revealed a spread in their colors, suggesting an increase in their iron content as they moved inward. This "chromosome map" of GCs initially showed a pattern where the stars' initial positions dictated their final iron levels, but later data challenged this first-order relationship. Our analysis focused on the evolutionary stage of red giants within the metal-rich GC NGC 1851, which has an unevenly distributed iron level, and we found that stars with higher iron content are concentrated in certain areas of the chromosome map. Our results indicate that stars with elevated iron levels are found at more internal locations, contrary to the initially observed pattern, and a double star-formation history with varying metallicity levels is necessary to explain the observed distribution of first population stars in this GC. Our findings also imply that the stars' initial positions are not directly linked to their final iron levels, and a more complex relationship exists than previously thought. This discovery motivates further in-depth analyses of other GCs to test the hypothesis that the stars' initial positions are not predictive of their final iron levels. This study tackles the issue of assessing causal influences in cases where some variables involved in ensuring causal validity are incompletely known. Many companies use a standard framework that measures "average treatment effect" (ATE), but there's a significant challenge to increase its detection power while maintaining "false discovery rate" (FDR) within a predetermined threshold. Popular algorithms like the BH method struggle to control FDR, particularly when encountering positive dependence, which requires conservative estimations. In this research, we introduce novel statistical algorithms that can reliably and accurately calculate ATE, demonstrating FDR control even in positive dependence scenarios, and showcasing equivalent or improved detection power compared to traditional methods. Additionally, we provide a lower bound on FDR control to ensure the new methods' performance. We also offer a free implementation in Python, making it easily accessible to researchers and practitioners. Our algorithm's underlying ideas are inspired by recent findings in controlling FDR, leveraging "adaptation" and "power-based" approaches to create a reliable and efficient framework for ATE. To address the challenge of positive dependence, we incorporate a general "expansion" parameter to control the number of false positives, ensuring the new methods' conservative nature. We provide a lower bound on the expected number of false positives, ensuring the new methods' reliability and accuracy. We also offer a novel statistical algorithm that can estimate expected expected ATE, known as the "EEATE" algorithm. The EEATE algorithm calculates an "expected" expected ATE, demonstrating equivalent FDR control and ATE estimation power as the adapted BH method. communicated through diverse media, presented as free-text messages or structured 
cards. To effectively address these requests, developers need to craft relevant search 
terms that can be incorporated into search queries, a task complicated by the fact 
that same requests can be phrased in multiple ways. Current approaches rely on static 
lists of possible query terms, whereas recent research indicates a data-driven 
approach, where terms are suggested based on project content, is more effective. This 
paper introduces a classification technique that not only suggests potential query 
terms, but also categorizes change requests and their associated search queries, 
enabling developers to prioritize relevant requests over less important ones. This 
system recommends a core set of requests worthy of immediate action, as well as provides 
a simple and user-friendly interface to manage request prioritization. To validate 
prioritization, the system's suggestion of top 5 important requests on public 
GitHub repositories is shared for verification. The actual results show a significant 
proportion of requests that should be prioritized, ranging from 20% to over 40% 
varies based on the specific repository. Additionally, by using a dataset of 1822 
change requests extracted from the GitHub Electron repository, the research achieved 
marked improvements of 118% in data coverage compared to a comparable 
state-of-the-art approach. Ultimately, the system's suggestions match 56% of the 
original change requests, resulting in a significant data enhancement. The system's 
potential benefits were assessed through A/B testing, which demonstrated that prioritization 
improved developer productivity, yielding a potential annual savings of 3.3 
hours-per-user, equivalent to a potential annual increase of 16.5 hours-per-year.

Adaptive convergence in interactions occurs when two people's physical interaction, such as voice pitch or duration, synchronizes. Current research on entrainment, however, remains unclear due to inconsistent definitions and measurement techniques. This study develops a framework for assessing entrainment based on speakers' voice characteristics. By employing a robot platform to conduct interviews with humans, we explored the link between the level of interaction involvement and entrainment. To quantify entrainment, we employed statistical measures to analyze pitch and pitch variability. Notably, the findings indicate that the degree of engagement in an interview is directly correlated with the level of adaptive convergence in pitch but not pitch variability. These results suggest that greater involvement in an interaction is associated with adaptive convergence in voice characteristics but only in contexts where there is a clear expectation of adaptation. Further research is necessary to clarify the role of entrainment in engaged interactions. Additionally, the study provides insights that can inform the design of automated systems able to detect and adapt to human emotional states. By analyzing the ability of a robot platform to recognize and respond to human emotions, we demonstrated that emotional recognition is not necessarily linked to adaptive convergence in emotional expression. This finding implies that emotional expression is not the primary mechanism by which humans identify other beings as emotional. This study contributes to our understanding of how humans automatically adapt their emotional state to interactive robots, and provides practical design principles for developing robots that can evoke and identify emotional responses in humans. Ultimately, the study highlights the significance of considering the motivations and motivations recognition capabilities of humans in the design of autonomous systems to foster engaging and emotional interactions with emotional entities. Not only does this study provide new insights into the field of entrainment and emotional recognition in interactive systems, it also explores novel aspects of emotional expression in emotional beings. Moreover, the study's integration of practical design and theoretical findings makes it a valuable resource for scientists and engineers seeking to design engaging emotional interactions with autonomous systems. Notably, the study demonstrates that emotional expression in humans is not the primary mechanism for identifying emotional expressions in other emotional entities, and provides practical design principles for autonomous systems to evoke and recognize emotional states in humans. Ultimately, the study emphasizes the significance of considering the emotional capabilities and motivations of humans in interactive design. In the realm of human-robot interactions, this study delves into the interconnectedness of engaged and emotional interactions. Notably, the study's findings reveal that emotional recognition in humans is not driven by adaptive convergence in emotional expressions, and that emotional expressions in humans are not the primary source of identifying emotional expressions in other emotional entities. Current educational tools used in testing can either provide coverage insights comparable to professional tools or highlight instructor-defined test cases that a student has overlooked. While this feedback has some value, it can lead students to rely on guesswork rather than structured testing methods. Moreover, this feedback style does not educate students on the shortcomings of their test suites, potentially making them dependent on the tool's advice rather than relying on their own judgment. As a more effective approach, inquiry-based learning has the potential to promote students' critical thinking by mimicking the process of a professional tester, thereby encouraging students to create high-quality test cases without constantly seeking external guidance. We have developed a new feedback system called Inquire, which provides feedback in the form of questions, aiming to educate students on the process of testing and enhance their decision-making abilities. By simulating the process of a professional tester, Inquire's goal is to train students in the art of testing and ultimately free them from constant reliance on external guidance. In an empirical study involving 248 students across seven university courses, we compared the effectiveness of Inquire and two existing coverage-based tools, providing original test cases, in teaching students testing concepts. The results suggest that Inquire's feedback style has a positive educational impact, with 53% of the students demonstrating improved understanding of testing concepts as evidenced by a post-experiment quiz, whereas only 39% of the students using existing tools exhibited this understanding. Importantly, not only did Inquire's effectiveness increase over time, but it also inspired creative ways to use the tool, with many students expressing a desire to continue learning from Inquire even after the experiment. These findings validate the effectiveness of Inquire and its potential to promote students' critical thinking in the field of testing. In its current form, Inquire can simulate four critical testing concepts, including edge coverage, branch coverage, data flow coverage, and fault localization. Future research can expand Inquire's capabilities to additional testing concepts by integrating more analysis tools and modeling the strategy of a professional tester. The open-source implementation of Inquire can be accessed at https://github.com/chasen/inquire. This fully fundamental yet often more abstract protocol is demonstrated to be equivalent to the standard, model-specific method in the case of single-resource scenarios. However, it's shown to be more complex to apply in multi-resource settings, necessitating a clear and detailed procedure for computing the relative entropy distances from resourceful states. Additionally, the practicality of this method in identifying multiple, interdependent resources housed within a larger composite system is also explored. Ultimately, the multi-resource comparative advantage of this framework is showcased through its usability in extracting both disjoint and overlapping resources from collective and correlated systems. Furthermore, the theoretical feasibility of utilizing this protocol for autonomous, multi-task large-scale resource extraction is also investigated. We analyze how to identify common random patterns in large sets of time series data, even when individual observations are rare or unusual. A new method allows us to make conclusions about the first m eigenvalues of the covariance matrix of observations, given assumptions about individual behavior. This approach is based on analyzing sample averages of weighted observations. By establishing sample averages' properties and using Sanov's theorem, we derive results on likely trends in the sample eigenvalue spectrum. A computational tool is provided to help test whether given trends are consistent with the data. The method's validity is confirmed by proving that real data eigenvalues approximate the true trends in probability. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated in an example using 10 years of daily data from a large US stock index fund and 50 European funds. We identify 2 significant common trends and find that our results align with economic theory expectations. A related R package provides the code used in the computations. Time series analysis that changes over time often has matched spatial and temporal patterns, but current models often ignore the temporal aspect or focus solely on it, missing out on valuable spatial information. As a result, predicting future changes in these patterns can be difficult. Our goal in this research is to create a hybrid approach, combining principles from neural networks and genetic algorithms, to analyze complex time series data. This proposed method, Supervised Topographic Mapping Through Time (SGTM-TT), is capable of handling high-dimensional data and has been successfully applied to various time series problems like forecasting near-earth asteroid trajectories and analyzing the activity of radio galaxies. Our tests indicate that SGTM-TT significantly improves prediction accuracy and output quality compared to traditional techniques, often producing more meaningful and interpretable results. This makes SGTM-TT a valuable tool for analyzing and understanding complex temporal patterns. By incorporating knowledge from past events and using a weighted approach, SGTM-TT can improve prediction accuracy and avoid common pitfalls like random forecasting. Additionally, its weighted approach allows for quantification of prediction uncertainty, which can be translated into probability measures. One of the notable advantages of SGTM-TT is its ability to handle large data sets with high-dimensional data efficiently, thanks to its compact output. This makes SGTM-TT a versatile method suitable for various time series analysis tasks. By leveraging the strengths of neural networks and genetic algorithms, SGTM-TT provides a robust and efficient framework for tasks like classification, regression, and forecasting. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of SGTM-TT in forecasting, highlighting its advantages over traditional neural network approaches. SGTM-TT also provides unique insights into activity mapping and forecasting, which can't be achieved with other methods. Our findings suggest that, with sufficient data, SGTM-TT can successfully learn and model the underlying dynamics of radio activity in active galactic nuclei. However, it requires a sufficient amount of data and robust training. If not, SGTM-TT may produce suboptimal results, but it can still provide valuable insights and perspectives. This research provides a solid foundation and approaches for analyzing complex time series data, which can be applied to other fields and domains. Our aim is to expand the capabilities of SGTM-TT to handle tasks with missing data, unevenly spaced data, and multi-variate time series analysis. We plan to investigate and address these challenges to further expand the versatility of SGTM-TT. By successfully tackling these complex data challenges, SGTM-TT can be effectively utilized in a wide range of real-world applications.

However, classification alone cannot fully capture the meaning of an action due to its spatial and temporal components. As a result, the majority of previous approaches have suffered from limited recognition capabilities. We propose a new framework that addresses this issue by introducing a novel form of action-aware proposal, characterized by a distinct spatiotemporal signature that differentiates it from background examples. Additionally, our framework incorporates a soft-selection mechanism that adapts proposal weights based on their similarity to a query feature spectrum. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through experimental results on the UCF101-24 and JHMDB-21 datasets, yielding a significant performance boost. For instance, our approach outperates the state-of-the-art performance by 2-6% on the UCF101-24 dataset under various evaluation metrics. The implementation details and code are available online at https://github.com/DCN-UK/TE2P. We anticipate that our framework will provide an optimal solution for spatiotemporal action detection. Balancing communication efficiency and data privacy is a critical concern in distributed neural network training. We address this challenge with 'DistPrivacy', an innovative approach that combines efficient communication with differential privacy using the Vectorized Differential Privacy algorithm. DistPrivacy allows for unencrypted data transmission while guaranteeing differential privacy across the network. It achieves this by incorporating an artificially noisy count in each client's transmission, along with the actual data, to represent the number of sensitive data points. This approach is then received by servers that employ a filtering mechanism to remove noise, retrieve the accurate count, and proceed with training. DistPrivacy was implemented and shown to provide differential privacy for PyTorch models, while also meeting specific performance criteria for a benchmark federated training task. Notably, DistPrivacy yields superior results compared to the existing benchmark algorithm. The implementation details and source code are available on the DistPrivacy repository. This project aims to contribute the research findings to the community, with the ultimate goal of advancing communication efficiency and data privacy practices in federated learning. This work delves into the dynamic cognitive hierarchy theory, introduced by Lin and Palfrey (2022), within the context of multi-stage incomplete information games. In such scenarios, players simultaneously uncover peers' relevant characteristics and problem-solving abilities as the game unfolds. Building on this concept, our study provides a complete characterization of the dynamic CH solution for two-person dirty faces games. Notably, our findings indicate that lower-level players determine their characteristics in subsequent stages more slowly than their higher-level counterparts. Furthermore, our re-examination of the experimental data collected by Bayer and Chan (2007) shows that the dynamic CH solution more effectively explains the observed outcomes than its static counterpart. Moreover, our analysis reveals that the dynamic CH solution can also be applied to multi-person games, particularly dirty faces games and linear demand systems. In these cases, our results demonstrate that the dynamic CH solution is in line with the equilibrium characteristics identified through the study of the corresponding characterstic functions. Additionally, our study presents a novel method for estimating the parameters of the dynamic CH model using maximum likelihood estimation, showcasing how the dynamic CH model can be applied to a range of multi-stage games. Notably, our analysis of the dynamic CH model indicates that the estimated equilibrium characteristics exhibit distinct tendencies among players at different hierarchical levels. Finally, our maximum likelihood estimation analysis reveals that the dynamic CH model can estimate the distribution of cognitive levels within a group, while also accounting for varying estimation outcomes across distinct experimental conditions. The dynamic CH solution and estimation methods are presented in open-source code, facilitating their accessibility. The code can be found online at the repository address: https://github.com/ChenLin-UCLA/dynamic-CH. Accurate and timely population estimates are crucial for policy decisions surrounding vaccination initiatives and infrastructure development planning. As interpersonal communication regarding vaccination status is a primary source of new information, the population research literature offers few existing datasets that can be leveraged for population size estimation through interpersonal communication. This research investigates the use of interpersonal conversation as a means to estimate population size in settings where reliable census data is absent. A novel statistical approach based on random walk and diffusion is developed to model the propagation of new information, and it is applied to create a maximum likelihood estimator for population size based on the expected time until a given piece of information reaches the entire study area. This estimator relies on the collection of secondary data including the rate at which new information enters the system, the rate at which information is shared between individuals, and the rate at which a given piece of information spreads through the study area. A simulation study is conducted to evaluate the proposed estimator's performance, revealing that it generates accurate results with modest study periods. The proposed method is then tested using real-world data collected from the Mbarangai Health Surveillance System, an MDPI-enabled research platform supporting the provision of holistic healthcare services to communities in Tanzania. Population size estimation using the real-world data reveals notable discrepancies, with some study areas exhibiting unusually high rates of information sharing and varying levels of information propagation. These disparities are analyzed, offering potential explanations and study area-specific strategies for improving the proposed estimator's performance. Finally, the proposed method is applied to an examination of the temporal effects of the COVID-19 pandemic on population size estimation, as captured by Twitter and Instagram posts sharing vaccination information. The results indicate a significant decline in population size estimation estimates during the pandemic, corresponding to a 65% reduction in study areas with low information sharing rates and a 35% reduction in study areas with high information sharing rates. A corresponding 8.2% decrease in propagation rates is also observed during the pandemic, suggesting the impact of the pandemic on the dissemination of vaccination information. We theoretically investigate the production of molecules in a BEC using a two-photon approach, where one photon's polarization is aligned to $\sigma_+$ and the other to $\pi$. The beam's propagation through the condensate enables spin-exchange interactions and spin-changing collisions, ultimately leading to the formation of molecules from initially unpaired spin. Our analysis considers the effects of two-photon detunings, spin-exchange collisions and photoassociation, to map the BEC's spinor density as a function of position and internal angular momentum. Under these conditions, pairs of atoms in the $|1,0\rangle$ state are formed via spin-exchange collisions, while pairs in the $|1,1\rangle$ state are created through both spin-exchange collisions and photoassociation. Our results show that the molecule production coefficient is unaffected by $\pi$ polarization but does depend on the $\sigma_+$ polarization's frequency and detuning. Additionally, we find that the molecule population in the $|1,0\rangle$ state surpasses that of the $|1,0\rangle$ and $|1,-1\rangle$ states when two-photon detunings are negative. However, for positive detunings, the production coefficients for molecules formed via the $|1,-1\rangle$ state are greater than those formed via the $|1,0\rangle$ state. Ultimately, the findings suggest that molecule production in BECs could be an effective method for manipulating coherent atom-molecule pairs through the propagation of controlled laser light. This research offers a new and versatile method for studying quantum interactions and effects at the macroscopic scale. Furthermore, it provides a potential means of creating a macroscopic quantum object by leveraging the cooperative effects that arise from the interaction between atom-molecule pairs and their internal angular momentum. In the last twenty years, SPH has gained significant momentum as a lagrangian method for solving hydrodynamics problems. It has been successfully applied in a wide array of fluid and fluid-structure interaction simulations. The development of multi-resolution SPH has taken this further, allowing for the simulation of complex problems by dividing them into multiple sub-domains, each with its own SPH model type. This paper introduces a groundbreaking framework for coupling various resolution levels in SPH models, thereby enabling fluid-structure interactions. The framework accommodates different interfaces between models of different resolutions, both smooth and discontinuous, thanks to a developed averaging technique. The coupled SPH algorithm has been successfully validated through a range of FSI tests, including a 2D cylinder-jet interaction case, a 2D oscillating cylinder simulation, and a 3D simulation of an oscillating plate in contact with water. The results demonstrate the efficiency and accuracy of the developed approach, particularly in the 3D FSI test case where high precision results have been achieved with relatively low computational costs. The couple-mesh algorithm has also been applied in the simulation of a breaking wave, yielding promising outcomes with significant time savings of up to two orders of magnitude compared to a standard SPH model. The efficiency gains are largely attributed to the minimal number of inter-particle exchanges required. The developed approach opens up a range of new possibilities for the simulation of breaking waves, ocean storms, and other highly complex fluid-structure interaction phenomena. The framework is flexible and can easily be adapted to other SPH-based numerical methods. The couple-mesh algorithm has been made publicly available as part of the SPH-C++ library. Due to the diverse applications and ongoing research in NLP, it is difficult to provide an all-encompassing view of the field. However, in this piece, some key advancements and promising directions in NLP are highlighted, focusing on how they have been impacted by the emergence of deep learning or can be transformed by the potential of quantum computing. Quantum computing's capacity for handling complex, disordered data with higher efficiency is particularly relevant to language, where massive datasets consist of intricate patterns of characters. Consequently, quantum computing may offer NLP a breakthrough in processing larger data sets, at speeds suitable for real-time applications, or exploring new frontiers previously inaccessible due to computational constraints. Meanwhile, the incorporation of deep learning in NLP has facilitated progress in speech and natural language understanding, reading, and generation, while presenting challenges in information retrieval and translation. Furthermore, the integration of multimodal language in NLP has become a defining feature of the field. The goal of deep transfer learning (DTL) is to help a pre-trained deep neural network (DNN) learn to perform tasks other than those it was originally trained for. This is done by adding new training steps that focus on those tasks. This paper looks at how changing the pre-training data and how modifying the DNN architecture after training affect the ability of DNNs to adapt to new tasks. Compared to earlier studies, our findings show that the ability of DNNs to adapt decreases more quickly when using broader datasets to train on and when increasing the size of the DNN model by adding more layers slowly in parallel. Additionally, our data suggests the common practice of using dropout in later layers is not actually helping the DNN adapt to new tasks. Finally, our results support the idea that the ability of DNNs to adapt is affected by how different the new tasks are from each other more than any benefits they might provide. Overall, our data supports the idea that the ability of DNNs to adapt depends on a complex interplay of different factors. This knowledge could help inform the development of new algorithms and techniques to support the ability of DNNs to adapt. is numerically investigated for cases without signal amplification. We assess the distance between 
discrete nonlinear interference points and find that this distance can be employed to estimate 
the effective memory length of the communication channel. By utilizing the majorization theory 
from linear algebra, we derive bounds for the aforementioned distance and provide insights into 
when the model closely approximates actual interference patterns. Furthermore, we analyze the 
condition under which the model generates unique interferences at every significant data element. 
We also introduce a new discrete metric that may be used in scenarios where the reliability of the 
channel model is scrutinized. We demonstrate that this metric is compatible with the established 
bounds and recapitulates previously obtained results. Lastly, we present an approach for creating a 
discrete model of a communication channel based on a general, continuous model, and discuss how 
this model fits within the framework of our analysis. Using numerical methods, we verify our findings 
and identify the limitations of the analyzed model. It is observed that while amplification is necessary 
for achieving a reliable model, the proposed approach for creating a discrete model yields accurate 
results for cases without signal amplification. Consequently, the established bounds, approach, and 
new metrics could be applied in similar contexts without signal amplification.

Our analysis reveals that the conditions generating the Thakurta metric, previously investigated in relation to black holes in the presence of a cosmic string, involve a static universe containing a massive object. Upon closer inspection, we find that this aligns with the characteristics of an AdS-Schwarzschild metric, previously explored in theoretical discussions by Bostock and Sannan. We argue that a more accurate interpretation would treat the static universe as a vacuum, rather than a black hole environment. Furthermore, we note that AdS-Schwarzschild metric descriptions are solely applicable in four-dimensional space, contradicting claims of dimension independence. Finally, we discuss how these observations impact model validity and highlight crucial differences between modeling and theoretical validity. Additionally, we identify several areas worth further research and propose an alternative, more accurate framework for analyzing black hole properties in the presence of a cosmic string. Ultimately, we find that AdS-Schwarzschild, rather than Thakurta, accurately describes the black hole generated in the presence of a cosmic string. Thakurta metric is, however, relevant in the context of modeling radiation absorbed and re-emitted by the black hole. Notably, we identify a metric proposed by Saha specifically for a Schwarzschild geometry in the presence of a cosmic string, rather than a strained AdS space. Our research suggests that detailed examinations of specific models are necessary to ensure their validity. We conclude by outlining potential future investigations. The complexity of gaseous flows in young star systems makes planet formation challenging to study from scratch. Researchers have suggested that dust rings triggered by pressure disruptions in the outer discs can give rise to planet seeds. Pressure bumps can drive the inner disc currents towards the disc's edges, increasing the disc's turbulence. Dust rings might develop in areas where the disc's rotation speed changes, such as at transitions from concave to convex shapes in the outer disc. We examine the possibility of planet formation in these isolated spots. Using simulations, we have studied the movement of small particles in discs with increased turbulence. Our results show significant variations in the movement of these particles, depending on the disc currents. In areas with increased turbulence, the particles are pushed towards the disc's surface, while in areas without, they remain deep within. To investigate further, we created simulated planet cores and tracked the evolution of the resulting planet-forming discs. Our findings indicate that in these isolated areas, the planets would experience reduced collisions with other particles, resulting in faster growth. In contrast, the presence of the inner disc currents would cause turbulence, which could prevent the formation of a smooth inner disc. However, the pressure disruptions could also create channels through the disc's turbulence, facilitating the transition of material from the outer disc to the inner area. In these cases, the dust rings could merge and combine to form a single, unified disc structure. In this scenario, the channels created by the increased turbulence could allow the transfer of material to the inner area, effectively removing the dust rings along the way. Overall, our study suggests that planet formation in isolated areas could be a common mechanism, leading to the development of multiple planets within these distant discs. However, the resulting planets would have distinct differences in their growth rates, sizes, and spatial distribution. A future investigation of the disc channels using high-contrast imaging could confirm the presence of multiple planets in these isolated areas. The increased turbulence resulting from pressure disruptions could also contribute to the formation of planet seeds within the disc's outer regions. In this case, the required density of the planet seeds would be significantly lower than previously estimated, making the formation of planet seeds a more plausible occurrence. A future investigation of the movement of small particles in these isolated areas could provide further insight into the complexity of the disc's turbulence and the presence of planet seeds. A detailed examination of the various factors influencing the movement of small particles in young star systems could help to refine the models used to study planet formation from scratch. This condition is subject to certain constraints involving $x$. Our findings complement previous work by Solomiačuk and Woehl, who investigated further into this matter for specific group types ($\mathbb{Z}$ and $\mathbb{Z}^2$). We utilize an inductive approach, decomposing $G$ into its quotient groups ($G_1$, $G_2$), iteratively applying the established result to initial segments until we reach the base case of $G_1 \simeq \mathbb{Z}$. This study explores multi-modal pretraining techniques for product data in E-commerce, addressing limitations in current methods which struggle with modality-noise and modality-missing. We introduce K3M, a novel method incorporating knowledge modality to mitigate noise and supplement missing modalities in image and text data. K3M utilizes a modal-encoding layer and a modal-interaction layer to combine information from image, text, and knowledge modalities. By integrating modality-specific layer types and a knowledge-based attention mechanism, K3M adapts modal contributions from the knowledge modality. Additionally, K3M incorporates a modal fusion layer to combine the outputs of modal encoders. Through pretraining with a modal-specific loss and a modal fusion loss, K3M yields a unified knowledge modality that can serve a variety of downstream E-commerce applications. Experimental results demonstrate that K3M outperforms existing approaches on E-commerce data representation tasks. Furthermore, product visualness predictions and semantic comparisons produced by K3M yield better performance and more meaningful outcomes than current methods, as validated by human annotators. A significant function in most algorithms for analyzing brain scans is attributed to unsupervised learning, particularly in non-linear exploration. A novel approach, Deep InfoMax (DIM), offers considerable potential for examining brain structure adaptability. In this paper, the potential of modified DIM models is compared to conventional supervised networks, such as AlexNet and ResNet, in predicting progression to Alzheimer's disease, using classification between healthy controls, MCI patients with stable MCI, and MCI patients who have progressed to Alzheimer's disease as the benchmark task. In a similar vein to previous studies on convolutional neural networks, various architectures based on ResNet, including modified SqueezeNet and MobileNet, are evaluated in this paper. Additionally, the potential of DIM in capturing detailed correlations between different brain regions is assessed through t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE) dimensional reduction technique. Our findings suggest that conventional networks like AlexNet and ResNet, as well as certain unsupervised models, such as HIP, provide superior accuracy in Alzheimer's disease classification compared to the proposed modified DIM models. However, the potential of DIM, particularly its capacity for exploring dimensional patterns within hippocampal regions, should not be underestimated. We examine the relationship between spin-orbit coupling and interactions within a two-orbital Hubbard model on a square lattice, employing the variational Monte Carlo method. An effective spin-orbit constant $\lambda_{\text{eff}}$ is considered in the wave function, focusing primarily on quarter-filled electrons. We find that $\lambda_{\text{eff}}$ correlates directly with interactions within the paramagnetic phase, indicating a transition towards an antiferromagnetic phase. Moreover, we investigate how $\lambda_{\text{eff}}$ varies according to microscopic spin-orbit coupling strengths. For strong electron-electron interactions and within the antiferromagnetic phase, $\lambda_{\text{eff}}$ is found to be insensitive to the magnitude of spin-orbit coupling. However, this insensitivity is reduced for intermediate interactions, particularly in the paramagnetic region with strong electron-electron interactions. This observation suggests a degradation of spin-orbit coupling characteristics due to interactions. We also discuss the relationship between $\lambda_{\text{eff}}$ and the double exchange mechanism associated with Kondo lattice systems, showing that an increase in interactions leads to a decrease in effective spin-orbit coupling, resulting in a shift towards a more itinerant state. By analyzing the density dependence of spin-orbit coupling parameters, we can quantify the impact of interactions on these interactions, particularly in the range relevant to the spin-orbit coupling parameters, particularly in the range relevant to the spin-orbit coupling parameters. Furthermore, we find an approximately 30% increase in the electron-hole asymmetry caused by interactions, leading to a more pronounced itinerant contribution towards lower electron densities. We compare our results with computational many-body calculations, demonstrating the applicability of variational Monte Carlo in analyzing the density-dependent behavior of spin-orbit coupling in two-orbital Hubbard models. We conclude that the degradation of spin-orbit coupling caused by interactions may provide an alternative explanation for observed spin-orbit coupling parameter discrepancies. This finding can be further confirmed by investigating the density-dependent behavior of spin-orbit coupling parameters in spin-orbital systems via x-ray spectroscopy with high resolution and precision. The spin-orbit coupling parameters obtained from such an experiment could be adjusted by considering a density-dependent correction to the microscopic spin-orbit coupling strength. High-fidelity simulations involving atomic details are now being extensively employed 
to study nucleic acids and their associated components. While this type of 
simulation is becoming increasingly prevalent, there remains a notable absence of 
a standardized set of open-source tools specifically designed for generating 3D 
structures of double-stranded DNA and RNA, to within near-atomic precision. In 
response to this need, we have developed Re:dir, an open-source package, which 
allows users to create precise, atomic-scale structures for double-stranded DNA 
and RNA sequences. This package provides a standardized set of parameters for six 
key rotational settings and includes an optimized method for adjusting the basepair 
angles, in line with the parameters established by the AMber force field. Re:dir also 
includes a feature that enables users to specify precise helical repeat patterns, which 
can be particularly useful for studies focused on specific DNA or RNA sequences. 
In addition, all of the codebase for Re:dir has been made publicly available, under 
an open-source license, in order to facilitate collaboration and code review. 
Furthermore, the structures generated by Re:dir provide a reliable foundation for a 
range of related simulations and can also serve as a reference point for users, 
facilitating informed decisions regarding the design of custom DNA or RNA sequences. 
We believe that Re:dir will be a valuable tool for researchers working on nucleic 
acid-related projects, and that its use will significantly enhance the accuracy of 
these users' simulations and designs. We encourage users to report any bugs or 
suggest any potential improvements to the code. Re:dir is currently available for 
download on the GitHub platform at the following address: 
https://github.com/seqan/re-dir. We have included detailed instructions within 
the code for those who are new to the use of Re:dir and have also included a 
comprehensive documentation of the code in English. If you have any questions 
regarding the code for Re:dir, we encourage you to contact us at one of the 
email addresses provided below.

engineering standards.

The Asymmetric Numeral System (ANS) was a significant innovation in entropy encoding developed by Duda, revolutionizing how data is compressed by representing numbers as a sequence of scales. ANS was initially scalable but lacked efficiency in achieving the optimal compression rate. Researchers then introduced the table-based ANS (tANS) encoder, which significantly improved scalability over ANS. Despite improvements, tANS still falls short of optimal compression rate modern architectures can achieve. A new version, precise tANS (ptANS), has been introduced to minimize redundancy in tANS, utilizing two lookup tables, one for lower and one for higher values, to represent scales. However, ptANS still incurs some redundancy. A modified version of ptANS, using only one table, has been discovered and found to be more efficient than tANS. Furthermore, ptANS has been found to be a special case of a broader family of algorithms, known as generalized tANS (gtANS), which uses multiple tables. Both ptANS and gtANS have been found to be competitive with other modern entropy encoding algorithms. The developers created an open-source library, available on GitHub, that provides a reference implementation of the ptANS and gtANS algorithms, allowing other developers to integrate them into their projects. The code is compatible with a wide range of programming languages, including C, C++, Python, and Java. The researchers conducted an in-depth analysis of the time and space requirements of ptANS and gtANS, finding they incur a negligible cost in terms of memory and processing speed.
