In a forthcoming letter, we examine how sensitive the Two Higgs Doublet Model is to a crucial parameter, $m_{12}$, which can be adjusted to accommodate a variety of observed Higgs boson properties. To do this, we explore how this model performs when using several popular Higgs and related particle constraints, specifically focusing on the following aspects: 

- Higgs couplings with standard model particles, particularly the Higgs-strahlung process
- Associated production of a Z boson and a Higgs boson
- Decays of heavy fermions
- Lightest supersymmetric particle (neutralino) direct and indirect detection

Our research shows that certain observables are highly sensitive to $m_{12}$ changes, particularly in scenarios where one Higgs doublet dominates the model's vacuum. However, in a scenario where both Higgs doublets coexist, $m_{12}$'s impact is more subtle. To accurately understand the origins of anomalies potentially arising from this model, it will be essential to carefully analyze these constraints and identify any remaining discrepancies that cannot be explained by $m_{12}$'s variation. 

Additionally, we identify parameter regions where $m_{12}$'s changes can make the model compatible with all examined constraints under both competitive and collaborative vacua assumptions. However, these solutions raise questions about CP-violation searches, as they may be beyond reach of upcoming facilities. 

In conclusion, our research emphasizes the need for further investigations into $m_{12}$'s variations in the Two Higgs Doublet Model's effects on related particle phenomena, particularly in the competition between collaborative and competitive vacua assumptions. To effectively analyze these phenomena, it is recommended to use multi-observable approaches that account for various Higgs and related particle constraints. 

Our research also includes supplementary material with detailed discussions and tables examining how certain Higgs and related particle constraints perform against data, as well as a comprehensive comparison of the model's performance under all examined constraints in the competition between collaborative and competitive assumptions.

We examine the RDF data exchange process based on relational data, constrained by Shape Expression schema. Our research involves addressing two critical issues: first, determining the feasibility of solutions for source data instances; and second, developing a single comprehensive solution that represents all possible outcomes. To achieve this, we incorporate typed IRI constructors to form RDF IRIs from relational values and translate Shape Expression constraints into target dependencies. Additionally, we have identified certain data exchange settings as 'key-covered', a determinable property that ensures consistency. Furthermore, we found this condition necessary and sufficient for a specific subset of weakly-recursive Shape Expression constraints to have universal solutions. Our findings build on existing research by generalizing the 'universal relation' assumption to any arbitrary source data instance. As a result, our data exchange process can accommodate various source data instances. Moreover, a particular instance is valid if the resulting RDF data satisfies the given Shape Expression constraints, and we used Turovsky's definition to establish this connection. Furthermore, our data exchange process is efficient and can be implemented in polynomial time. This is particularly notable given the high complexity of optimizing solutions in general RDF data exchange processes. We extended our research to include RDF data exchange with certain recursive constraints, identifying limitations and proving that certain properties are both necessary and sufficient for a specific subset of such constraints. Our findings also reveal that certain types of constraints cannot be optimized universally. However, we were able to develop a specialized data exchange process for a specific subset with bounded recursion depth. This process is both feasible and can be completed in polynomial time. To achieve this, we first converted the recursive constraints into their equivalent relational forms using a recently developed method. This process ensures that the resulting RDF data satisfies the given constraints. Finally, we used typed IRI constructors to form RDF IRIs from relational values and develop a specialized data exchange process for this particular application. Our process is both feasible and can be completed in polynomial time. This is particularly notable given the high complexity of optimizing solutions in general RDF data exchange processes. Our research is the first to address RDF data exchange based on relational data, constrained by Shape Expression schema, and is applicable to various real-world scenarios where data needs to be converted between different formats. To facilitate the understanding of our research, we have included several practical examples that illustrate the key concepts and findings of our work. These examples highlight critical issues and provide insights into the complexities of specialized data exchange processes. Our example scenarios cover different constraint types and settings, and is particularly notable in showing cases where certain constraints cannot be optimized universally.

Pre-trained language models possess knowledge of the world, which can be leveraged to enhance tasks unrelated to the model's original training. In the realm of NLP, multiple syntactic parsing representations have been developed over the years. We propose a novel approach to distill the language model's knowledge into a basic syntactic parsing form utilizing self-attention and linear projection matrices. Notably, the linear projection matrices for self-attention queries and keys hold crucial information for parsing the structure of sentences into subword units. We have implemented this method using the German BERT model, transforming it into the BERT-SP, and evaluated it against the recently introduced DEP parser. The results indicate that BERT-SP achieves superior performance, especially in parsing sentences with uncommon structures, surpassing the state-of-the-art in 88.9% of German Test Cases. Furthermore, we have incorporated an unsupervised procedure for extracting subword-boundary parsing representations, leading to a significant improvement in the BERT-SP model. The unsupervised BERT-SP outperforms its supervised counterpart in 93.6% of Test Cases, while also surpassing the state-of-the-art in 91.7% of cases. The BERT-SP model, along with its unsupervised variant, can be accessed on GitHub. We aim to introduce a standard representation of the BERT model as a parser, similar to the standard representations of ELMo and ULMFiT in the language models paradigm. We believe this representation, along with its unsupervised variant, can serve as a starting point or basis for further development in the self-attention mechanism. We plan to make an in-depth investigation into the properties of the BERT model in the context of syntactic parsing in the future. If this work is accepted, we will remove the BERT-SP model and replace it with the actual implementation, ensuring that the new version attracts the same number of views as the original. By sharing our code, we aim to enable the replication of our results and allow researchers to build upon our work. Additionally, we provide insights into the potential limitations of the BERT-SP model, which can be viewed as a basic syntactic parsing representation. In the knowledge transfer paradigm, we believe the BERT-SP model represents the smallest possible unit of information that can be transferred from the BERT model to the parsing paradigm. The accuracy of speech-based applications heavily relies on high-quality Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR). Despite having access to advanced ASR tools, the lack of sufficient training data in certain languages hinders their optimal performance. This study aims to address this issue by utilizing existing resources in ASR to mitigate the data scarcity in large-scale ASR modeling for languages with limited data available. We achieved this by incorporating spoken data from Wikipedia into the training process, effectively expanding our data pool. Our experiments focused on German ASR and involved two distinct training approaches: direct training with the enriched data and incremental training, gradually adding data to the model, mimicking a real-world scenario. Notably, training with the Wikipedia data significantly improved the model's performance, surpassing even that of a state-of-the-art model trained with extensive, manually transcribed data. Furthermore, the study shows that incremental training does not provide additional benefits over direct training with the enriched data, suggesting an efficient method to address data scarcity in ASR modeling for low-resource languages. This research offers valuable insights and practical solutions to combat the challenges posed by data scarcity in ASR. Additionally, the spoken data from Wikipedia provides a valuable resource for languages with limited data, serving as an important step in developing ASR technologies for those languages. Given its utility, this data is recommended to be collected for languages with insufficient ASR datasets. Moreover, the study's findings have been made publicly available, providing a basis for future research. This paper demonstrates a Faber-Krahn type inequality for the first eigenvalue 
of the Hermite operator when subject to Robin boundary conditions, showing 
that the optimal configuration is a half-space, and achieves equality if the 
Robin coefficient is non-negative. A similar result is also obtained for the 
second eigenvalue under certain conditions on the Robin coefficient. These 
results are validated using a variational approach based on a weighted Poincaré 
inequality. Furthermore, the methods employed in this study may be adapted to 
examine eigenvalues of other Sturm-Liouville operators. Additionally, the study 
demonstrates that certain conditions on the Robin coefficient are necessary for 
the second eigenvalue inequality to hold. This investigation may be seen as a 
extension of prior research focusing on the first eigenvalue under Robin 
boundary conditions, and may also be utilized to examine eigenvalues in 
microelectronic contexts. A supplementary paper will delve deeper into these 
microelectronic applications. 

Key words: Robin boundary conditions, Faber-Krahn inequality, Hermite operator, 
Robin parameter, optimal configuration, second eigenvalue.

Deep neural networks, known for their robust performance across various tasks, are often difficult to understand. This interpretability issue severely hampers their use in critical fields such as medical imaging. A promising approach, neural tangent kernel, offers some level of interpretation by mirroring a kernel machine's properties. In an attempt to enhance classification and layer understanding, we've merged NT-K with kernelized layers. For layer combination, we've introduced a new method that maintains NT-K's layer and model interpretation. To prevent a significant loss in model performance, we've adapted a technique that adaptively balances NT-K and traditional deep neural network layers. We've successfully demonstrated these improvements on a range of datasets, including CIFAR-Net, CIFAR100, and MiniImageNet. Additionally, we've observed that merging NT-K layers leads to lower memory usage and faster training times. You can access the merged code at: https://github.com/AdityaCr/NtkResNet. A more refined NTKResNet variant, incorporating pre-training and hard sampling, is available at: https://github.com/AdityaCr/ResNtkSota. This variant yields state-of-the-art results on datasets such as CIFAR, ImageNet, and CIFFER, significantly outperforming NTKResNet in terms of training speed and memory requirements. Furthermore, we've observed that pre-training and refining the model leads to more consistent gradient flows, and as a result, better model generalisation. Despite extensive research on topological systems, classifying non-Hermitian one-dimensional systems remains an unresolved issue. By applying a generalized extension of the Kitaev-Fidkowski classification method, we have developed a comprehensive topological classification of non-Bayer-Friedmann insulators and superconductors, allowing for general correlation between sub-systems. Our findings significantly deviate from those of Hermitian systems when sub-system correlations exist, indicating the presence of various novel topological insulator/superconductor phases. Notably, we have identified an exotic phase displaying "folding" topological classification at double the winding number constraint of the system's boundary mode(s), which occurs regardless of the strength and nature of on-site correlations. Our work provides a systematic framework for classifying topological insulators and superconductors beyond Hermitian systems. Furthermore, it paves the way for the analysis of non-Hermitian topological systems with higher spatial dimensions. The predicted phases can potentially be observed in active/active lattice systems. Building upon previous research, we have extended the classification to active/active lattices with various phases, including a unique phase displaying "multi-mode" behavior. The findings from both studies are compatible and can be mapped onto each other. Our work may inspire further experimental and theoretical investigations into the fascinating realm of non-Hermitian topological systems. Our current research builds upon our earlier findings where we identified acoustic characteristics essential to synthetic speech perception as warm and competent. We now aim to explore how these derived vocal attributes contribute to their creation. We've specifically examined the potential of spectral flux, F1 mean, F2 mean, and their combinations in fostering warmth in synthetic speech within the context of speech synthesis. We present a multi-layer quiver in this paper, using which we can build a higher dimension (n+1) algebras of infinite complexity from a given n-dimensional algebra. This process enables the creation of such algebras in the form of matrix and tensor products of lower-dimensional algebras. Consequently, it results in equivalence of module categories for certain types of quivers and n-dimensional algebras. Building upon previous research by Ringel, we generalize his findings to establish a connection between these quivers and n-dimensional algebras. Furthermore, we define n-dimensional algebras as representations of multi-layer quivers and prove that a full subcategory of module representations is closed under taking extensions and limits. Moreover, it is linearly ordered in the case of n=2, which generalizes a finding by Asano and Kitano. Additionally, we introduce the concept of n-dimensional slices of infinite complexity and prove that these are equivalent to representations of multi-layer quivers. Furthermore, we establish the equivalence of co-slices of higher dimension (n+1) to representations of quivers with n-dimensional co-coordinates. Lastly, we outline several open questions related to multi-layer quivers and n-dimensional algebras.

A starting point for understanding this inherited information is a measure of entropy, which represents disorder in a system, increasing over time unless counteracted by its production rate. Research has shown that organized patterns only last as long as their entropy production rate outweighs the system's overall rate. In this study, the interplay between a system's localized connections and global trends is explored using complex networks. Simulations show that areas with high production rates are more likely to appear in systems with localized connections, rather than those with random or global trends. These findings suggest that Earth's evolutionary path has been shaped by regions with high production rates, leading to an increased likelihood of lasting connections over time. These regions may also play a crucial role in pre-biotic and biological processes, making them a significant factor in the emergence of inherited information. Quantum particles experiencing tunneling can be studied through the Larmor precession in a magnetic field, which measures the tunneling time. This concept has sparked debate and controversy. A numerical and experimental investigation conducted using a double-slit setup found no evidence of a tunneling time related to the Larmor precession frequency. This conclusion holds for the entire tunneling process as well as specific portions. Ignoring the initial and final phases of tunneling, the Larmor precession frequency remains constant. These findings highlight the intricacies of extracting tunneling times from the Larmor precession frequency. (Figure adapted from J. Appl. Phys. 116, 104707 (2014).)  See also arXiv:1409.7622 and arXiv:1409.7623 for additional context and related research.

This research presents a novel Proportional-Integral-Derivative-Accelerated (PIDA) control strategy, integrating a derivative filter, to enhance quadcopter stability in chaotic and unpredictable flight conditions. The mathematical framework is established based on a highly accurate model that effectively accounts for non-linearities, uncertainty, and interdependence. The integration of measurement noise and uncertainty can lead to flight instability, and our proposed controller paired with a heuristic Genetic Filter (GF) addresses these issues, achieving a significant reduction in root mean square error. The PIDA controller is tuned using a Sensitivity Analysis technique, and the combination of a GF and PIDA control structure demonstrate improved performance, with the GF acting as a disturbance observer to refine the PIDA's estimation and feedback signals. The application of the GF-PIDA control structure yields a substantial reduction in root mean square error, specifically a ~46.56% decrease compared to the PIDA structure alone, and a ~51.51% decrease compared to the PI controller. Furthermore, the GF-PIDA control structure exhibits more accurate tracking capabilities, with a coarser but still acceptable phase shift of approximately 0.15 radians. The proposed GF-PIDA method exhibits superior performance, outperforming the robust control structure control method and achieving a more accurate comparison with experimental results. Importantly, the proposed control structure does not require bounding the disturbances, and can effectively account for time-varying parameters, ensuring robust stability. The efficacy of the GF-PIDA control structure is confirmed through numerous simulation trials. Overall, the integration of a GF with a PIDA control structure results in a more accurate and robust approach to quadcopter attitude control. The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) is one of the primary detectors in the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN, tracking particle interactions resulting from high-energy collisions. As part of the CMS system, the silicon pixel detector forms the innermost component responsible for navigating the trajectory of particles. Although initially operational between 2009 and 2016, it has been replaced with an upgraded variant in 2017. During a preceding period of shutdown for the LHC, an upgraded sensor layer was implemented. In this study, simulation models were created for the upgraded sensor, incorporating data from layer-hit simulations, to calculate detection efficiency, efficiency in locating hits, and signal-to-noise ratios. These parameters were then compared to actual measurements following the 2017 upgrade. Hit efficiency and efficiency in locating hits showed comparable values with the original and demonstrated sensitivity to minimal signal levels of around 600 electrons. Epidemics on massive contact networks with millions of individuals pose significant challenges for analysis and containment due to their immense scale. However, for networks that can be segmented into groups, describing the spread of an outbreak between these segments is significantly more manageable. Typically, studies have relied on dividing individuals into clusters based on their transmission history, but these classifications often lack relevance to the early stages of an outbreak. By disregarding this limitation, researchers have previously defined clusters based on random contact observations, yet these clusters lack a direct connection to the transmission history. We present a new, data-driven approach that leverages machine learning to identify and label clusters in a network, allowing for accurate segmentation. This method is demonstrated on a well-documented outbreak in a close-contact setting, revealing clustered arrangements that correlate with factors such as living arrangements and work schedule. By segmenting the population in such a manner, researchers gain the ability to study the movement of an outbreak between discrete groups, making epidemic analysis and control more tractable. This segmentation also enables the development of targeted interventions tailored to the characteristics of these clusters. As data becomes increasingly available, the segmentation of population subsets is set to play a vital role in the analysis and control of epidemics. With the proposed approach, researchers now have a flexible tool for producing meaningful and relevant clusters, both in offline investigations and real-time investigations. We anticipate that this segmentation method will have far-reaching applications across various types of data, extending beyond infectious disease studies to other areas such as vaccine distribution, physical distancing measures, and computational modeling. Furthermore, the segmentation of networks may uncover previously unknown relationships between population characteristics, such as age, geography, or other relevant factors, contributing to a deeper understanding of the underlying epidemiology. The presented work is a first step in a multi-disciplinary effort aimed at leveraging data-driven contact network segmentation to inform public health policy and modeling. The maximum likelihood estimator used in CMB map-making provides optimal, unbiased results as long as the underlying data model is accurate, but inaccuracies often arise due to sub-pixel structures like beams, sidelobes, or instrumental defects. To address these issues, a Bayesian approach to map-making incorporates prior knowledge about the model to produce a more robust solution that can mitigate inaccurate data models. This work demonstrates the Bayesian approach, which involves minimizing the distortion of the observed sky values to match the predicted sky values, and shows its effectiveness by applying it to PLANK data maps, specifically in terms of preserving the beam's sub-pixel structure. Using simulated maps with known beam profiles, the study assesses the ability of the Bayesian approach to maintain accuracy in the presence of errors. Furthermore, a detailed analysis of the necessary computational steps is performed, and the required CPU time is quantified in relation to the specific signal power spectrum. Finally, the robustness of the Bayesian approach is evaluated by examining its performance under various levels of instrumental defects simulated within the data. According to the findings, the Bayesian approach can successfully mitigate sidelobes and instrumental defects by several orders of magnitude more effectively than traditional maximum likelihood estimator based map-making methods. This superior performance is attributed to the much lower computational cost of the Bayesian approach, with a required CPU time that is roughly one-tenth the value of the maximum likelihood estimator based approach. This low computational cost allows the Bayesian approach to be easily integrated into data processing pipelines operated by large scale surveys, such as the CMB B-mode polarization survey, which is currently being conducted with an estimated processing time of approximately 40 days. This low computational cost is sufficient for the successful integration of the proposed method. Ultimately, the final processed maps generated using the Bayesian approach demonstrate notable improvements over and beyond those generated with the maximum likelihood estimator based approach, with the former exhibiting a 2 times lower root mean square error in the residual noise levels. This improved outcome is expected to result in a higher signal to noise ratio in the final processed maps, with the estimated gain expected to be in the order of the square root of the reduction in the residual noise levels. Consequently, a 2 times lower root mean square error in the residual noise levels corresponds to a 2 times higher signal to noise ratio. Based on the noise levels of the maps generated using the two different estimator based methods, it can be concluded that the maps generated using the Bayesian approach exhibit a 2 times higher signal to noise ratio compared to maps generated with the maximum likelihood estimator based approach.

Interpreting teaching instructions with natural language can be compromised by the complexity of meaning, often leading to misunderstandings. Learners may misinterpret the intentions behind teacher-provided information when object characteristics are ambiguously described, a problem known as referential ambiguity. We explore how principles from cognitive sciences, such as teaching strategies (tailoring instructions) and adapting to agent preferences, can mitigate referential ambiguities through induction. Our experiments involve training two artificial agents to accomplish a simulated robotic task: one the teacher, and one the learner. The teacher adjusts its instructions in real-time to match the learner's preferences, resulting in significantly improved task completion by the learner. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of these induction strategies in addressing referential ambiguities. Additionally, we found that incorporating induction techniques via agent interaction outperformed traditional methods of task-oriented learning. These findings suggest that addressing communication complexities through life-long learning can be a promising approach. Like state tomography, characterizing an arbitrary quantum channel necessitates a massive number of measurements, exponentially increasing with the number of quantum bits involved. Recent advancements in shadow tomography, specifically in state measurement, have revealed the possibility of extracting crucial state information using only polynomially many measurements. This study brings the concepts of shadow state tomography to the forefront, addressing the challenge of process characterization and leveraging the Choi isomorphism to derive stricter measurement bounds. We aim to derive precise bounds for the Cheeger constant using a range of geometric attributes such as area, perimeter, inradius, circumradius, minimum width and diameter. Our approach involves establishing tight inequalities among these measures specifically for planar convex bodies, along with formulating new conjectures that stem from numerical experiments. Additionally, we develop a concise expression for the Cheeger constant in terms of perimeter and minimum width, and prove that the optimal ratio of perimeter to minimum width across all convex European polygons does not exceed approximately 4.672. This ratio is shown to be strictly less than 5, and we speculate that it should be below 5 exactly. Moreover, we verify the optimality of the previously suspected value of approximately 4.672 for the Cheeger constant itself. Our research also includes a statistical analysis of the Cheeger constant's distribution among all convex European polygons. The advent of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) holds great potential for transforming communications in underserved or destructive-affected areas. In this chapter, we explore a strategic combination of UAVs and terrestrial nodes (TNs) to establish efficient wireless communication networks. Initially, we derive optimal strategies for deploying UAVs as base stations to serve a randomly dispersed population of users. Next, we address a more complex problem in which TNs can also act as base stations to compare the effectiveness of these two approaches. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this combined approach can outperform a method relying solely on UAVs by reducing energy consumption and enhancing battery lifespan. Moreover, by distributing population data among UAVs and TNs, we can enhance the security of these communication networks. Finally, we examine how this hybrid approach performs under variable conditions, including different population distributions, UAV-TN pathloss patterns, and availability of terrestrial infrastructure. In addition to these numerical results, we also investigate how this hybrid approach can be optimized using deep reinforcement learning. Here, we develop a suitable neural network architecture for this optimization problem and demonstrate the efficacy of this neural network through training, as well as compare its performance with other key benchmarks. Overall, this chapter provides a comprehensive analysis of the potential benefits of combining UAVs and TNs to establish efficient and reliable communication networks. In particular, it highlights the advantages of a hybrid approach for population-serving strategies, security considerations, variable conditions, population distribution, pathloss patterns, and learning schemes. Finally, this chapter suggests potential areas for further research into the effective deployment of UAVs in real-world settings. The internet of things encompasses a network of interconnected devices, which includes various non-standard gadgets, at a lower cost than typical PCs, yet still requiring data security measures. Consequently, devices require data encryption and decryption capabilities, necessitating secure algorithm implementations. Current encryption methods are unsuitable for low-power devices due to high computational requirements. In an effort to address this issue, this research presents a crypto library, designed to run on embedded devices, which supports multiple encryption algorithms, including those that are key exchange and random number generation capable. Introduced in the 1990s, this concept is an extension of the earlier idea by Arnold in 1971, which concerned matrices under similarity transformations. We use this method to establish a minor-free graph treewidth bound of at most $O(\sqrt{d\log d})$ when mapping to a bounded degree graph. This is significantly tighter than the $O(d^{3/2})$ treewidth bound achieved through the Selective Sampling lemma. Our result also implies a minor-free graph cut bound of at most $O(\sqrt{d\log d})$ edges in its expander construction, optimizing a decades-long area of study. We combine our treewidth bound with a linear programming technique to develop a minor-free graph half-integer tesselation of a $d$-dimensional sphere in $O(2^{d+1}\mathrm{poly}\log d}$ time. We also apply our treewidth bound to develop an $O(2^{k+1}\mathrm{poly}\log k}$ time algorithm that finds $k$-homogeneous polynomials on the $d$-dimensional sphere when $d$ is at least $2k+3$. A group of researchers from the University of Sydney and the University of Melbourne proposed a series of unitary transformations, B_V, that allow for the transformation of bosonic-excitations on a quantum circuit to qubit-excitation evolutions. This set of transformations, along with the corresponding fermionic-excitation evolutions, can serve as an alternative to the well-known Jordan-Wigner transformation in the simulation of quantum many-body systems. Unlike the Jordan-Wigner transformation, evolutions of qubit-excitation are immune to local measurement operations, making them more desirable. Additionally, the cost of applying a qubit-excitation evolution is independent of the system size, at a cost of O(1), when compared to the O(L) cost of a fermionic-excitation evolution. This presents an advantage for the use of qubit-excitation evolutions in the simulation of quantum many-body systems on a circuit. We have demonstrated the relationship between these transformations, either in the form of Hamiltonian simulations or the solution of linear systems with a quantum circuit, through a generalization of a well-known result in the simulation of quantum many-body systems. This presents a set of novel applications for the use of qubit-excitation evolutions in the solution of linear systems with a quantum circuit. The discovery of a changing speed of gravity over cosmic distance could be attributed to a primordial background of random gravitational waves produced during the early stages of the Universe's expansion. If the early Universe passed through a rapid expansion period, for example during an inflationary phase, the resulting spacetime fluctuations would have significant effects on the evolution of the Universe's expansion history, potentially altering the predicted development and observable consequences of this background. In this study, we investigate how inflationary fluctuations impact a wide range of backgrounds with different spectral characteristics, and find that their effects can be quite substantial, often shifting the predicted spectra in a manner that defies conventional expectations. We also identify a particular limit in which these fluctuations have an unmistakable and uniform impact on all backgrounds - they cause a systematic shift in the natural frequency of the background. This shift can be calculated by taking into account a particular measure of deviation from homogeneity. Notably, even in cases where the background's natural frequency remains constant, the shape of the predicted spectra is significantly affected by the fluctuations, with varying degrees of shift. In a particular case where the natural frequency remains constant, the shift is proportional to the fluctuations in an related measure of deviation from homogeneity. This particular case is particularly relevant when considering an inflationary model based on inflationary fluctuations in a particular type of cosmic fabric called braneworlds. In this model, the fluctuations in the background's natural frequency are bounded by a particular constant, suggesting a corresponding upper limit on the maximum shift. This upper limit is significant in this particular model and could have substantial implications for its predicted spectra in a particular case where the background's natural frequency remains constant, such as a particular type of gravitational wave pattern known as a $f^{-2}$ pattern. Our study presents the initial findings from a survey of the gas phase in a comet using the Sub-Millimeter Array. The research focused on water and other volatile molecules in the coma of comet C/2015 ER61 (T2), a short-period comet with unusual properties. We aimed to understand the relationship between the comet's activity and the abundance of certain molecules. By analyzing spectral lines, we detected H2O, CO, CH3OH, and HCN in the coma. The water column density showed a unique, horn-shaped pattern, not previously observed. This could be due to either hydrogen recirculation or hydrogen enrichment in the inner coma. In addition, we estimated the production rates of H2O, CO, and CH3OH, and found that CO and CH3OH seemed overabundant compared to typical comets, while HCN was relatively underabundant. The unique properties of T2's activity and the spectral line profiles may suggest a complex H2O distribution within the comet's nucleus. Furthermore, we found evidence supporting the idea that the H2O snow surface is an important factor governing the temperature distribution at the surface. The findings also highlighted the importance of direct gas-phase recycling of volatiles in the comet's evolution. Overall, the study provided new insights into the composition and structure of cometary nuclei. The survey of the gas phase in the inner coma of the comet offers significant implications for understanding the composition and structure of cometary nuclei. The data collected through this survey awaits analysis in a forthcoming paper. We propose an unsupervised speech synthesis approach that builds on recent research in automatic speech recognition and existing neural-based speech generation methods. Employing only raw, unlabeled audio and text without any corresponding labels, our system aims to mimic the function of a manually annotated dataset, as supplied by the TTS software, without requiring any annotations whatsoever. As a starting point, we draw on existing models for speech-joint synthesis and learning, specifically a sequence-to-sequence neural model with a joint learning mechanism. However, this initial approach proved impractically slow due to the extensive amount of computation required by the sequential processing of audio and text data. To overcome this limitation, we devised a method to parallel-process the audio and text data using a waveNet-based approach, greatly speeding up processing times. In addition to these innovations, we developed a neural language model to generate vocabulary and phonetic representations, reducing errors in the speech synthesis process. Ultimately, we tested our approach using the LibriSpeech test dataset, with the results showing significant improvement in comparison to existing solutions, notably a mean opinion score (MOS) of 3.97, closely rivaling that of TTS software with an MOS of 4.22. At the same time, our approach far surpasses existing solutions in processing speed, generating speech in a mere 0.53 seconds, in stark contrast to the 3.97 seconds required by the previous method. Consequently, we conclude that our approach marks a major breakthrough in unsupervised speech synthesis. Furthermore, our findings suggest that speech analysis is a rapidly evolving field, and that future research is likely to challenge traditional assumptions about processing speech in a sequential vs. parallel manner. Ultimately, we envision a future in which speech analysis can operate at processing speeds comparable to that of automatic speech recognition. Given the extensive range of potential applications, we believe this future to be highly promising and plausible. Multi-objective mixed-integer non-linear programming problems frequently appear in real-world contexts, particularly in fields like manufacturing and engineering. Researchers have suggested combining approximation algorithms like the non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm II and branch-and-bound techniques for solving MOMILP's hybrid approach. This proposed method, BnB-NSGAII, is a potential solution that leverages computational strengths of both methods. When dealing with high-levels of computational expense, the hybrid approach can provide more accurate results by integrating them. Although previous studies have demonstrated some use of this technique, there remains a significant knowledge gap regarding its practical application and implementation. This paper provides a thorough description of incorporating NSGAII as a node solver within a hybrid approach. Additionally, it introduces enhancements such as approximate dominance checks, Pareto-rank hybrid usage, and pseudo non-dominated sorting to optimize this method. Furthermore, this study implements this approach using the CEPLEX hybrid algorithm and demonstrates its feasibility using multi-objective practical problems like the multi-objective multi-product multi-family housing problem. Results show that this method can significantly improve computational efficiency, allowing it to solve problems with hundreds of variables and objectives within minutes, despite taking hours with the non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm II alone. This study also includes a comparison with Cepa2, a state-of-the-art multi-objective hybrid approach, demonstrating that BnB-NSGAII can provide competitive results. This presentation outlines the Dynaswap architecture, a cybersecurity framework specifically designed for molecular modeling simulations on large cyberinfrastructures, such as molecular modeling simulations. By identifying potential threats and developing an intelligent security system, Dynaswap protects user data from unauthorized access, data breaches, and malicious activities within the infrastructure. With the ability to monitor system events in real-time through Dynaswap's interface, users can rest assured that their data and system are secure. This architecture has been successfully implemented and tested on the Pangea cyberinfrastructure platform. This project's findings will be shared, including challenges we encountered, such as implementing the architecture within the existing cyberinfrastructure setup, and potential issues that Dynaswap's adoption may present. Finally, we will discuss future plans to expand Dynaswap's capabilities.

We studied the solar wind energy flux near the inner edge of our solar system using data from four different close approaches to the sun by the Parker Solar Probe, where we recorded data for 1.0 to 1.13 solar radii around the orbit's perihood. These data were gathered over a total of 13 solar rotations and covered four campaigns between 2018 and 2020. During this time, we observed a wide range of low-energy particle behavior, where the energy levels varied significantly, but overall, we found the solar wind still behaves similarly to its observed behavior at greater distances from the sun. After normalizing the energy levels to 1 solar radius, we found an average energy flux of around 6.40 +/- 1.00 mW/m^2, which means the solar wind's energy output decreases about two times as you get closer to the heart of the sun. By using this data, we found that the solar wind's energy, momentum, and dissipation relationship remains consistent, but the issue of particle acceleration in the solar wind still hasn't been fully resolved. Additionally, we found the solar wind's behavior could be described with a specific value of the polytropic index of around 1.1 +/- 0.2, which matches the results from other studies, or with a specific value of beta, which represents the ratio of thermal energy to magnetic energy, around 0.16 +/- 0.03. When the solar wind's behavior is compared to other models, we found the solar wind's energy flux near the heart of the sun doesn't match the predictions of specific types of models such as the switch-back model or the Alfvén wave dissipation model. However, we still think these types of wave dissipation models might be the key to explaining the solar wind's behavior. Finally, we found the solar wind's energy flux near the heart of the sun doesn't match the predictions of specific types of models such as the critical balance model either, which means the solar wind's behavior still remains a bit mysterious. Further research needs to be done to explain the solar wind's behavior.

In a previous study (arXiv:2012.13744), the concept of R-negative scissors states was introduced for a system of classical bodies, with a specific example provided for the Two-Rotors Model. However, a crucial aspect of these states, namely their asymptotic decay, remained unexplored. This gap in knowledge was addressed, with a detailed proof obtained for the Two-Rotors Model. Additionally, a generalization of the R-negative scissors states concept was developed for systems with multiple scissors, with associated general asymptotic stability results supported by relevant numerical simulations. This generalized framework encompasses a wide range of configurations, including those with multiple scissors, based on a general formula for R. Relevantly, the Two-Rotors Model was found to be equivalent to a particular instance of the Manning--Rosen potential when considered in quantum form, allowing for a better understanding of the latter's spectrum through analysis of the R-negative quantum scissors states. With a specific example, the idea that the eigenvalues associated with system energies, as described by the Manning--Rosen potential, can be generated through system angular momentum values was demonstrated. This discovery was also confirmed by numerical quantum simulations, with resulting findings compared to the findings in arXiv:2012.13744. With evidence supporting the relevance of the R-negative quantum scissors states, a new approach was developed for constructing the Manning--Rosen spectrum using a specific algebraic method. One of the primary objectives of Information Extraction involves recognizing event descriptions along with their related entities within a given text. This task has received significant research attention, yet efforts focused on detecting events within Chinese text have been relatively limited. To address this gap, a new dataset for Chinese Event Extraction has been developed, featuring a diverse range of 22 different event types. This dataset comprises 3,862 event instances, carefully annotated by experts. To further explore the limitations of current advanced models in handling this task, the accuracy of their predictions on this new dataset was assessed in detail. Additionally, a new model specifically designed for Chinese Event Extraction was developed and tested. This model, built with the Universal Schema approach in mind, utilizes a sequence-to-sequence architecture, supported by Universal Encoder encoder layers and Bi-LSTM decoders. Moreover, a universal attention decoder layer was developed and tested, showing improved performance over more traditional approaches. Experimental results demonstrate that this model outperforms other leading models in this field. Moreover, a new dataset for English Event Extraction, featuring 16 different event types, was developed, consisting of 14,068 event instances. This dataset is currently under review for public release. For the purposes of this research, the accuracy of the models was assessed using F1-measure. This work also involved examining the role of pre-trained Chinese models, such as BERT and ALBERT, in facilitating Event Extraction. Ultimately, a combined model consisting of a sequence-to-sequence architecture, pre-trained Chinese models (specifically BERT and ALBERT), and a new universal attention decoder layer was developed, showcasing state-of-the-art performance on both the Chinese and English Event Extraction datasets. This model is currently being made available online at https://github.com/zhuyifeng1999/Chinese-Event-Extraction. For the purposes of the English dataset, the code is hosted at https://github.com/CLU-NF/U-Schema-English-Event-Extraction. A public release of the Chinese dataset is currently in progress, with the code being hosted at the same location. Both the Chinese and English datasets were developed with the support of Wangyi News and TMT. A special thank you is extended to all parties involved. Recent observations of fast radio bursts (FRBs) have led to a range of theories attempting to explain their mysterious origins. These theories encompass a variety of magnetic fields, relativistic flows, and radiation mechanisms. Observations of FRBs 20191214 and 20200723 by the CHIME FRB Collaboration revealed a connection between radio flare brightness and energy, suggesting a pattern that could be explained by the interaction of a relativistic flow and a magnetic field. However, a study has now challenged these findings, instead arguing that the data supports a synchrotron radiation mechanism emanating from a magnetically dominated region. According to this argument, the relationship between brightness and energy can be accounted for by a region largely free of particles, and the absence of a flaring plateau in the case of FRB 20200723 can be attributed to a changing radiation efficiency. Furthermore, numerical simulations of a relativistic jet have failed to produce results consistent with the CHIME FRB data, instead suggesting that the synchrotron radiation mechanism is the more plausible option. Finally, the implications of these findings are explored in the context of observations of gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), suggesting that FRB energies may be comparable to those of GRBs, and that the potential for GRBs to produce FRBs (GRB-FRB) may not be as limited by energy constraints as previously thought. Nonetheless, further observational evidence is required to definitively resolve the origins of FRBs. Observations of FRBs 20181110 and 20191214 using the Low Frequency Array (LOFAR) revealed a connection between radio flare brightness and energy, but with a notable discrepancy in the case of FRB 20181110, where a plateau in the flux-energy relationship persisted, and the absence of a notable flare at its peak energy. A comparison of these observations with the results of simulations of a relativistic jet suggests that the presence of a plateau may indicate a failure of the synchrotron radiation mechanism, and the potential for other mechanisms (such as inverse Compton scattering) to contribute to radiation in less magnetically dominated regions. Ultimately, the synchrotron radiation mechanism appears to be the more plausible option, and further observational evidence is required to definitively resolve the origins of FRBs. We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports stealth addresses in conjunction with Delegated Proof of Stake, resulting in Delegated RingCT.
In the Delegated RingCT scheme, the sender partitions a transaction output into multiple tokens and assigns a stealth value to each, where the token amount is predetermined by the sender.
Token values can be imported from external sources, such as Bitcoin, allowing widespread adoption of Delegated RingCT.
Despite being a modular design, our Delegated RingCT is the only comprehensive solution for DPoS-based cryptocurrencies, enabling truly private payments.
Furthermore, a pioneering Delegated RingCT implementation is presented, showcasing the feasibility and security of the protocol through integration with Nano, a leading DPoS cryptocurrency. The implemented Delegated RingCT features a compact and efficient design, using approximately 33 bytes per token, along with an innovative token splitting method. Moreover, Delegated RingCT was successfully integrated into Nano, yielding a lightweight and easy-to-use wallet interface for private payments. Our online survey with 235 Signal users revealed that users can be divided into two categories: those who understand the function of PINs (enthusiasts) and those who do not (casual users). Surprisingly, only 12% of users declined to use a PIN, indicating successful encouragement of PIN adoption in Signal. While enthusiastic users predominantly employed complex PINs saved in password managers, casual users mainly used simple numerical PINs. To strengthen the security of casual users, enhancing awareness about the purpose and features of PINs could be beneficial. Additionally, introducing a simple and visible interface for displaying generated PINs could help these users better understand their significance. Lastly, engineers should consider the trade-off between introducing features that may deter casual users from using PINs, but also strive to improve the overall security of PIN interaction in Signal. 

Key findings:
- The majority of Signal users (88%) use a PIN.
- Enthusiastic users predominantly generated complex PINs using password managers.
- Casual users mainly used simple numerical PINs.
- Introduction of a simple and visible interface for displaying generated PINs could improve the user experience for casual users.
- Enhancing awareness about the purpose of PINs could help casual users better understand their significance. 

Recommendations:
- Implementing additional features to encourage users not using PINs may improve security.
- Introducing a simple and visible interface for displaying generated PINs may improve the user experience for casual users.
- Raising awareness about the purpose of PINs may improve the understanding of PINs among casual users.

The method's ability to produce accurate results with minimal evaluations is particularly beneficial due to the solar irradiance function's non-smooth, highly oscillatory nature. Examples demonstrating the method's effectiveness include calculating the energy absorbed by a thin, uniform solar absorber and the absorbed energy of thin-film materials, taking into account their complex optical properties and varying thicknesses. However, current methods based on automatic differentiation and Kronecker-factored block diagonal approximations disregard noise in mini-batch datasets. We propose a new algorithm, NOCONV, that leverages the convexity imposed by the per-example noisiness and cross-batch structure of the Hessian. NOCONV also demonstrates the ability to decrease memory usage while maintaining performance, making it a more efficient option. Experimental results demonstrate NOCONV's superiority using a relatively simple implementation on standard classification and generative adversarial networks, achieving performance on par with current state-of-the-art methods for training deep networks. Numerous languages attribute gender not just to living entities but also to inanimate objects. This study investigates whether this "grammatical gender" influence is eliminated when extracting word embeddings or if it lingers, potentially impacting relationships between inanimate nouns. Our investigation reveals that in these embeddings, nouns sharing the same gender tend to be closer to each other than those with different genders. This implies that grammatical gender could still be a determining factor in the representation of inanimate nouns. To quantify the exact impact, we developed a grammatical gender-based metric that measures the similarity between embeddings of inanimate nouns from different grammatical genders. The results show a noticeable disparity; specifically, a significant 0.08 to 0.14 F1-score difference was observed. Additionally, our analysis demonstrates that this influence is most pronounced for less common and more contextually dependent inanimate nouns. Finally, an experimental probing task was conducted to assess whether state-of-the-art models, specifically BERT and FLAIR, have inherited this grammatical gender bias, which they indeed have. Interestingly, our findings suggest that BERT learns this bias much faster than FLAIR during pre-training. Overall, our research highlights the importance of considering multiple factors, including grammatical gender, as a means of improving the representation of inanimate objects. This work may prompt the development of more effective methods for extracting higher-quality embeddings. Estimating an object's pose is a crucial aspect of most visual pipelines in robots and 3D vision as a whole. This study tackles the challenge of accurately positioning new objects with no prior knowledge. This method builds on previous work by removing the need for category-specific models and replaces them with generalizable principles. Through end-to-end training, our system learns an intrinsic object shape language that remains consistent across categories. This allows our pose estimation approach to operate effectively on unseen objects despite having no explicit category labels. This study showcases our findings using the YCB object dataset, featuring 98 diverse objects. It also highlights the importance of a specific type of data enrichment, known as "easy" rotations, to enhance our results. This study presents a novel, generic technique for performing causal inference that leverages a Structural Causal Model (SCM) along with mixed causal networks, where some nodes have multiple potential outcomes. Existing techniques for mixed causal networks are limited to specific types of SCM configurations, but our approach can apply to any SCM setup within the Markov Lagrangian framework, enabling us to derive a universal formula for causal inference that accommodates any target outcome. Additionally, our method extends the ANM algorithm to facilitate causal inference between arbitrary pairs of nodes, regardless of outcome type. We demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed framework using a variety of examples, encompassing both simple and complex causal configurations. Furthermore, all the proofs for key theorems and a detailed explanation of the proposed method and its underlying reasoning are provided in the supporting documentation. Moreover, an R package called 'CausalInference' has been developed to facilitate the implementation of our proposed algorithms. This package is available for download on CRAN. Lastly, using a simulated Anneal dataset, we validate our proposed algorithms by assessing their performance in a real-world causal inference scenario. The results show that our proposed algorithms have superior accuracy compared to established benchmarks. 

The main contributions of this research are:

1. A general mathematical representation (Formula \eqref{eq:universal}) for performing causal inference on any Structural Causal Model (SCM).
2. A novel algorithm for performing causal inference on mixed causal networks that can handle an arbitrary number of configurations.
3. An extension of the ANM algorithm for causal inference between any pair of nodes with arbitrary outcomes.
4. An R package called 'CausalInference' for implementing the proposed algorithms.
5. An empirical evaluation of the proposed algorithms using simulated Anneal dataset safety data, which showed superior performance compared to benchmarks. 

The supporting documentation contains additional information and comprehensive mathematical proofs for all the main contributions. 

The provided R package offers six functions for performing causal inference based on the proposed algorithms. 

The corresponding Python code for the package can be found at https://github.com/ali-akbar-zadeh/causal-inference. 

The provided research contributes significantly to causal inference and outcome variable inference by expanding the framework to any Structural Causal Model (SCM) and its underlying Markov Lagrangian framework. 

The offered Python code at https://github.com/ali-akbar-zadeh/causal-inference surpasses current benchmarks by implementing the ANM algorithm for any pair of nodes with arbitrary outcomes.

Blazars with certain spectral energy distributions display a notable increase in ultraviolet and soft X-ray frequencies, which can be attributed to distinct radiation mechanisms. By analyzing the polarization patterns of UV and X-ray emissions from these blazars, scientists can gain a deeper understanding of the complex astrophysical environment surrounding blazar jets, allowing them to distinguish between competing emission models. This research employs a novel Monte Carlo code, ADCITY, to simulate the polarization characteristics of photonic and leptonic radiation, acquired through adiabatic deceleration of particles, in close proximity to a relativistic flow. A comparative study involving the blazars Mrk 501 and 1ES 1440+122 shows that ADCITY produces predictions in line with the scope of WISE, XMM-Newton, and Swift observations, indicating a solid match for Mrk 501 but somewhat lower agreement for 1ES 1440+122, likely due to observed polarization patterns being more pronounced than predicted. A proposed explanation for this discrepancy could involve a delayed particle flux triggered by a major flaring event in Mrk 501, aligning theoretical simulations with observational data, as well as a previously unaccounted radiation component emanating from 1ES 1440+122, in close proximity to its jet base. This discovery presents an opportunity for a lepton-photon beam to connect the jet and the broad-line region of Mrk 501, in accordance with the unified model. A detailed video explanation is available at the URL: https://youtu.be/6b6B9sQo8Rc.

Baryons are generated through a process that is straightforward to understand, which involves a QCD string breaking up into causally linked parts. A simplified model, representing a QCD flux tube with properties tied to the mass of a compact object within it, effectively reproduces the masses of a range of baryons. This approach also allows for the creation of hyperons, which is achieved through similar mechanisms. A key benefit of this approach is its ability to describe relations between different types of hadronic states. While this discussion primarily centers around static properties of Baryons, it also touches on dynamics and how this segmentation impacts the creation of causal surfaces in space-time. As an extension, this framework's potential to describe the interior of black holes that have causal surfaces is explored. Because this discussion is rooted in a quantized framework for QCD, it provides a novel framework for describing physics within black holes, their masses, and the way they evolve. A review of how this framework relates to the information paradox is also provided. A potential connection between this framework and the concept of entanglement is also examined. Light field technology is currently a focal point of interest for the research community due to its potential to dramatically enhance image capture and reconstruction speed, as well as reduce noise. Compared to conventional imaging methods capturing a single 2D frame, light field imaging can capture and isolate 4D light field data, consisting of spatial and angular variations. However, this dense data comes with a high price, resulting in an exponentially increased data load with a high risk of noise, making data processing a complex challenge. We have developed a novel, advanced deep learning approach, dubbed LFCAN, which is specifically designed for noise-affected light field data interpolation and reconstruction. By combining 2D and 3D Convolutional AutoEncoder models, LFCAN separates spatial and angular components, then uses a multi-stage refinement process to fully leverage the rich information present in 4D light field data. Through rigorous testing on both real-world and synthetic datasets, LFCAN has demonstrated superior performance over existing state-of-the-art light field reconstruction methods across a range of performance metrics, including PSNR, SSIM, MS-SSIM, and LFIQM. Our results show that LFCAN is capable of achieving up to a 2 dB improvement in PSNR for 16 angular slice datasets and a 1.3% increase in MS-SSIM for 33 angular slice datasets, all while achieving this performance at a significantly reduced computational cost. Our source code for LFCAN is available online at https://github.com/hccuse/LFCAN. Additionally, our dataset used for real-world experimentation can be found at https://datawanghui.cn/datasets/dl4lf/. Moreover, the 4D light field datasets used for both real-world and synthetic evaluation can be accessed at https://datawanghui.cn/datasets/dl4lf/. Lastly, the 4D light field datasets used for training and testing the models can be accessed at https://datawanghui.cn/datasets/dl4lf/. Moreover, our pre-trained models for both real-world and synthetic datasets can be accessed at https://datawanghui.cn/datasets/dl4lf/. Lastly, our demo video can be found at https://youtu.be/6b8B8o2BQsA. Our research contribution has the potential to open up new applications and domains for light field technology, and our results demonstrate that a deep learning approach can be used to make light field technology more reliable and accurate, particularly in a wide range of real-world scenarios

In cross-lingual information retrieval using vectors, two fundamental models, 
interactive and non-interactive, prevail with synchronous and asynchronous 
query-document embeddings, respectively. Weighed against retrieval accuracy and 
computational efficiency, each approach excels and falls short. This study combines 
the benefits of these two frameworks through the development of a semi-interactive 
mechanism that constructs a non-interactive framework but unites document embedding 
with multiple associated queries in parallel, thus enabling interactive-style cross-lingual 
feature acquisition. By leveraging the word embeddings and a distillation process of an 
optimized interactive model, we augment our proposed method, initialized with the M-BERT 
multilingual language model, and validate it on datasets generated from real search engine 
inputs. Results demonstrate that our approach substantially enhances both accuracy and efficiency 
over existing benchmarks, specifically reducing computation by a factor of 100 while 
improving first passage retrieval by 11%. Furthermore, this study initiates the promotion of 
cross-lingual retrieval vectors as a standard tool for the entire industry, paving the way for 
a new era of cross-lingual retrieval research, and makes the associated source code and 
information available at https://github.com/ashishng25/clirvectors. Also, this study 
demonstrates first passage retrieval videos on WMT-19 Shared News Topic Exploration, 
available at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Qb8p2B8C9E.

Demographic research, particularly in public health policy, heavily relies on per capita rates, such as disease incidence and healthcare expenditure. Existing studies have demonstrated the potential for spatial analysis of per capita rates to identify distinct subpopulations. However, the results are often marred by bias resulting from the survey's sampling design, where sampled data is linked to specific geographic areas. Our proposed method utilizes geostatistical models, accounting for the sampling design's impact, to remove bias from the per capita rates. This involves using weighted versions of the sampling design and a weighted version of the Kriging estimator. We show that the weighted Kriging estimator is unbiased and efficient, with the sampling design's properties determining the distribution of the estimates. Simulations reveal the significant improvement in estimating spatial variation when accounting for the sampling design, compared to standard methods. The benefits are particularly evident in smaller studies, where the bias is most pronounced. This method is highly adaptable across various types of surveys, sampling designs, and study variables, making it a versatile tool for analyzing per capita rates from spatial surveys. Furthermore, the method can be extended to accommodate multiple variables and multi-level sampling designs, allowing it to adapt to a wide range of challenging data sets. Overall, the method provides an efficient way to accurately spatial analysis based on surveys with complex sampling designs. This method is applicable in various fields, such as public health, environmental science, and urban planning. Examples in public health policy demonstrate the significant improvement in detecting hotspots and estimating prediction intervals when using the method, in contrast to standard approaches. Overall, the method provides an efficient way to accurately spatial analysis based on surveys with complex sampling designs. Further research is needed to address issues of data sharing and study replication. The R code and data used in this study are publicly available online. Astronomical observations from ground-based telescopes can be distorted by Earth's atmosphere due to differential dispersion that varies by wavelength. Observations made off-axis, other than directly at the zenith, necessitate the use of Atmospheric Dispersion Correctors. Current designs of these correctors are based on atmospheric models which have yet to be verified through on-site measurements. We've carried out a corrector calibration process using data collected off-axis from 17 bright stars, applying a linear model in the process. The results of this analysis demonstrate the effectiveness of the new model in reducing dispersion after applying the new solutions, in contrast to other models, by an average factor of 2.2, with the benefit of being linearly representative across the entire wavelength range covered by WIFS, our wide-field imaging system. Furthermore, we've identified six stars that could serve as reference points for similar ADC calibration systems in the future. We're particularly interested in systems like WIFS which cover a wide field of view and are equipped with multiple detectors, enabling us to Simultaneously correct and record observations of numerous off-axis reference stars across the entire field of view. During these observations, we've calculated accurate measurements of stellar radial velocities. To further reduce errors, we've carried out high-precision measurements of stellar magnetic field velocities. We've calculated the average errors of these measurements to be 2.3 km/s and 16 km/s for radial and magnetic field velocities respectively. We've also explored and discussed potential applications and extensions of this technology in the context of systems like WIFS and other wide-field imaging systems. We've successfully demonstrated how this technology can be used for observations of objects of interest such as asteroids, comet tails and other celestial bodies. Moreover, we've determined that using this technology in systems equipped with multiple detectors is possible as long as there are sufficient reference stars available within the field of view to accurately calibrate the dispersion. In order to further reduce errors, we've explored the use of using BIS, a technique based on spectral information, to calculate atmospheric dispersion. In systems like WIFS, which covers a wide field of view and is equipped with multiple detectors, we've demonstrated how BIS can be used in conjunction with information from all available detectors to calculate atmospheric dispersion. Traditional stacked RNN and DBN models lack the capability to incorporate tendencies spanning multiple periods and often overlook redundant input variables, which contribute nothing or negatively affect predictive power. By integrating the hierarchical latent variable model with multiple transition periods and a Bayesian neural network, our approach effectively mitigates the "damping" effect associated with RNNs and eliminates the overfitting issue posed by DBN models. Additionally, the model's ability to project high-dimensional time series onto a lower-dimensional representation through PCA enhances the variational approximation of Gaussian distributions, significantly improving the efficiency of inference and prediction. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach consistently surpasses the performance of RNN, DBN, and PCA models on both artificial and real-world datasets, showcasing its immense potential for applications involving multi-period time series forecasting. The remarkable effectiveness of deep learning has sparked interest in incorporating ethics into deep learning frameworks. Previously developed ethical modules, however, are often limited to specific, narrow applications or have raised serious concerns regarding their own ethical implications. This paper presents a pioneering attempt to develop a flexible and adaptable ethical module using conceptual roles, an innovative knowledge representation technique. The proposed framework allows for the interpretation of an aggregation function (an aggregation function is a relation that holds for a group of inputs) without having to specify it for each individual input. Due to the limitations of current natural language processing capabilities, the developed system relies on a simplified ontology. Nevertheless, the proposed framework holds great potential for expansion to a more comprehensive ontology in the future. The research also examines and highlights several crucial ethical dilemmas associated with deep learning, including bias, transparency, and security. The demonstrated results show that the proposed framework can effectively address these issues. Moreover, the utilization of the provided ontology and the implementation of the REGUL role-based inference mechanism incur negligible computational costs in terms of time and resources. This is particularly evident in applications requiring high-speed processing, such as self-driving cars. The proposed framework is currently suitable for a wide range of applications, such as image classification, object recognition, and speech recognition. The research outlines a possible methodology for developing a comprehensive, all-encompassing ontology to further enhance the proposed framework. The proposed framework may serve as a precedent or template for the development of similar modules and roles, and the associated code and ontology are freely accessible upon request. The paper discusses the challenges and limitations of the proposed framework, including its inability to effectively handle instances of inherent ambiguity and context-dependent ambiguity. The research also delves into the computational complexities associated with the proposed model. The proposed framework is currently under implementation as part of the DEEP LEARNING ETHICS CHALLENGE initiative. The challenge aims to develop a framework similar to the proposed one and is open to participants until the deadline. Object detection has been significantly advanced by recent deep learning-based techniques. Many proposed methods have achieved impressive results, yet they require extensive annotation time and cost. One goal is to leverage pre-existing image classification models, which are already extensively annotated, to tackle object detection tasks. Zero-shot object detection methods aim to achieve this by using the classified image labels to forecast object bounding boxes. In order to bridge the gap between image classification and object detection, we introduce a novel framework known as Object Bounding Box Guessing (OBBG). OBBG incorporates a bounding box guess network (OBBN) to generate bounding boxes based on pre-existing image classification models. The key components of the OBBN consist of a Bounding Box Frame (BBF) and a Object Bounding Box Number (OBBN) code. The OBBG framework also introduces a BGF-MLP that predicts the BBF and refines the OBBN code to generate the final bounding boxes. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to introduce the concept of learning a bounding box frame to generate bounding boxes. Our experiments demonstrate the success of OBBG, which achieves impressive results on the PASCAL VOC and COCO datasets. Our findings suggest that OBBG outperforms previous zero-shot object detection methods, including the recently introduced Object-BBox Det model. OBBG has also achieved superior performance to weakly-supervised object detection methods. One notable aspect of OBBG is its ability to produce bounding boxes with minimal extra supervision. Mortality forecasting models built on the classical factor framework, such as the Lee-Carter model and its variants, often oversimplify real-world conditions. The models assume factor loadings remain static over time despite the significant influence of variables such as advancements in medical technology and environmental shifts. We expand the classical model to create a factor model that accounts for the evolution of factor loadings over time. We introduce two methods for forecasting factor loadings and apply them to a model that effectively captures the changing relationships in mortality datasets. Additionally, we highlight the challenges associated with forecasting factor loadings in real-world applications. We conclude that the proposed approach improves forecasting accuracy for both short-term and long-term mortality outlooks. The methods' code and the mortality datasets used in this study can be accessed through a public repository. Reducing neural architecture search cost has proven to be a costly endeavor. One potential approach to minimize this cost is to eliminate the need to recompute architectures for each model, with smaller operator sets, particularly in latent space, resulting in decreased random searches and increased shared operator usage among child models. Notably, research suggests a direct correlation between the number of unique operators and interference caused by shared operators. Consequently, employing latent space operators with minimal interference is crucial for efficient search. However, retaining operator details in memory and reloading them after each model training is an ineffective strategy, as it fails to leverage the benefits of shared operators. In contrast, loading and fine-tuning pre-trained operator latent spaces yields superior performance, as it effectively minimizes the impact of shared operator interference. Building upon this concept, S2NAS efficiently performs NAS at a significantly reduced cost by incorporating the following innovations: 1) incorporating structural diversity into the operator latent space to minimize interference between child models and reduce reliance on the history of the operator latent space, 2) employing a novel random search strategy that prioritizes top-performing architectures and those using the fewest shared operators, 3) applying a novel constraint strategy that prioritizes architectures using the fewest shared operators, and 4) introducing an innovative efficient architecture evaluation approach known as the $l_0\cdot F$ score. When evaluated on CIFAR-10, Cleb, ImageNet, and STL-10 datasets using various search spaces, S2NAS demonstrated notable improvements over existing low-cost NAS methods. For instance, it achieved a 82.11% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet (similar to the performance of ResNet-50) at a significantly reduced cost of 4840 architecture evaluations (approximately 90% less costly than the best previous NAS method). Furthermore, it also yielded top-performing results on Cleb, achieving 65.80 top-1 accuracy at a significantly reduced cost of 1040 evaluation (approximately 99% less costly). Given its impressive performance and cost efficiency, S2NAS has significant implications for real-world applications in a resource-constrained setting. It also outperforms the best previous method in several benchmarks, achieving a top-1 accuracy of 65.80 on Cleb (similar to the performance of MNIST+SVHN at 65.83). reduces their size while maintaining their performance, and can even reveal smaller
sub-networks with higher accuracy than their full counterparts. Our study focuses
on understanding the inherent biases of these "lucky network subsets." We looked at
the effects of iteratively pruning a basic neural network on a specific type of task,
finding that the remaining connections create localized patterns. Our analysis
suggests that data influences the structure of the pruned networks. The characteristics
of the pruned networks are surprisingly similar to those of manually-designed neural
networks, opening the possibility of automating the process to discover more
efficient network configurations for a variety of tasks and data sets. However, we
also found that the pruned networks perform poorly when extended to more complex tasks. 
This issue highlights a limitation of current pruning techniques. 
Further investigation is required to discover more efficient network configurations.

structure of the pruned networks, and show that it offers a simpler alternative to
the pruned networks. 
The basic neural network, which we call manual-prune-net, is derived from observations
of the pruned networks and their inherent biases.

terms of performance and model complexity on a specific data set.
