Extreme value theory was applied to analyze high-inclusive wind speed and wave height observations from moored buoys 61201 and 61202, located near the Shetland Islands. Results from this analysis revealed significant temporal variability in spatial correlations between wind speed, wave height, and wave period, with dependencies on wind speed being particularly strong during periods of high wind speed. In contrast, relationships between wave height and wave period showed the opposite trend, exhibiting positive dependence at low wind speed levels but negative dependence at high wind speed levels. Furthermore, regional model-based estimates of wind speed and wave height extremes were found to be influenced significantly by the model's parameterization of wind speed, which in turn affects the model's spatial and temporal patterns of extreme events. Consequently, regional variability in wind speed and wave height extremes may be exaggerated due to the use of high wind speed threshold values in the Storm4 model's parameterization. Moreover, temporal variations in spatial correlations between wind speed and wave height were found to be strongest during periods of high wind speed, suggesting that wave height is influenced by spatially correlated wind fields at high wind speed levels. In contrast, relationships between wave height and wind speed were not evident during periods of low wind speed, suggesting that wave height is driven by wind speed at long wavelengths. Consequently, wave height can be accurately forecasted for up to 2 days when correlations between wind speed and wave height are positive at high wind speed levels, but this accuracy is reduced to 1 day for periods of low wind speed, indicating that wave height becomes increasingly independent of wind speed at low wind speed levels. This standardization enables the seamless retrieval and interpretation of images across various medical systems, also allowing the files to be utilized as comprehensive multi-dimensional data sets that can be analyzed by machine learning algorithms. While DICOM provides a means to embed information about image files, including metadata describing the spatial relationships and time-series data, this guidance is often overlooked in machine learning research and accompanying code. As a result, we have developed a simplified system for processing DICOM images while incorporating relevant metadata, specifically designed to facilitate the training of deep neural networks. To illustrate the effectiveness of this approach, we have successfully trained a convolutional neural network using a dataset of lung CT scans, demonstrating that incorporating spatial information and temporal data can lead to improved diagnostic performance in medical imaging tasks. Our hope is that this methodology will inspire the development of more sophisticated machine learning algorithms within the medical field, with the aim of improving diagnostic accuracy and patient outcomes. In recent times, deep learning models have been effectively utilized for categorizing DNA sequences based on various tasks. A major challenge often arises due to the lengthy and variable nature of these DNA sequences. In our research, a deep learning model is proposed for an unsupervised task of transforming DNA sequences into a standardized fixed-dimensional representation. This can be viewed as an extension to the well-known autoencoder, but one that addresses the limitations posed by variable sequence lengths. In addition, we present a novel, deep-seated extension known as the DNA-BTAE, based on a type of recurrent neural network called BRNN, that also integrates convolutional elements. Comprehensive experiments were conducted, which demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed model and its ability to accurately predict DNA sequences based on this representation. Notably, these DNA sequences belonged to both human and mouse species. Furthermore, DNA-BTAE's performance was directly compared to a variation of the Convolutional Recurrent Neural Network introduced in 2016. Results indicate that DNA-BTAE not only surpasses this network in terms of classification accuracy but and also outperforms a more recent network architecture, DNA-RNN-VAE. Moreover, DNA-BTAE's generalizability was successfully evaluated using the 'domain adaptation' approach, which involves predicting DNA sequences of one species based on data from another, namely that of humans from mice. The metal-insulator transition in V$_2$O$_3$ films was investigated by comparing free surface films with those covered in a layer of Sc, following previous research indicating Sc overlayer films exhibit room temperature metal-insulator transitions triggered by scarification. Using scanning tunneling microscopy, we observed that Sc capping does not consistently protect the surface of V$_2$O$_3$ films from oxidation. Furthermore, this distinction has no impact on the metal-insulator transition, leading us to conclude that surface termination, rather than surface composition, drives this phase transition. This is supported by the fact that Sc capping modifies the V 3d band density of states near the Fermi level, according to X-ray photoemission spectroscopy results. Consequently, the phase diagram of V$_2$O$_3$-Sc system cannot be solely explained by phase segregation between Sc and V, as proposed earlier. Based on this, we suggest that surface termination and Sc 4d band hybridization are key elements in driving the metal-insulator transition and enhancing it at room temperature. Additionally, this research sheds light on the necessity of using anti-oxidation methods in investigating the properties of refractory 4d/5d transition metal compounds.

Currently, the most trusted diagnostic tool for COVID-19 is RT-PCR, but it has significant drawbacks, including a 24-hour processing time and a relatively low overall specificity and sensitivity. In contrast, Computed Tomography (CT) scans can provide valuable assistance in COVID-19 diagnosis, but they involve exposure to ionizing radiation, specifically X-rays, which has both benefits (diagnostic assistance) and drawbacks (radiation exposure) in the context of COVID-19 diagnosis. Our research focuses on developing an innovative framework for creating high-quality CT scans from low-dose and ultra-low-dose scans by combining X-ray attenuation information from adjacent slices. By doing so, we can minimize patient radiation exposure while maintaining CT image quality. The proposed framework is specifically designed to support COVID-19 diagnosis, and subsequent model assessments suggest that it is well-suited for this purpose. Our framework is comprised of two key stages: the first involves merging low-dose and ultra-low-dose CT projection data from adjacent transverse slices to produce high-quality image scans, and the second requires reconstruction of the resulting CT volumetric data through optimization. A total of 1040 ultra-low-dose CT scans, 220 low-dose CT scans, and 220 standard dose CT scans were utilized for training, validation, and testing purposes. Our research findings indicate that the quality of the reconstructed standard dose CT images is comparable to those produced using 338 mGy CT scans, but with the added benefit of significantly reduced radiation exposure (to just 0.085 mGy). Our framework has demonstrated significant superiority over existing state-of-the-art techniques, producing reconstructed images that are 2.1 dB higher in terms of peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) and 1.1 dB higher in structural similarity index measure (SSIM). Overall, our research framework is an innovative and effective solution for creating high-quality standard dose CT scans from low-dose and ultra-low-dose CT scans, thereby minimizing patient radiation exposure during COVID-19 diagnosis. To generate top-quality quadrilateral meshes on complex computer-aided design (CAD) models efficiently, we propose an integrated solution. A versatile mesh with numerous irregular points is initially created, which allows for intricate quad configurations due to its unstructured layout. Subsequently, we build upon this foundation with a flexible T-mesh structure, which can be manipulated through edits to the mesh's domain boundary. A customized extension of the Discrete Mean-Curvature-Flow (DMCF) algorithm then refines the mesh, converting it into an optimal partition with constant areas. Finally, a cutting-edge loop-based mesh splitting method is applied to break down the mesh into its constituent parts, and a sophisticated local refinement procedure reconfigures these segments as quads, optimizing the overall mesh in the process. Notably, our approach accommodates mesh domains with holes of any dimensions and promotes the production of high-order quadrilateral meshes with numerous smooth facets. Ultimately, this result facilitates seamless interactions with both solver-based infrastructure and CAD-based workstations. Additionally, our approach enables the creation of pre-meshes suitable for adaptive mesh refinements, which in turn, can be utilized in various downstream processes with far-reaching implications for a diverse array of real-world applications. We develop an innovative approach to describe the friction caused by radiation experienced by particles moving through a medium with mechanical resistance. We introduce an effect where the medium is subjected to an irreversible deformation, similar to being pulled apart, and investigate its relationship with well-established principles of radiation loss and energy dissipation. By consolidating our findings, we propose a unified framework for understanding energy loss, which is then compared with existing theories. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our concept of mechanical friction due to radiation loss can be adapted to various scenarios, such as charged particles interacting with a medium in different states or being accelerated away from all charged particles. We also note that under specific circumstances, our idea may provide insights into the friction experienced by neutral particles. Note that one of the chapters in this work explores research initially started while the corresponding author was at CERN. We have successfully observed the charge-tunneling phenomenon occurring between a quantum dot and a superconducting island using a technique that employs radio-frequency sensing. Our approach has allowed us to distinguish between different types of tunneling events, specifically those driven by individual particles as well as by pairs of particles called Cooper pairs. Furthermore, we've found that the quantum dot can be utilized to detect changes in the superconductor's electronic state without needing traditional electrical current measurements, providing us with insight into previously inaccessible subgap energy states. Our findings offer valuable insights for future research focused on detecting parity-dependent interactions between these quantum dots and superconducting islands, potentially revealing the existence of elusive Majorana modes. The observed parity-dependent behavior could also be leveraged to implement a parity-dependent electrical current switch at the nanoscale. Lastly, our radio-frequency sensing method can be used to monitor the electronic noise present within the superconducting island, allowing us to establish an experimental limit on the charge tunneling events known as shot noise. This limit can be further restricted by taking into account various systematic noise sources, hinting that our current setup may not be capable of detecting tunneling events occurring at the superconducting gap edge. Therefore, future research could focus on reducing electronic noise to the level where the charge tunneling events at the subgap energy states can be directly quantified. The application of deep neural networks in medical image classification has shown great promise due to their advanced image mapping capabilities, potentially leading to significant improvements in patient diagnosis. However, standard training datasets are often marred by significant annotation errors, which can range from missing or incorrect labels, as well as the propagation of noisy data. These shortcomings necessitate a robust training method that can effectively mitigate noisy data and produce reliable diagnostic models for medical imaging applications. This research presents an innovative solution to address this challenge by developing a decision-making mechanism that can accurately predict the likelihood of a sample's correct classification in the presence of noisy data. By utilizing a parameter adjustment strategy, the sample with the highest clean likelihood is selected as the training candidate, thereby substantially enhancing the training process' resistance to noisy data. Experimental evaluations conducted on two medical datasets demonstrated that the proposed method achieves a higher overall accuracy of 92.80% compared to the 91.03% achieved through traditional cross-validation. Furthermore, the research indicates that the proposed method's performance is largely impervious to varying levels of noisy data. The outstanding outcomes achieved by the proposed method make it an exceptionally reliable choice for medical image classification tasks plagued by noisy data. In a total functions logic such as HOL, defining functions that can potentially run indefinitely is challenging because it's impossible to express non-termination within the logic. To overcome this issue, a clock axiom is introduced in a new logic called HOL$_{\omega}$$, which allows for the efficient inclusion of total functions from the natural numbers to the natural numbers without requiring the concept of non-termination. Using this clock, HOL$_{\omega}$$ can easily provide definitions for functions with infinite runs and prove properties involving non-terminating functions. Furthermore, HOL$_{\omega}$$ has been implemented in Coq v8.13.7, demonstrating the practical benefits of using clocks in formalizations. To further expand on HOL$_{\omega}$$, a decision procedure for first-order logic with a limited number of functions is provided. This decision procedure can be applied to any theory contained within HOL$_{\omega}$$. It enables the resolution of decidability issues within HOL$_{\omega}$$, such as the infinite version of Church's conjecture. It has also allows HOL$_{\omega}$$ to easily tackle other challenging problems within logic, including the bisimulation problem for B\"uchi automata. Ultimately, HOL$_{\omega}$$ offers a flexible framework for creating a logic with a decidable first-order theory through the introduction of a decidable clock. To facilitate the adoption of HOL$_{\omega}$$, both the source code and formalizations of various results have been made available on GitHub. Specifically, the formalization of the first infinite version of Church's conjecture can be found in HOL$_{\omega}$$. Clocks can also be used to make other formalizations involving non-terminating functions more efficient within HOL. For instance, the clock can be applied to the formalizations done by Huet, Paulin, and Miller, with the latter requiring further adjustments due to the use of congruence rules. To confirm the practical value of HOL$_{\omega}$$, a formalization of the fundamental theorem of arithmetic was successfully proved within HOL$_{\omega}$. This proof, requiring around 6,800 lines of code, relies heavily on HOL$_{\omega}$$ and clocks. To facilitate future applications, both the source code and formalizations of HOL$_{\omega}$$ have been made available under a Creative Commons license. Notably, beyond this threshold, the material experiences a unique phase where it hosts nodes with high orbital angular momentum, a phenomenon previously suggested for the chiral liquid state in the context of topological insulators. This phase shows characteristic signs in the material's specific heat, affecting its thermal conductivity in the presence of an external magnetic field. Researchers have discovered that this high orbital angular momentum semimetal state is not an anomaly unique to this particular model; rather, it is a universal state that likely exists in various related scenarios, such as the phase transition between the chiral liquid and the semimetal states in the context of topological insulators. Therefore, it is likely that this high orbital angular momentum semimetal state is a common intermediate state found between the chiral liquid and the semimetal states across different related scenarios. In the case of a specific number and arrangement of Weyl nodes, the material transitions into a type of semimetal with nodes of high orbital angular momentum, while time reversal symmetry's restoration is a requirement for this transition to occur. The study examines various oversampling methods to classify multi-class topics, particularly focusing on the performance of SMOTE, a popular method for generating new samples based on minority class examples, and its two variants, the random oversampling method, and the AdaSynthetic oversampling method adapted from AdaBoost. An evaluation of these algorithms was carried out using seven datasets and a comparison with the clustering approach for oversampling, through a robust test suite that assesses their resilience to noise. According to the results, SMOTE synthetic samples successfully passed the robustness test, and surpassed the performance of other algorithms, including random oversampling and the original AdaSynthetic method, in several classification tasks. Furthermore, an analysis using the Bayesian risk criterion suggested that AdaSynthetic exhibits more robust characteristics than SMOTE. Overall, the study provides insights into the performance of SMOTE, and suggests its potential application in classification-related research, particularly in the context of topic modeling. It is expected that this algorithm could be a useful tool for developing topic modeling applications with a focus on text analysis. This study analyzes data from an online monitoring system of U.S. local news to explore connections between COVID coverage, regional case and death rates, and characteristics of news outlets and their audiences. Using a distinct dataset of over 750,000 articles from over 300 outlets between April 2020 and February 2021, our results show a shifting correlation between local news coverage and COVID metrics across different time periods. Specifically, we find that initial increases in local news coverage correlated with declining national death rates at the start of the pandemic, but this inverse relationship became stronger over time. Meanwhile, we discover opposing patterns in individual states with high case counts, and observe a more consistent positive correlation with death rates. Furthermore, our analysis highlights variations in local news coverage frequency and tone tied to demographic factors such as age, education levels, and political affiliations. This study also sheds light on the COVID-related information delivered to local audiences through their preferred news sources. By quantifying the role of national vs local issues in the news, as well as audience preferences for specific types of COVID coverage, we can better understand the complex interplay between local news and COVID metrics in each U.S state. Ultimately, our results emphasize the importance of considering context and time in data analysis. They also indicate that local news can act as a crucial public health tool, helping to track the pandemic's progression and inform individual actions, and ultimately contributing to a more effective national response to the crisis. Given the enduring impact of COVID-19, this study provides valuable insights for policymakers, public health officials, and the general public. They show that local news can be leveraged as a means of communication between public health officials and community members to address the ongoing epidemic, and may need to be specifically targeted in targeted advertising campaigns to reach key demographics. They also highlight the limitations imposed by local media reach and coverage frequency on the ability to effectively track the pandemic nationwide. They suggest exploring alternative communication channels with broader reach, such as social media platforms, as a supplementary means of communication. Smoothed particle hydrodynamics possesses innate conservation capabilities, which remain flawless when accurately integrated, maintaining machine-precise levels of total mass, energy, and linear/angular momentum. Notably, this property holds significant value in computational astrophysics for processes such as binary interactions and compact object mergers. Although the inclusion of gravity in such applications leads to excessive computation in pairwise interactions, a Fast Multipole Method variant addresses this by substituting interactions between distant particle clusters, which however introduces a new concern of ensuring conservation. Our research develops a novel FMM-based SPH implementation for gravitational interactions that not only meets the conservation criteria but also minimizes higher-order derivatives, thus preserving physical laws and maintaining the SPH dimensionless numbers. This implementation has successfully passed multiple conservation tests, including static scenarios, adiabatic compressions, and Kihara comptonization tests. Notably, our implementation ensures the exact preservation of energy and linear momentum in the fast-SPH algorithm, while achieving a high accuracy of at least 90% in the full-SPH algorithm. Furthermore, significant advancements have been made by utilizing Taylor series expansions to accelerate the calculation of fluid properties, such as density and energy. which in turn enables the use of conventional SPH algorithms without compromising the overall scheme. Additionally, detailed analysis of implementation strategies is provided, including an optimal particle distribution policy derived from the Kelly-Soudris criterion. All implementation details are open-source and available on GitHub at https://github.com/edward-spo1/FastSphFMM. Furthermore, a detailed case study utilizing the newly developed fast-SPH algorithm is presented for a critical astrophysical process, namely the merger of a binary neutron star, utilizing a full-SPH simulation with a high-resolution particle count of $2.5\times10^6$ and an associated mass of $1 M_\odot$ for both objects. A detailed comparison is made between this high-speed algorithm and standard SPH, demonstrating a substantial increase in computational efficiency of around one decade in a single-core scenario, which in turn is expected to translate to multi-core scenarios in a linear fashion. We develop a novel, yet efficient, training method that can be applied to both reinforcement and imitation learning. This method integrates synthetic data, specifically environment dynamics and agent trajectories, into the training process. Synthetic data can be generated without interactions with the environment, making it a promising approach for limited budget training. We create a policy that incorporates linear relationships, trained in a two-stage process using synthetic data. First, network weights that capture linear relationships are identified through the minimization of a regression loss. Subsequently, an optimal coefficient matrix is derived through the minimization of a trajectory loss. Our results on various benchmarks indicate a substantial increase in performance with limited synthetic data, exceeding the capacity of current reinforcement learning benchmarks with real data. Moreover, the training method demonstrates efficiency, processing a dataset in under 10 seconds, and outperforms random sampling, requiring minimal sample pairing or optimization. We believe this method has the potential to bridge a significant gap between imitation and reinforcement learning. Synthetic states could potentially replace real-world observations, making imitation possible without direct access to environment dynamics or observations. We propose a new framework, called Linear Discrete Dynamics (LDD), that can be used with high-dimensional continuous dynamics, providing discrete dynamics based on a reduced representation. Our findings also indicate that policies trained with limited real-world data successfully adapt to a variety of challenging scenarios. We further investigate the use of synthetic data in real-world applications, observing a transfer of our policy to a real-world robotic arm after training with synthetic data based on a simulated robotic arm. We provide a more in-depth understanding of the proposed method in a video available at https://youtu.be/0B9O2T1Q6Q4. Researchers at the CMS experiment have analyzed data, which total 137 fb$^{-1}$ of LHC proton-proton collisions, to investigate a phenomenon where two Higgs bosons are produced. These data do not reveal any signs of such a process in the searched areas, which included various combinations of the Higgs bosons decaying into bottom quarks, gamma gamma, or pairs of bottom quarks. A predicted outcome in accordance with the Standard Model has been established as a benchmark. As a result, the likelihood of observing this phenomenon, which does not involve resonance and is produced at a maximum rate, is estimated to be less than 3.0 times 10 to the -3. Furthermore, our study demonstrates the unique strengths of each participant models, including a notable increase in word accuracy for unseen text, and a notable decrease in word insertion errors. Our code and the dataset used to train the model have been made publicly available.

In probabilistic learning, organisms sometimes opt for a less than optimal strategy known as probability-matching, which means choosing options based on their reward probabilities, as opposed to the optimal strategy, maximization, which involves consistently selecting the option with the highest reward.  Despite years of study, the factors leading to probability-matching are still unclear and an interesting aspect is the similarity between this and maximization at a brain level.  We provide evidence that explains a range of behaviors by developing a model.  This model, which is founded on a variation of the leaky integrate-and-fire neuron with modulated excitability, demonstrates through both numerical and analytical methods that it successfully replicates a wide array of probability-matching performance across various tasks.  Furthermore, it suggests that the similarity between probability-matching and maximization at a neural level could be a result of different groups of neurons contributing to different processes.  One group of neurons, which could potentially be located in different brain regions, may be responsible for a variety of tasks including probability-matching, while another group of neurons, which could exist in the same or different brain locations, may be required for task switching.  This suggests the possibility of distinct regions of the brain for different types of cognitive switching behaviors.  Overall, the model offers an innovative understanding of the neurobiological basis of probability-matching and its connection to maximization.  It proposes that the probability-matching maximization duality could arise from the combination of two types of excitability strategies, which may be implemented by two distinct sets of neurons, which could be located either in the same or different brain locations.  This study suggests the possibility of distinct regions of the brain for different types of cognitive switching behaviors, which could be tested through experiments involving various stimuli and tasks. To mitigate systematic measurement errors on quantum computers, current methods employ anti-coherent strategies, which utilize multiple qubits to eliminate systematic measurement biases. While effective, these methods can't account for anti-decoherent effects, which decrease the probability of measuring a state. We develop a new approach, the linear mitigation method, which turns out to be a maximum likelihood estimator for measurement errors under specific assumptions. This new method not only accounts for both anti-coherent and anti-decoherent effects but also makes the most informed predictions about them. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the linear mitigation method in a real-world scenario involving a trapped ion quantum computer. Compared to the best available anti-coherent method, it significantly improves accuracy in predicting measurement biases. Additionally, we find that the linear mitigation method naturally leads to the detection of physical decay effects when applied to quantum circuits. This new method is compatible with a wide range of quantum devices, including those with complex qubit structures, and it shouldn't increase the number of required measurements. We suggest incorporating the linear mitigation method into the standard measurement process. As a result of this approach, it's now possible to accurately predict quantum evolution, a crucial element in more sophisticated quantum algorithms and applications. This research investigates how incorporating network coding into a network of devices influences energy efficiency. We first consider a general model for a class of wireless devices called the generalized success probability model, and derive an exact formula for finding the optimal coding depth to maximize energy efficiency in a randomly connected network. The findings of our analysis extend existing success probability models, including those developed by Gupta and Kumar and by Sae-Id and Love. We then compare the energy efficiency of a network that uses maximum diversity network coding with one that does not incorporate coding. The results show that incorporating network coding can improve energy efficiency by a factor of at least 13. Additionally, we demonstrate that certain design parameters such as the number of devices and transmission power can be optimized to achieve specific goals. Finally, we consider a scenario where the channel state information is not perfectly known and derive an expression for the expected energy efficiency, which indicates that network coding can still improve energy efficiency under these uncertain conditions. The analysis shows that a moderately high level of uncertainty in channel state information can be compensated for by incorporating network coding. Specifically, we find that if there is some chance of devices having identical channel state information, then network coding can improve energy efficiency even in this uncertain environment. The probability threshold below which network coding can improve energy efficiency is given by $p_{\textrm{th}} = 1 - \left(1+\frac{2\sigma^2}{\mu^2}\right)^{-\frac{\eta}{2}-1}$. Here, $\eta$ represents the additional energy expended to transmit one bit, while $\sigma^2$ and $\mu^2$ represent the variance and mean of the channel state distribution respectively. Notably, our results show that incorporating network coding can improve energy efficiency by at least 25% even in this uncertain environment. To address this, we propose a general approach to unifying these traditional methods with machine learning.  This technique combines the strengths of traditional methods, specifically NDT, n-link, and scale-radius graph, with deep learning.  By employing a deep learning framework, we leverage the ability of these traditional methods to provide accurate point cloud alignment and accurate error bounding while also accommodating changes in distribution.  Furthermore, this technique allows the model to learn from its experiences, providing a measure of uncertainty in its predictions.  To demonstrate the capabilities of this technique, we tested it on a variety of 2D and 3D point cloud datasets and observed that it consistently produces accurate and precise error bounds and uncertainty estimates. A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, specifically protostellar and starless cores.  Protostellar cores are found to possess greater mass than their starless counterparts, with mass discrepancies holding true even after correcting for the effects of temperature and opacity.  We interpret this observed mass difference as a sign that protostellar cores have progressed to a stage where they are enveloped by massive infalling envelopes, a characteristic common among protostellar cores.  This unique distinction is consistent with the hypothesis that protostellar cores are destined to become the parent stars of our solar system.  Using a straightforward model for the growth of cores, we are able to estimate the average mass of the parent cores from which the sun and planets formed, finding their average mass to be approximately 0.16 solar masses.  Importantly, this estimate is consistent with the core mass function observed in nearby star-forming regions, a disparity that is instead predicted by simulations of star formation.  This result is an initial sign of a larger disparity between the theoretical models of star formation and the accurate data collected through the study of nearby star-forming regions.  Further research into this topic is necessary to confirm the disparity between the theoretical models of star formation and the accurate data collected through the study of nearby star-forming regions. Our revised assessment combines two key measures: the portfolio's absolute value and its performance relative to that of a chosen benchmark. A mathematical proof derives the exact distribution of a node's attachment probability in this model, and numerical computations verify that this hybrid scheme generates networks with precisely the same degree distribution as a typical preferential attachment network, particularly those exhibiting a power-law distribution. Additionally, this model's spectral properties have been extensively studied using numerical computations. Interestingly, a distinct characteristic of coexisting networks emerges when examining the relationship between a graph's largest eigenvalue lambda_one and the number of nodes N, leading to a difference of at least 1/4 in terms of how lambda_one scales in comparison to N. This distinction is in contrast to typical preferential attachment networks where lambda_one scales at a rate of O(1 log N). This model's ability to capture a range of real-world graph phenomena by combining different attachment rules has significant implications for its understanding and representation. Furthermore, this model's potential applications in the study of various domain-specific networks have been explored, including automaker-partnerships, the evolution of the internet, and the world trade network. This discovery highlights the need for a hybrid approach to domain-specific network analysis, emphasizing the importance of accurately representing a network's attachment rules in order to achieve meaningful results. To grasp the impact of gravitational forces on both quantum systems moving at varying speeds and stationary systems, we must consider how these forces interact across different energy levels. Typically, gravitational interactions are negligible for systems of finite energy, but they become significant when considering the collective behavior of numerous particles, as seen in Bose-Einstein condensates. Despite its minimal effect at the individual level, the gravitational interaction can become significant at the macroscopic level due to the universal nature of gravitation. Consequently, it is required by principles such as the one by Durr and Herdegen that govern the behavior of quantum particles in accelerating frames and those by Baccaro and Fagnola that govern quantum particles in resting frames. Consequently, we use examples to illustrate that well-known approaches to gravitational interaction on the quantum level are insufficient and we also compare their effectiveness with the principles of gravitational interaction that satisfy the requirements proposed by these approaches. Furthermore, we discuss an open problem related to the behavior of quantum particles in accelerating frames.

Introducing Spartan, a novel approach for training neural networks with pre-defined sparsity. This method effectively leverages a combination of two techniques: soft parameter pruning through optimal transportation and hard parameter sparsification during forward passes. This research showcases Spartan's sparsity capabilities, surpassing previous state-of-the-art methods such as SNIP, SigOpt, and AutoPrune. In software development, test code is created to ensure the proper functioning of programs, but its quality can be compromised due to subpar design or implementation techniques, resulting in software issues during testing or development processes. To help address this, a method called Squeezem was developed to identify test code flaws, also known to as test smells, which can lead to software problems during development and testing phases. By utilizing machine learning with support from development community experts, Squeezem was refined to detect a range of test smells and improve the quality of test code. By analyzing the quality characteristics of test code, Squeezem can pinpoint relevant features that contribute to different types of test smells and evaluate the effectiveness of the method in identifying test smells compared to previous studies. Our findings suggest that Squeezem outperformed other approaches in detecting test smells within software repositories. Through controlled experiments, we verified that the identified test smells can be fixed both manually and automatically, with the use of automated remediation resulting in lower maintenance effort. By examining open-source projects, we discovered that Squeezem was successfully applied to various software development paradigms and found that the most prevalent test smell, specific to Java, is long methods, followed closely by high NBD and high LCOM. These findings highlight the importance of quality characteristics in identifying test smells and the need for further studies on Java-specific test smells. Based on these results, future research directions have been proposed, including the investigation of other relevant quality characteristics and the exploration of other interesting test smells that affect software quality. By sharing the source code on our public GitHub repository, we facilitate future research to be replicated and extended. Additionally, we have made available a repository containing the identified test smells from 15 popular Java software projects and have included a representation of the method length distribution. By doing so, we have made key research artifacts available to the software development community. In the context of software development, test code is an essential resource that requires continuous maintenance to ensure its quality and effectiveness. By examining the source code of tests, we have identified several characteristics that contribute to test code quality, including its length, complexity, and organization. By comparing different coding styles and quality characteristics, we have found that the length and complexity of test code both impact its quality, with longer and more complex test code being less effective. These findings suggest that the length and complexity of test code are significant factors that influence its quality, with better test code being characterized by its brevity and clarity. This paper investigates the existence and uniqueness of solutions to a modified version of the sweeping process, first proposed by J.J. Moreau in the early 1970s as part of plasticity theory. The proposed modification involves a novel combination of the prox-regular moving set and two types of perturbations: a Carathéodory mapping and an integral forcing term with an integrand dependent on time variables. To address this new integro-differential sweeping process, a novel discrete version is introduced, and stochastic stability is demonstrated for a specific case in a Hilbert space environment. The proof of stability relies on an original application of the Lyapunov-Krasnoselskii type condition. The study also explores the connection between the modified sweeping process and a type of variational inequality involving an unbounded constraint, with an infinite relative recession cone. A representative example is provided to illustrate the application of the obtained results. The example is drawn from a system of uncountably many tangentially constrained differential equations, featuring a unique integral dependence on time variables. The modification of the sweeping process is seen to encompass a broad range of evolutionary variational inequalities with integrands subject to time variables. The paper's findings are published in a format that allows for generalizations and extensions, with full details of the new discrete version and general proofs included in Section 3 and Section 4, respectively. The research is dedicated to the memory of the late French mathematician, J.J. Moreau, a pioneer in the field of contact mechanics and plasticity theory. The modification of the sweeping process was motivated by his seminal work in multidimensional static problems, with generalizations to other types of differential systems proposed in the final section of the paper. Measuring inter-beat intervals from ECG signals can provide early warnings for cardiovascular diseases. However, identifying IBIs from noisy signals is difficult, especially when they are heavily distorted by motion noise, which is common in individuals who are highly active. Researchers working on remote health care and wearable technology have been exploring ways to identify IBI trends using signal processing. Recently, a deep learning approach known as a conditional normalization autoencoder was proposed for estimating IBI trends from noisy ECG signals. This method employs a type of convolutional neural network trained with a combination of signal reconstruction and IBI estimation losses. During testing, the model produces IBI estimates by conditioning the input signal on previous predictions. While promising in ideal settings, the model struggles with severe electrode noise and missing R-peak issues in real-world applications. This paper presents an enhanced version of the CN-AE approach, incorporating an additional module for direct IBI estimation using convolutional neural networks. By separating IBI estimation into signal reconstruction and direct estimation paths, the model effectively mitigates motion noise and significantly improves IBI detection rates. Experiments conducted using an in-house ECG dataset have shown the model can accurately estimate IBIs even when the signal quality is severely degraded. Compared to the original approach, the enhanced model achieves an average increase of 25% in IBI detection accuracy. This improved performance translates to a 90% detection rate in the most difficult electrode noise scenario, which is far beyond current conventional methods. Overall, the augmented CN-AE architecture significantly outperforms existing techniques for IBI estimation on the tested dataset. Our findings demonstrate that deep learning methods can effectively estimate IBIs even when the signal quality is poor. By automating IBI detection, these approaches can significantly improve remote health monitoring systems. The model's code and dataset are available for public review. To utilize contemporary computing systems efficiently, an important consideration is reducing the communication cost associated with data transfer, especially when calculating the tensor singular value decomposition (t-SVD) in just a few data passes. The prevailing subspace randomized methods used to compute the t-SVD require 2q + 2 passes over the tensor data, where q represents a positive integer variable for iteration refinement. In this paper, we introduce a new randomized algorithm for t-SVD calculation, allowing for an arbitrary number of passes 'q', not constrained to even integers, building upon existing matrix-based approaches adapted to tensors. The error margin of the proposed method has been statistically quantified. Through practical experiments, we demonstrate that the algorithm's efficiency and usability are well-supported, and we apply this method to develop a faster computational solution for tensor completion. In comparison to existing methods, our approach results in significant reduction in communication cost, accompanied by notable acceleration in computation time. Network analytics heavily relies on embedding static graphs in lower-dimensional spaces to facilitate node classification, link prediction, and visualization, with more recent research extending this approach to dynamic graphs capturing network changes over time. This survey presents an in-depth comparison of state-of-the-art techniques for embedding dynamic graphs in fixed-dimensional spaces, with a focus on their theoretical foundations, limitations, and implementation strategies. Additionally, the survey highlights existing challenges and potential future research directions in this area. While achieving optimal results for node classification and link prediction in dynamic graphs remains a pressing issue, the survey reveals that this field has progressed significantly in the past few years. Several competing methods have been developed, with some approaches integrating additional information to enhance embedding results. This survey reviews these techniques, highlighting their respective advantages and limitations, as well as proposing directions for future research. Specifically, the survey discusses node representation, edge prediction, edge classification, component identification, and component classification tasks in dynamic graphs. Consequently, the survey presents a unified picture of current research in this area, with key performance metrics and utilization examples for each technique also reviewed. Ultimately, the survey outlines existing obstacles and provides insights into potential future research avenues in dynamic graph embedding. Several open-ended questions are posed to encourage interest in this area, with one such question pertinent to the survey itself: Can dynamic graph embedding be reduced to a single task? The survey concludes by providing a comprehensive reference list, complete with relevant papers published in preprints and conference proceedings. A Python library called DynGCN, implementing the methods discussed in this survey, is also made publicly available at https://github.com/DynamicGraphLearning/DyGCN. Determining the fundamental parameters of star clusters is a vital component of astrophysical research. Utilizing the Gaia DR2 survey provides an opportunity for precise assessments of star positions, parallax, and motion based on uniform photometric data, thus enabling the determination of accurate cluster parameters. Focused on the Melotte 72 open star cluster, our study incorporates new Gaia DR2 data, light curves, and color-magnitude diagrams to establish the cluster's precise parameters. Evaluating a total of 1354 Gaia DR2 members reveals a genuine age of 22.2 million years, 1.0 kpc distance, and an actual galactic latitude of -18.8 degrees. Additionally, our findings indicate the cluster moves at a speed of 11.8 km/s, and existing red clump star rates the mass of the cluster at 26000 solar masses, while estimating the core radius to be 1.7 pc. Moreover, our study identifies Melotte 72 as a relatively small and sparse star cluster. Using e-MERLIN radio observations, our research detected only 3.4 solar masses young stellar object within the cluster, indicating a scarcity of Class I and Flat spectrum young stellar objects. This implies that Melotte 72 is an exceptional example of a star cluster due to both its unique characteristics and the scarcity of both the YSOs within it. In robotics, calibrating an eye-in-hand camera using image information is an essential task that has been extensively researched. We investigated using artificial intelligence-based methods for this purpose by leveraging only a single color image, utilizing exclusively simulated data to train the models. Our experiments involved comparing three approaches: one method predicting the camera's positioning directly from the image, another using 2D keypoints and subsequent PnP calculations, and a third method using estimated depth and segmentation maps to calculate the camera's position through iterative closest point alignment. When evaluating the methods against each other and established traditional approaches, we found an unexpected result in which direct prediction outperformed other strategies. Further analysis into these findings involved assessing the methods' performance under various noise levels. We found that deep learning-based methods excelled when images were affected by Gaussian and white noise but struggled when there were pixels with noise. When characterizing the depth estimated by the deepest model under different levels of noise, we found a noise-resistant property. By using the estimated depth and segmentation maps from a noise-free image, we calculated the camera's position and position vector with minimal noise. These findings suggest that using deep learning-based methods for camera calibration in realistic scenarios is viable. Furthermore, direct prediction is the most efficient method, requiring the least amount of computations. Leveraging simulated data to train models that use only images is also recommended in real-world scenarios. Lastly, using the deepest model' s estimates of depth and segmentation maps has a similar effect to adding noise to the traditional approaches, demonstrating its potential in the development of future autonomous robots. These conclusions and the underlying code will be shared with the community through an open-source repository located at https://github.com/mulanml/eye_in_hand_camera_calibration. Evaluating the direct prediction method on real-world datasets to compare its performance to that of other strategies is the next step in this research. To achieve this goal, we plan to collect and analyze real images and compare the estimated positions to the actual camera positions, which will enable a complete comparison of the methods' performance. These findings and the accompanying code will be shared with the community through an open-source repository located at https://github.com/mulanml/eye_in_hand_camera_calibration. Ultimately, directly predicting the camera's position using deep learning is the most effective strategy, requiring only an image to calculate the camera's position, and it excels under various levels of noise. These conclusions and the accompanying code will be shared with the community through an open-source repository located at https://github.com/mulanml/eye_in_hand

One notable strategy to embed physical laws into machine learning is physics-informed neural networks (PINNs). These networks can be trained alongside other data sources, like observation data, to create a more comprehensive framework. PINNs have demonstrated the potential to utilize limited data efficiently and improve the performance of both data-driven and physics-based modeling methods. Building on this concept, we now introduce the idea of integrating PINNs with uncertainty quantification techniques. By combining physics-informed learning with Bayesian deep neural networks, we can create a more robust framework that leverages the advantages of both PINNs and uncertainty quantification. We examine and assess various strategies for incorporating uncertainty into PINNs, including Markov chain Monte Carlo and its adaptations, as well as approximate posterior networks. Our numerical experiments involve common problems like ordinary differential equations and partial differential equations with both noisy and noise-free conditions, and our results showcase the benefits of using uncertainty quantification with PINNs. These benefits include enhanced prediction intervals, more accurate expected values, and improved quantification of uncertainty. Additionally, we find that combining PINNs with MCMC-based uncertainty quantification allows for the use of a smaller number of samples to achieve a more precise approximation of the uncertainty quantified posterior distribution. Furthermore, we propose a future research direction that involves integrating neural networks with exact sampling techniques. These techniques, like Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, could significantly reduce sampling requirements, as current techniques like slice sampling can be incorporated with little modification to utilize sampling techniques with PINNs. Overall, our work highlights the potential of combining uncertainty quantification and physics-informed neural networks to create a more reliable and accurate approach to solving complex problems. This framework has numerous applications in real-world scenarios and can potentially be used in high-stakes decision-making environments. We analyze the spectral characteristics of a discrete-time linear bandit algorithm known as the Follow-the-Ordered (FOTO) method. We establish a lower bound on the expected regret rate of FOTO, which is proven to be in accordance with prior studies assuming certain conditions were met. In action spaces that meet those conditions, we demonstrate FOTO's suboptimality matches this lower bound, thereby establishing a minimum bound for its regret rate. Furthermore, we examine how the spectral properties of a design matrix affect its regret rate, revealing that a dimensionality increase can actually lead to worse performance, and that a design matrix's eigenspectrum is a reliable indicator of a linear bandit algorithm's regret rate. This insight presents opportunities for developing new algorithms, and suggests that forcing a method to avoid areas with large eigenvalues in its design matrix may lower its regret rate, and could provide a practical approach to creating more efficient algorithms. Building on this idea, we design a new algorithm, Linear Adaptively Designed (LAD), which produces a smaller eigenvalue profile over time. In action spaces that meet certain conditions, we demonstrate LAD's regret rate is bounded below by a lower bound we established, and above by a higher bound we established, and through experiments, we demonstrate LAD outperforms FOTO. We also show LAD's regret rate can be controlled by adjusting a parameter in its design, and provide guidelines for setting this parameter to achieve optimal performance. Lastly, we demonstrate LAD's effectiveness in action spaces that do not meet the conditions for comparability, and through experiments, we demonstrate LAD outperforms FOTO. We also show LAD outperforms FOTO across various action spaces, and provide guidance for setting its parameter to achieve optimal performance. In general, these findings suggest designing algorithms that exploit a method's spectral characteristics can be a reliable way to reduce a method's regret rate, and provide practical approaches to creating more efficient algorithms based on this principle. Graphene with gaps has been proposed to exhibit the orbital Hall effect, where the unusual integer quantum Hall effect arises from charge motion within the gap, characterized by the orbital angular momentum rather than the traditional electron velocity. By calculating the single-electron Hamiltonian, we show that the orbital Hall effect can occur without true decoupling of layers in the experiment, and that the orbital angular momentum is sensitively regulated by tunable coupling between layers, revealing that the orbital Hall effect is essentially a hybridization-driven phenomenon. Additionally, we establish that the orbital Hall effect is distinct from the ordinary quantum Hall effect, with its threshold for observation determined by a sharp sensitivity threshold, which is far below classical room temperature. Using the single-electron Hamiltonian to analyze "bilayer graphene", which has previously been shown to exhibit decoupled layers, we find that the orbital Hall effect can occur even in this situation, and that the effect is controlled by a single-electron Hamiltonian parameter that is variable in the laboratory. Since this single-electron Hamiltonian parameter corresponds to a single-electron interaction that is known to be variable in laboratory settings, this implies that the orbital Hall effect can be observed in bilayer graphene at ordinary temperatures. Furthermore, the single-electron Hamiltonian calculations also reveal an unusual single-electron transition associated with the orbital Hall effect that is distinguishable from ordinary single-electron transitions, suggesting the possibility of creating an orbital Hall effect through a single-electron photo-transition. Overall, our findings indicate that the single-electron Hall effect is a hybridization-driven phenomenon, where the single-electron transition can initiate the orbital Hall effect, and that the single-electron transition can be experimentally manipulated to induce the single-electron Hall effect. Over the past few years, research has gained momentum in graph adversarial attacks but there is still a significant gap in understanding such threats, particularly in the context of Graph Classification. This investigation aims to explore the state-of-the-art graph adversarial attacks and present a comprehensive survey of the existing literature. We examine the different types of attacks, offer insights into the challenges associated with them, and discuss the potential techniques to mitigate such attacks. Moreover, we outline future research directions in this domain. It is worth noting that this survey primarily focuses on Graph Classification, thereby limiting its scope to that area. The survey of graph adversarial attacks within the context of Graph Classification is a highly areas of study, however, but it is an area that is still relatively under-explored compared to other fields such as natural language processing and computer vision. As such, this survey aims to provide a thorough overview of the current state of the art and offer guidance to researchers in the field. The rest of this paper is organized in this fashion: Section II discusses the types of graph adversarial attacks and present a taxonomy, Section III covers the state of the art in graph adversarial attacks, Section IV discusses potential countermeasures, and Section V outlines future research directions. This paper concludes with Section VI and VII, respectively.

In this research, we explore minimal vertex covers of hypergraphs, which are subsets of vertices that encompass all edges containing at least one vertex from the subset. A vertex cover is considered minimal if removal of any vertex from the subset results in a non-vertex cover. The problem of identifying a minimal vertex cover (MVCP) has been established as NP-hard and we have found that solving it on smaller hypergraphs can be challenging. To advance our understanding of MVCP, we have devised a parameterized algorithm for hypergraphs with a limited number of edges that surpass a certain threshold, which demonstrates an improved computational efficiency as the threshold is approached, thus providing an illustrative case of parameterized hardness and mixed computational complexity. The algorithm's performance is further validated by testing it on various types of hypergraphs, which shows that it effectively solves MVCP for a short threshold in a shorter time compared to an alternative method based on the standard brute force approach. The code for the developed algorithm is openly available at https://github.com/JakubGajarsky/MVCP_Algorithm. Additionally, we have found that an existing algorithm based on the neighborhood technique is effective for small hypergraphs but fails to scale for larger problems due to an exponential time complexity. The problem of identifying an independent vertex cover, which is the hypergraph analogue of the well-known problem of finding an independent set in graphs, is also explored and we have established that this variant of MVCP is NP-hard, which provides an explanatory case of NP-hardness. The independence number (i.e., the size of a maximum independent vertex cover) can be determined using an adaptation of a known algorithm for graphs and we have found that an algorithm based on the neighborhood technique is effective for small hypergraphs but also exhibits an exponential time complexity that hampers its scalability. The time complexity of MVCP and IVCP (which stands for identifying an independent vertex cover) were investigated using the standard worst-case complexity measure of Big Oh and we have determined that under certain constraints, MVCP can be solved in O(n^k) time, which compares favourably to the time complexity of O(2^k*n^k) observed in the unparameterized case. The time complexity of IVCP was also explored and we have found that under the same constraints, IVCP can be solved in O(n^k) time, which is an improvement compared to the unparameterized case with a time complexity of O(2^k*n^k). Domain-specific knowledge is frequently captured using comprehensive, formally structured concept relationships called ontologies. In fields like biology and medicine, vast ontologies comprise hundreds of thousands of interconnected concepts. Effective visual representations are particularly crucial when dealing with large, complex ontologies, enabling easier comprehension and exploration. However, existing visualisation tools predominantly focus on hierarchical structures and overlook other types of associations. This paper introduces OntoPlot, an innovative visualisation system designed to seamlessly balance the exploration of all concept relationships and large hierarchical structures. OntoPlot's novel hybrid visualisation incorporates icicle plots, interactive elements, and space-efficient visual compression to enhance understanding and reduce visual clutter. Through a user study involving domain experts, we compared OntoPlot's usability to that of Protégé, the industry-standard ontology editor, finding that OntoPlot surpassed expectations in facilitating association-related tasks and earned widespread endorsement from domain specialists. The OntoPlot prototype is open-source and accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/visual-ontologies/onto-plot. Additionally, we have released Protégé 7.0.0 with OntoPlot-based visualisation. Furthermore, this study's findings have been presented at the 2021 Workshop on Visualisation for Ontologies.

One of the most significant issues arising from agnostic domain shift in domain adaptive pedestrian detection is the prevalence of false positives.  As labeling each target domain's bounding boxes is a resource-intensive task, another common approach is to align the target and source domains using unsupervised methods.  However, due to the diverse nature of target domains, directly learning from these aligned domains often results in a decrease in accuracy due to an increased frequency of false positives.  A potential solution to mitigate false positives is to utilize a refined mask assignment strategy by combining supervised information, as detected bounding boxes associated with semantic masks can significantly reduce false positives.  This insight led to the development of a new approach, MA-CT, which utilizes a graph convolution network to align semantic masks from a pre-tagged dataset with the detection results in the target domain, followed by a mask-assignment technique that prioritizes true positives by incorporating supervised information, thereby learning an accurate bounding box classifier.  Through evaluations conducted using the Caltech, Citypersons, BUPT, and TUD-Angstadt datasets, MA-CT demonstrated state-of-the-art performance with a notable increase of up to 8.4% in average precision compared to existing unsupervised domain adaptive pedestrian detection methods.  Code implementations for MA-CT are available online at https://github.com/whs550/MA-CT. This study presents an innovative method for enhancing low-quality music recordings made on consumer-grade devices, which often include distortions like background noise, echo effects, and microphone distortion. A novel deep learning technique combines two processes: one removes background noise and another applies a reverberation correction. The first step utilizes a convolutional autoencoder, while the second leverages a separate convolutional autoencoder or a pre-trained Spectrogram-CNN. The performance of the proposed method was tested on a dataset of clean and distorted recordings contaminated with background noise and echo effects. It successfully recovered the distorted signals by learning the characteristics of the micrphone distortions, which were previously unknown, by applying the deep learning approach. The results show that this technique surpasses established methods like the Wiener filter, Wavelet Denoise, and U-Net, during both training and testing stages. When the reverberation component was removed, the method showed notable improvements in testing accuracy. Ultimately, the proposed approach yielded a significant signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) improvement of 10 dB, surpassing current best methods by approximately 4 dB. A practical demonstration of the technique was successfully applied to remove distortions and noise from a real-world piano recording made on a smartphone. The effectiveness of this technique was further validated through subjective testing among participants, which yielded significant improvements in terms of clarity and overall listening experience. We make the source code and pre-trained models for this research available for the general public at a specified repository link. Furthermore, the dataset used in this research, which comprises noisy and distorted recordings of music played on a piano, trumpet, and guitar, is also made available at a specified dataset link with the permission of the copyright holders. The credibility of astrochemical simulations largely relies on the accuracy of binding energy values that take into account the diverse structures and energy patterns found at ice-grain surface binding sites. We developed the Binding Energy Evaluation Platform (BEEP) to create a comprehensive database containing the full range of binding energies between molecules and an amorphous water surface model. BEEP employs highly automated quantum chemical methods to identify multiple binding sites on water clusters, allowing for the precise calculation of binding energies. Our research involved computing binding energy distributions for 11 deuterated water clusters, each having 6 binding sites. We used these distributions to create a statistical model that can be used as a guide for estimating intermolecular binding energies. Our proposed method is versatile and can be applied to various molecule-surface systems, enabling the direct assessment of molecule-surface binding energies. We tested our approach by calculating the binding energies of two prominent N2H+ and H2O isotopologues in the context of our database findings. BEEP's statistical model allows for a reduction in the number of explicit binding energy calculations required to validate a molecule-surface binding energy, thereby increasing simulation efficiency. However, it is essential to note the limitations and potential biases inherent in quantum chemical methods, which need to be considered in the context of our findings. The combination of quantum chemical methods and statistical models represents a promising strategy for accurately determining molecule-surface binding energies. Furthermore, the development of global potential energy surfaces could significantly enhance the accuracy of binding energy calculations based on existing molecular-scale simulations. This innovative 'depth-modulated' approach is a pioneering effort to tackle quantum complexity by leveraging the unpredictability of the measurement outcomes. To alleviate this issue, we explore various image enhancement strategies to minimize the necessity for labeled data. Ultimately, we investigate the performance of multiple advanced neural network architectures as chest X-ray semantic segmentation bases, training them with and without labeled ground truth to compare their overall efficiency. Our experiments reveal that training a U-Net model on augmented images significantly improves its robustness, outperforming even more complex neural network designs, such as U-gated ResNet. Furthermore, combining two advanced image enhancement strategies (color distortion and rotation) results in the best segmentation outcomes. Interestingly, using a neural network model specifically designed for image enhancement (U-rotation) yields U-Net level results, suggesting these enhancement strategies have educational value for the model. Overall, our findings indicate that employing strategically designed image enhancement strategies can substantially decrease the need for labeled data in semantic segmentation tasks. As a result, developing a system that automates these image enhancement strategies using minimal annotated data may significantly accelerate the application of deep learning to the field of computer-assisted medical diagnosis. Existing image captioning models often produce captions based solely on what they've learned from labeled data. But what if the goal were to enforce specific styles in the generated captions? For instance, some captions might focus on conveying information, while others aim to be more creative and capture emotions. To address this, we've created a style constrained image captioning model that takes into account both local caption content and the overall style. Our model relies on a hierarchical latent space to integrate the two elements, separating the semantic meaning from the stylistic characteristics. To customize the style, we utilize a database of regular captions, treating it as a set of latent space vectors. When processing an image, the model generates a range of possible captions by combining the image's embedded meaning with different style components from the regular caption database. Training is simplified by dividing the task into two separate optimization steps. As a result, our model can generate captions in the desired style and also incorporate the image's inherent meaning. Evaluations confirm our model's ability to produce high-quality, style-constrained captions. Additionally, our model's capacity for generating captions in multiple styles has also been confirmed. You can see the model in action here: https://sites.google.com/view/style-constrained-ic. Our code is available for free on GitHub at https://github.com/ziyi2018/StyleIC. We intend to build upon this research in the future. 

Keywords: image captioning, style constraints, latent space, database-driven, hierarchical decomposition.

As autonomous systems become increasingly prevalent, it is essential to establish a legal and regulatory framework for addressing harm caused by these systems to individuals. Previous attempts to define harm in philosophical literature have failed to address various real-world examples, leading some to consider abandoning the concept of harm. The existing definitions of harm, largely reliant on causality, surprisingly overlook the use of causal models and actual causality theories. This paper presents a new definition of qualitative harm, grounded in causal models and an established concept of actual causality, specifically emphasizing contrastive causation and default utility. The proposed definition demonstrates its ability to address challenges in existing literature and highlights its significance in evaluating scenarios involving autonomous systems. The utility of the definition is further showcased through its application to AI decision-making processes. The paper also suggests that the proposed concept of qualitative harm can serve as a transitional point between harm quantification and harm categorization. Finally, the study identifies and explores the differences between qualitative and contrastive aspects of harm, revealing the potential for these two concepts to be utilized in various contexts, such as distinguishing between harms and benefits, and in evaluating the ethics of autonomous systems. Speech-to-text translation involves converting spoken language into written language across different tongues. Conventional two-stage approaches using separate speech and translation models often fall short in handling unknown words through static vocabulary lists. By contrast, one-stage models using tokenized vocabularies can better adapt to unseen words during translation tasks. Yet, they typically rely on static vocabularies, limiting their ability to tackle zero-shot translation scenarios, where input sentences contain words unknown to the model. To address this challenge, we introduce a speech-to-text model pre-trained using self-supervised learning that can translate to unknown words without prior knowledge, unlike existing models. Our proposed model modulates a learned vocabulary during translation by utilizing a separate bottleneck layer for neural language models. By doing so, it effectively tackles zero-shot translation using static vocabularies. Gaussian Process-based forecasting outperformed other methods, particularly at hourly time scales, and could improve network planning and operation by enabling more effective distribution of energy among a large number of customers, which in turn may rely heavily on peak demand. The growth of machine learning algorithms has not entirely resolved the issues affecting AI performance, primarily due to limited data and labelling resources. However, augmenting a model with relevant information can help address these challenges to some extent. The effectiveness of incorporating knowledge greatly depends on accurately processing and integrating it into the model, a complex task in itself. This survey aims to provide an overview of the various techniques employed to enhance knowledge integration within machine learning models, focusing on decision trees, under the umbrella of knowledge-aware machine learning (KAML). Additionally, it highlights existing knowledge integration methods related to decision trees, while discussing related challenges and presenting various implementation benchmarks. Finally, the survey identifies areas for improvement and presents potential research opportunities in KAML. Creating a reliable model for precise COVID-19 detection on chest CT scans poses significant difficulties. The issue often arises due to annotation biases affecting traditional supervised segmentation techniques. To address these challenges, we've developed an innovative framework, AnomDetect, which leverages anomalous region detection without requiring segmentations. This data augmentation method reduces biases by using unlabelled data and can be integrated into existing supervised models. We've also designed an unsupervised metric learning method that doesn't need manual segmentations to train a feature extractor. This allows the model to identify distinctive patterns in COVID-19 cases. To evaluate the effectiveness of our approach, we've created a novel anomaly detection metric and conducted comprehensive experiments on two unique datasets, finding that AnomDetect outperforms existing methods in detecting COVID-19 cases using a COVID-19 AutoNet Dataset and a large, diverse chest X-ray dataset. Compared to other approaches, AnomDetect has achieved superior AUC scores on both datasets. Furthermore, our approach has successfully detected COVID-19 cases on a diverse and large scale, matching the performance of expert radiologists who have not undergone any specialized training. This innovative technology has significant potential to improve the efficient and reliable detection of COVID-19 cases on a large scale. The code for AnomDetect is publicly available at https://github.com/Chen-Fei-DEIM/AnomDetect. This method leverages a two-pronged approach: first, it uses the Gapped Analytic Continuation method to determine the eigenvalues near the energy spectrum, and then applies the variational principle to optimize the entanglement measure. In experiments, we apply VSV to various optimizable entanglement measures, including the negativity of the density matrix and the geometric entanglement. Notably, our implementation of the variational principle demonstrates superior performance compared to the Gapped Analytic Continuation method alone. Constructing the matching cost is a critical step in estimating light field depth through multiframe estimation, where different approaches have been used by previous researchers. We introduce a novel cost construction method called SMCost, designed to be both efficient and effective by converting pixels with anomalous disparity offsets into a fixed code. This approach takes advantage of the small tolerated disparity error to significantly reduce the computational cost and memory requirements while preserving accuracy. Furthermore, SMCost enables a parallelization scheme that further enhances performance. Our comprehensive evaluation demonstrates that SMCost surpasses existing constructors in depth estimation while being several times faster in computation and using significantly less memory. Moreover, the basic framework of our cost constructor enables it to be applied to other similar problems, such as estimating motion from light fields, where we achieve better results compared to the previous state-of-the-art. Overall, the SMCost constructor sets a new benchmark in speed and accuracy for light field depth and motion estimation. This approach also facilitates a deeper understanding of the relationship between accuracy and computational efficiency, making it a valuable tool for researchers. Our code is now available online for public access at https://github.com/multiviewvpp/SMCost. Additionally, the results obtained from our evaluation are plotted graphically for easy reference. Evaluations were conducted using the LF-MPI-SIFT, LF-MPI, LFSTEREO, MPIF, MPIF-F, NUSPEDES, PE, and 5DFlow datasets. Alternative theories of gravity that go beyond the Riemannian framework have been proposed to explore quantum gravity and model systems with non-relativistic symmetry. However, developing these theories involves a complex task: deriving an action principle that accurately captures their behavior. This technical note utilizes the formulation of double field theory to create action frameworks for these alternative gravity theories. By doing so, it resolves the ambiguities associated with their corresponding motion equations. As a result, this note embeds three theories – Torsional Newton-Cartan gravity, Carrollian gravity, and String Newton-Cartan gravity – within double field theory and derives their respective action frameworks for comparison with previously established literature results. Additionally, it uses double field theory to extend these procedures to more general contexts. For String Newton-Cartan gravity, it even goes a step further and uses double field theory to explicitly derive the Tulli equation. This achievement lays the groundwork for future work that will utilize double field theory to extend and explore alternative gravity theories. To meet growing demands for next-generation home WiFi networks, improvements in performance are necessary to support emerging technologies like virtual reality and high-definition video streaming.  The integration of IEEE 802.11ax and the use of beamforming has enhanced multi-user home networks' ability to handle a high volume of traffic.  However, this network still poses challenges for large-scale parallel file downloads using the DL-DLR protocol, particularly in a home environment with physical barriers that affect network signal and cause interference.  In this research, a modified DL-DLR protocol has been developed to optimize network performance using available network signal data and download request information.  The protocol's effectiveness was evaluated in a home WiFi network environment featuring 20 MU-MIMO access points with varying levels of interference and compared to the standard DL-DLR protocol's performance.  The results showed that the modified protocol's throughput was significantly higher, with improved scalability and resilience to network interference.  The modified protocol was tested on a home network with 10 users and download requests of up to 80 per second, yielding a higher aggregate throughput of 253% compared to the standard DL-DLR protocol.  The modified protocol also demonstrated better parallelism and scalability, with a 253% and 133% improvement respectively, and showed increased resilience to network interference with an 83% improvement.  The modified protocol's performance maintained a low packet loss rate of 1.68% compared to the standard DL-DLR protocol's 21.27% packet loss rate.  The results indicate that the modified protocol's performance is comparable to that of a centralized scheduler with real-time network signal data.  The conclusion is that the modified protocol offers improved performance, scalability, and robustness for large-scale parallel file downloads in home WiFi networks with a high volume of traffic.  The results can be applied to future home networks with emerging IoT devices and their increasing data demands.  The research can be extended to include the download of large files and videos in a home environment with evolving technology advancements and network applications.  The proposed algorithm can be applied to other file download problems in home networks with real-time network signal data available.
